#5706. Hinge Health revenue jumps 52% in Q3 as it expands beyond MSK, eyes hardware acquisitions

Hinge Health revenue jumps 52% in Q3 as it expands beyond MSK, eyes hardware acquisitions" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Hinge Health is seeing early traction with its migraine and gastrointestinal care programs as it pushes beyond musculoskeletal care and builds a broader, multi-condition platform.

But the company's core MSK business remains the engine fueling its robust growth.

"Our vision has always been to automate the delivery of care using technology to close the gap between the care people need and the care they actually receive. We're now applying that same approach and the same trusted relationships with employers and partners in neurology and gastrointestinal care," Daniel Perez, Hinge Health co-founder and CEO, told analysts and investors on the third-quarter earnings call Monday. "We're not starting from scratch in each new category. We're extending a platform that's already proven into conditions that are often connected to the ones we already treat. We believe that's a fundamentally different and more powerful way to expand than what other companies in our space are attempting."

During a Q&A with analysts and investors on the earnings call, Perez asserted, "We’re not taking our eye off the ball in MSK. I think we’re actually widening our lead on MSK … But it’s allowing us to expand into other areas as well."

In the third quarter, the company posted $235 million in revenue, up 52% from $154 million a year ago, and above its guidance range of $223 million to $225 million. The company posted third-quarter adjusted earnings of 66 cents per share, exceeding Wall Street analysts' estimates of 60 cents per share. Hinge Health's non-GAAP income from operations increased 154% to $77.2 million in the third quarter.

Hinge Health, which launched in late 2014 and went public in May 2025, developed software combined with AI to automate physical therapy services for joint and muscle health. The company has designed its platform to address a broad spectrum of MSK care, including acute injury, chronic pain and post-surgical rehabilitation. To address the automation of care, Hinge has developed AI-powered motion tracking technology, a proprietary FDA-cleared wearable device called Enso, and an AI-supported care team to deliver scalable and personalized MSK care.

The company reported strong client growth, with 3,270 clients as of September 30, up 28% from a year ago. Last twelve months (LTM) calculated billings increased 54% year-over-year to $960 million as of September 30, compared to $624 million during Q3 2025.

The company also benefited from strong operational efficiency as it reported a gross margin of 87% in Q3, compared to 82% during the same quarter a year ago.

Free cash flow for the quarter was $113 million, representing a 51% free cash flow margin. The company ended the September quarter with total cash and equivalents of $359 million.

Based on strong Q3 and year-to-date results, Hinge Health boosted its 2026 outlook, now expecting full-year revenue to reach between $879 million and $881 million, reflecting year-over-year growth of 50% at the midpoint. That compares to the prior revenue target of $856 million to $860 million. The company now projects non-GAAP income from operations to be between $266 million and $268 million, reflecting year-over-year growth of 123% and non-GAAP operating margin of 30% at the midpoint.

Core MSK is still the company's largest revenue contributor by a wide margin, Perez noted, and that business is growing robustly. "We expect it to remain that way for years to come; the opportunity at MSK remains massively underpenetrated," Perez said.

"The MSK opportunity is still enormous. Musculoskeletal conditions are among the leading drivers of disability and healthcare spend in the United States, and the vast majority of people in America still don't have access to a digital MSK solution," Perez said during the call.

"We built something that works clinically, commercially, and economically, and we're still in the early innings of penetrating that market. We are the undisputed leader in this space, and we estimate 88% of lives within our markets are yet to be won, leaving a long runway for growth. That alone is a multi-year growth opportunity," he said.

The company is building on top of that MSK care foundation as it expands into migraine care and gastrointestinal care. Hinge acquired GI startup Cylinder Health in August for $105 million in cash.

The company's client base is up almost 30% year-over-year for its MSK care program and roughly 40% for its new GI Care Program since the acquisition announcement of Cylinder Health in August, Perez noted.

The company expects to make more acquisitions and is even looking at hardware acquisitions, Perez said. "I think too many technology companies, especially in healthcare, focus exclusively on software, but I absolutely firmly believe you will not automate care delivery without also investing in hardware. And we've shown we're pretty good at hardware," he said as the company internally developed its Enso wearable device.

Perez told Bloomberg last month that the company was interested in hardware that can augment virtual care.

"We will build organically first and use M&A when it accelerates our timeline. And our acquisitions, particularly in hardware, have historically been small tuck-ins of technology in a team, and then you build it out into something much larger," he added.

Looking at the company's new care programs, Perez called out notable early results from Hinge's migraine program, which is still in early access: 23% reduction in monthly migraine days, 28% reduction in migraine duration, equivalent to roughly five hours and just over half of surveyed members achieved a clinically meaningful improvement.

"We're also seeing a meaningful reduction in monthly prescription use days, which matters both for members and for the clients paying for their care," Perez said.

More than 800 clients, representing 9 million lives, now have access to the migraine program, approximately double the previous quarter, according to management. The migraine program was announced in May.

For the GI care business, Hinge Health is taking Cylinder's existing program and building it into the same app and care infrastructure it uses for MSK and migraine. The company is targeting summer 2027 for the fully integrated product. Meaningful revenue contribution should emerge particularly in 2028, after Hinge gets a fuller sales cycle with the integrated product, Perez noted.

Hinge Health sees an opportunity to offer health plans and employers one integrated care platform that covers multiple health conditions rather than separate point solutions.

Nearly one in two people with GI conditions also have MSK pain, and 70% of people withmigraine also have a GI condition, Perez noted.

"GI cost has been a growing pain point for employers and health plans, especially with the growth of GLP-1s, given GI side effects are so common, and our employer clients are very grateful for taking this on," he said during the call.

Hinge Health had a strong selling season in Q3, according to Aaryn Pure, Hinge Health's chief commercial officer, with three new Fortune 15 clients. "We've already received verbal agreements on more lives this year than we closed in all of last year, and last year was a record-breaking sales year for adding eligible lives," Pure noted.

More than 10 million lives across over 800 clients have access to multiple Hinge products, he said.

Small and midsize businesses are becoming an important growth channel for the company, even though Hinge began investing in that market just a year ago. Through Q3, Hinge Health closed nearly 1 million SMB lives, "demonstrating we're not just winning at the top of the market, we're adding clients across every size tier," Pure said on the call.

He also noted that some health plan and third-party administrator (TPA) partners are implementing or considering arrangements where Hinge Health is automatically embedded or offered on an opt-out basis in their SMB book of business.

"Being the first-mover preferred partner is allowing us to capture that market," Pure said.

The company also announced Monday that Jim Pursley will step down as president, effective January 1, and will join Hinge Health's board of directors. Following this transition, Pure will lead the commercial organization, the company said.

In an analyst note, Ryan Daniels, group head of healthcare technology and services at William Blair, wrote that Hinge Health demonstrates "market leadership with significant advantages both on the product and go-to-market fronts."

"With a nearly 150% increase in shares YTD, HNGE now trades at approximately 11 times our 2027 adjusted gross profit, a premium to mature, high-margin, growth-oriented healthcare IT peers. Still, at these levels, we believe the stock presents a compelling long-term risk/reward and see continued growth momentum and upside to operating income and free cash flow estimates," Daniels wrote.

#5705. Last Night's Blue-Tomic Bomb Probably Blasted Away Musk's Tesla-SpaceX Merger Dreams

Voters delivered a stunning rebuke of Republicans and everything they stand for Tuesday night, taking control of both the House and the Senate in a wave of wins that just kept coming. Democrats kept winning, again and again, wave after wave. A bluekkake, if you will. And while that's great news for the stock market, the Middle East, healthcare, trans kids' safety, and so many other hugely important issues, voters also rejected Elon Musk and his billionaire meddling. We won't be able to get rid of him overnight, but at least Musk's dreams of a Tesla-SpaceX-Twitter-xAI merger are probably dead.

If you remember, Musk has long been reported to want his companies all under one roof to complete Tesla's tranformation into an AI/robotics company (or stop making cars without crashing the stock price). xAI already merged with Twitter and stuck Musk's antisemitism-spewing, CSAM-generating chatbot in Teslas, then merged with Spacex ahead of its IPO. As previously reported, Musk had then ordered Tesla to look at spinning off its China business to help his main division merge with SpaceX more easily. Musk also floated the possibility with investors, and one of the Trump administration's lasting legacies will be its love of corporate mergers, so it sounded plausible.

With Democrats winning control of both the House and the Senate, likely finishing with 258 Representatives and 55 (or 56!) Senators, the left doesn't just have power, it has a mandate from the voters to put a stop to everything the Trump administration is doing. Raskin will chair the House Judiciary Committee, Garcia will chair the House Oversight Committee, and both have promised investigations into any criminal activity that's taken place. That's not exactly fertile ground for a major corporate merger, especially after Musk attempted to inflame a race riot in Ireland, campaigned for Germany's Nazi-adjacent AfD party, and blew hundreds of millions of dollars trying to elect Republicans.

Yes, our friends over at the Tesla Takedown kept a running thread going last night, highlighting every race Musk lost and how much money he wasted. #5703. Nabrawind’s Crane-Free Wind Towers Face a Supplier Test

Spain’s Nabrawind has developed a way to install exceptionally tall wind turbine towers without bringing an enormous crawler crane to the site. Its Nabralift system uses a tubular upper tower supported by a three-legged steel structure. Hydraulic equipment raises the assembled turbine while modular sections are inserted below it near ground level. The lifting frame can then be removed and used on another installation. This addresses genuine logistical and construction problems, particularly at remote sites where specialist cranes are expensive to transport and where wind can interrupt conventional lifting operations.

The company has progressed beyond demonstration-scale hardware. In September 2026, UL Solutions issued type certification for Envision’s 7.8 MW turbine on Nabrawind’s 188-meter tower. Fortescue is using 17 of those tower configurations at the 133 MW Nullagine wind project in Western Australia’s Pilbara region, where construction is underway. Nabrawind previously erected a 160-meter prototype in Spain in under two weeks and has supplied smaller commercial towers in Morocco and France.

The engineering benefits are credible. Nabrawind reports using roughly 20% less tower steel than comparable conventional tubular designs and reducing foundation concrete by as much as 80%, depending on the design and site. Those are supplier claims rather than independently established savings across all wind farms. The potential to avoid large cranes, simplify transport and raise turbines in windier conditions could also matter substantially to total installed cost and construction schedules. High hub heights only earn their keep when those costs are justified by the electricity generated over the project’s life.

The current deployment has an unusual commercial structure. Fortescue acquired Nabrawind in September 2025 and is building Nullagine to serve its own mining operations. Fortescue has the capital, internal electricity demand and industrial incentive to support a technology it owns. Successful installation in that context would be important evidence of construction performance, but it would not establish that an unrelated wind developer can finance and maintain the same system under ordinary third-party commercial arrangements.

Nabralift’s proprietary construction approach creates a procurement issue. Conventional tubular towers can be sourced from several qualified manufacturers, and experienced contractors can compete for much of their construction work. A developer selecting Nabralift currently depends on one supplier for the core tower system, specialist lifting knowledge and associated support. Wind turbine original-equipment manufacturers also create supplier dependencies, but concentrating another critical part of the project in a proprietary installation system requires its own contract and risk assessment.

A type certificate provides valuable technical assurance about the certified turbine-and-tower configuration. A lender or insurer still needs enforceable delivery schedules, long-term warranties, repair and maintenance provisions, clarity on replacement parts, and a workable remedy if the supplier’s capacity or commercial priorities change. These questions become more important when a wind farm must operate for 25 years or longer and there is no qualified alternative provider of the same system.

Nabrawind’s next important proof point is an independently developed and financed large wind farm that accepts those risks on commercial terms. Qualified installation partners, credible long-term service arrangements and greater competitive capacity could make its engineering advantages easier for developers to buy. The 188-meter tower has earned technical attention; its broader market depends on financing and procurement confidence catching up with the machinery.

My full TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment examines Nabrawind’s self-erecting design, Fortescue’s Nullagine deployment and the supplier concentration that independent wind developers would have to manage. It follows my earlier assessment of 300-meter wind towers, where construction economics were the central challenge.

#5701. GM Recalls Over 67,000 Chevy Blazer EVs And Cadillac Lyriqs, Vistiqs, And Even Celestiqs For Temporary Loss Of Braking

General Motors is recalling 67,380 Chevrolet Blazer EVs And Cadillac Lyriqs, Vistiqs, and even Celestiqs because under specific circumstances, a software defect can cause a temporary loss of braking ability. According to the NHTSA recall report, GM is aware of 20 minor accidents due to the fault, two of which resulted in minor injuries. Fortunately, the condition only arises at low speeds, but any loss of braking is a deeply concerning and dangerous occurrence. Two-wheel-drive Cadillac Lyriqs are not included in the recall, and the only Blazer EV trims involved are SS and Police Pursuit Vehicles.

Cadillac Lyriqs are hit hardest by the recall, which includes 474 2023 Lyriqs, 22,819 2024 Lyriqs, 11,926 2025 Lyriqs, 9,322 2026 Lyriqs, and 44 2027 Lyriqs. The recall also includes 13,627 2026 Vistiqs and 5,175 2027 Vistiqs, as well as 51 2025 Celestiqs, and 31 2026 Celestiqs. (This is one of our best glimpses yet into how many Celestiqs have been sold.) The only Chevrolets included in the recall are 562 2024 Blazer EVs, 2012 2025 Blazer EVs, 1,314 2026 Blazer EVs, and 23 2027 Blazer EVs. VINs are already searchable on NHTSA's website, and the remedy comes in the form of an over-the-air update for owners who have opted in to those, otherwise owners will have to take their vehicles to dealerships to have the software update downloaded.

The conditions that lead to the temporary loss of brake function are very specific. According to the recall report and GM's testing, "when the brakes are lightly applied at low speeds during a sharp turn and the vehicle encounters a bump or depression – such as at the end of a driveway – a momentary release and reapplication of the brakes may cause the software's slip calculation to misinterpret wheel movement. In some instances, this may result in a temporary loss of braking. The phenomenon is unique to certain vehicles equipped with performance all-wheel drive (pAWD, RPO X0E) and is resolved when the brakes are applied again."

GM already recalled 21,469 all-wheel-drive Lyriqs for a similar issue in 2024, but it found that vehicles built with the software changes following that recall and vehicles that already received the software update from that recall are still susceptible to the conditions described in the new recall, and they need the latest update. The latest software update corrects the slip calculation in the vehicle's brake system control module that causes the temporary loss of braking, which coincidentally is the same claim made on the 2024 recall. Hopefully this time it actually fixes the problem.

If you drive one of the cars included in the recall, be aware of the possibility of braking loss, and remember that if you experience braking loss, normal brake function should return on the next brake press. Dealers should already be notified of the recall, but owner notification is estimated to begin on December 14.

#5700. Medicare Part D premiums projected to rise 50% in 2027 without plan switching: KFF

Medicare Part D premiums projected to rise 50% in 2027 without plan switching: KFF" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Medicare beneficiaries who remain in their current stand-alone Part D drug plans could face sharply higher premiums in 2027 if they don’t switch to lower-cost plans during open enrollment, according to a KFF analysis.

The average monthly premium for stand-alone prescription drug plans, or PDPs, is projected to rise 50%, from $34 in 2026 to $51 in 2027, if current enrollees remain in the same plans, according to the analysis from KFF, an independent source for health policy research, polling and news.

The increase would widen the gap between stand-alone drug plans and Medicare Advantage plans that include prescription drug coverage. KFF projects that drug coverage through Medicare Advantage plans that offer Part D coverage, or MA-PDs, will average $9 a month in 2027, compared with $51 for PDPs. The average PDP premium would rise by $17, compared with an increase of less than $2 for MA-PDs.

For Medicare Part D prescription drug coverage, the average beneficiary has 28 Medicare Advantage prescription drug plans (MA-PDs) and 9 stand-alone prescription drug plans (PDPs) to choose from, with varying costs associated with these different options. KFF analysts examined premiums and cost-sharing requirements for Part D coverage in 2027 and how these costs have changed over time, based on Medicare plan landscape and benefits data from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS).

The $51 figure assumes current PDP enrollees remain in their existing plans. The actual average premium could be lower as beneficiaries switch to less expensive plans during open enrollment and new beneficiaries select coverage.

CMS projected a much smaller increase in the national average Part D premium, from $35 to $36. KFF noted that CMS, which based its estimate on September 2026 enrollment, did not explain its calculation methodology.

Among PDP enrollees who do not receive low-income subsidies, 76%, or 10.4 million people, would pay higher premiums if they keep their current plans. About 2.4 million would see their monthly premiums increase by more than $50.

That's a sharp increase from 2026, when only 38,000 enrollees faced monthly premium increases exceeding $50, according to KFF. The Trump administration’s decision to discontinue the Part D Premium Stabilization Demonstration after 2026 ended the additional premium subsidies that were provided to PDP sponsors and the cap on the maximum allowable monthly PDP premium increase, which was set at $50 for 2026, according to KFF analysts.

Another 4.1 million beneficiaries without low-income subsidies are enrolled in zero-premium PDPs this year, but no zero-premium PDPs will be available in 2027.

“With some plans increasing premiums substantially, the stakes are higher this year for people with Medicare stand-alone drug coverage if they sit on the sidelines during open enrollment,” Juliette Cubanski, a vice president and director of the Program on Medicare Policy at KFF, said in a statement. “There are relatively low-premium PDP options, but people facing large premium increases need to take action if they want to avoid paying significantly more.”

According to KFF's analysis, if PDP enrollees who are not receiving Part D Low-Income Subsidies (LIS) keep their current plan in 2027, more than half (55%), or 7.5 million people, will pay premiums of less than $20 per month, but nearly 30%, or 3.9 million people, will pay at least $100 per month.

Average monthly premiums for the eight national PDPs are projected to range from around $6 to $204 in 2027. Among national PDPs, the two lowest-premium plans are Centene’s Wellcare Value Script Rx, an enhanced PDP with an average premium of $6.50 for 2027, up from $5.80 in 2026,  and Wellcare Classic, a basic PDP with an average premium of $10.90 for 2027, up from $8.60 in 2026, according to the analysis. The national PDPs with the highest average monthly premiums are United’s AARP Medicare Rx Preferred at $204.50, up from $126.00 in 2026, and Humana Premier Rx Plan at $137.40, up from $119.60 in 2026.

The analysis also finds that most Part D enrollees will face a deductible of several hundred dollars for drug coverage in 2027, including 85% of MA-PD enrollees, up from 80% in 2026, and virtually all PDP enrollees, 99.8%, up from 96% in 2026, based on current enrollment. The average Part D deductible in 2027 will be $643 for PDP enrollees, up from $540 in 2026,  and $489 for MA-PD enrollees, rising from $360 in 2026. The standard Part D deductible in 2027 is $700, up from $615 in 2026.

Most Part D enrollees will also face coinsurance rather than fixed copayments for preferred-brand and non-preferred drugs, potentially making their out-of-pocket costs less predictable. Virtually all PDP enrollees will face median coinsurance of 25% for preferred brands and 35% for non-preferred drugs, according to KFF.

#5698. Tesla Allegedly Misled Thousands Of South Korean Customers About 'Full Self-Driving'

Usually, when we tell you that Tesla has gotten into hot water for misleading folks about its "Full Self-Driving" Level 2 driver assistance system, it has to do with Tesla overstating just how capable of a system it is. That's not the case in South Korea, though, where the Texas-based automaker has allegedly vastly overstated the legality of FSD usage and charged customers for it nonetheless. Now, tens of thousands of Korean Tesla owners are looking for answers.

Tesla apparently markets FSD in South Korea despite the fact that it knows the majority of its cars can't legally use the program in the country, the complaint from an advocacy group alleges. That means it can't be activated on the car. Soon, the complaint will be filed with the Korean Fair Trade Commission, a consumer protection agency, according to Reuters. Tesla will have to answer for why it marketed FSD to prospective buyers for years, even collecting the $6,726 lump-sum payment required for activation, even though it couldn't legally be used.

Currently, just 20% of Teslas registered in South Korea can legally use FSD because they're built in the U.S., according to a preliminary testimony given by Tesla Korea country manager Seo Young-deuk last month. Those specific cars meet U.S. vehicle-safety standards that South Korea recognizes as part of a free trade agreement. The thing is, most Teslas on the road in South Korea are manufactured in China, where no such agreement exists. It was only recently that Tesla started the process of obtaining FSD certification on China-made vehicles, even though it has been charging customers for the software for over three years.

Right now, it's not totally clear how many customers in South Korea bought FSD subscriptions on ineligible vehicles, but the automaker has sold over 170,000 China-made vehicles in the country since 2023, Reuters reports. The company continued to market FSD as sales of ineligible China-manufactured vehicles surged in South Korea in recent years, and last year, 99% of new Teslas sold in the country couldn't legally use FSD.

The complaint alleges that last year, Tesla promoted FSD as "coming soon" and posted a demonstration video filmed in South Korea without clearly disclosing that the tech could only be used in a tiny fraction of the vehicles it was selling, according to Reuters. The consumer advocacy group accused Tesla Korea of deceptive marketing and has asked the KFTC to issue a temporary cease-and-desist order on marketing FSD for ineligible vehicles, impose fines and refer the case to state investigators.

It may be an uphill battle, though. Just last month, a court in Seoul dismissed a lawsuit filed by Tesla owners seeking refunds for the FSD option, Reuters reports. The court rejected the claim that Tesla had failed to deliver the driver-assistance system. Instead, it put the onus of the issue on regulatory and legal restrictions that had limited the company's ability to roll out future functions.

Man, that feels like one weak ahh argument to me.

#5697. CVS Health plans to split pharmacy business from Aetna, Caremark

CVS Health plans to split pharmacy business from Aetna, Caremark" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The healthcare giant announced Wednesday morning that it would divide its business units into two companies. The first houses its retail pharmacies and Health 100 technology businesses, and will operate as CVS Pharmacy. The second includes Aetna, Caremark, Oak Street Health and Signify Health and will be referred to as CVS Health on an interim basis.

CVS said in the announcement that it expects the separation to be completed in the first half of 2028, subject to closing conditions, and until then, it will continue to operate jointly. The move will reverse CVS' historic acquisition of Aetna for $69 billion in 2018.

Current CVS CEO David Joyner will become chief executive of the new CVS Health, while Prem Shah, group president of CVS Health, will become the CEO of the new CVS Pharmacy unit.

The company said that the decision "follows a comprehensive strategic review" by its board of directors.

Joyner said during the company's earnings call Wednesday morning that the shift comes "from a position of strength" after multiple years of hard work at CVS to shift its strategic approach and drive improvement. That includes significant investments in technology across the enterprise, and an overhaul of its leadership team to drive needed change.

He said that the "environment around us is constantly changing" as the company pushes toward this new strategy.

"We can take this strategic action today because of our tremendous progress since 2024," Joyner said.

"We will be better positioned to address this changing environment as two strong independent healthcare leaders," he continued. "Following a thoughtful and deliberate strategic review by the board and senior management, we have a structure and plan that are built to win and represent the best path to create value over the long term."

During this process, the team has identified significant opportunities for greater integration between Aetna and Caremark and has leaned on those to support key strategic initiatives, like advancing value-based care, Joyner noted. However, the pharmacy business has generally "operated behind a firewall."

"It has always been an arm's length negotiation and structure, which again, just reinforces the fact that there are integration opportunities, but nothing that we cannot solve for with a commercial agreement," Joyner said.

While there are clear synergies that exist between the pharmacies and Caremark, those commercial deals can maintain what's working, he added.

"We don't need the integration in an operating structure," Joyner said. "We need to make sure that we're aligned around where we believe that there can be value creation and make sure that there's an appropriate commercial agreement in place to support that."

CVS' strategy over the past several years has been built on four key principles: delivering on best-in-class execution, rethinking the consumer experience, becoming a go-to partner and harnessing capabilities across the company.

Following the split, both companies will continue to lean on these concepts, CVS said. Each individual entity will also benefit from a more focused strategy and the ability to adapt more nimbly to its own unique goals and strategic needs.

The future CVS Pharmacy will continue to identify ways to expand the reach of its pharmacists and identify further partnerships across the healthcare spectrum, while CVS Health will adapt in new ways to serve its clients, the company said.

Joyner said the company will continue to be transparent about its progress during the separation process.

Shares in the company were up 3% pre-market as of about 7:30 a.m. ET. CVS also reported its Q3 earnings on Wednesday, posting $2.2 billion in profit and $108.4 billion in revenue for the quarter.

Joyner said on the earnings call that post-split, investors will own shares in both companies.

#5695. NASA's Swift Space Telescope Re-Enters Atmosphere With Five Times More Risk Of Casualties Than Anticipated

On Wednesday, NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, a space telescope that's been in orbit since 2004, finally re-entered Earth's atmosphere above Indonesia. However, it appears to have done so with a risk of casualties five times beyond what NASA technical standards mandate. How and why this happened isn't immediately clear; NASA Public Affairs Specialist Alise Fisher told Jalopnik, "In the leadup to Swift's Nov. 20, 2004, launch, NASA determined the risk was consistent with mission requirements as allowed by agency policy." Somewhere between launch and reentry, that risk assessment shifted. It's unlikely that anybody made a specific mistake; this is probably the result of, well, space being hard. Still, it does highlight that our main defense against the detritus of astronomical ambitions is pure luck.

Swift is only crashing to Earth because it ran out of fuel to stay in orbit or adjust its trajectory. To NASA's credit, it did throw $30 million at a private company in an unprecedented attempt to rescue Swift with another satellite that would pull it back up into safe orbit. Sadly, the rescue satellite itself failed, dooming Swift to this fate.

In formal terms, Swift suffered an "uncontrolled reentry," which basically means it had no propulsion and just fell from space. NASA's own requirements, most recently updated in 2021 but going all the way back to 2001, state: "For uncontrolled reentry, the risk of human casualty from surviving debris shall be less than 0.0001 (1:10,000)." If you're not aware, there's no actual law requiring that satellites de-orbit in some sort of safe way that won't, you know, crash into a city or kill anyone. So our shield against the skies is just statistics. This is the threshold at which NASA feels the risk is acceptable. For reference, in all of history, just about 10,000 satellites have de-orbited, so... statistically we're due. And that was before we were putting tens of thousands of satellites up every few years.

In Swift's instance, however, NASA played its cards a little close to its chest. For one thing, it did not put out a risk assessment for the reentry, which is unusual. Then, in the middle of a longer announcement, the agency mentioned that Swift's risk of human casualties was actually "1 in 2,100." That's a risk of human injury or death five times beyond what it was meant to be.

Fortunately, the odds appear to have resolved in our favor. There are no reports of anyone being struck by space debris from Swift. Most of the satellite was expected to burn up during reentry; the trouble would come from whatever survived, likely dense pieces like the telescope lens or the reaction wheels. If any of those made it to the surface, there doesn't appear to have been a person around it.

That's a roll of the dice, though. At some point, as thousands of satellites de-orbit per year in our new megaconstellation era, laws should be passed to manage this formally. That would likely mean requiring controlled reentries, when the satellite still has a little fuel left to navigate to a safe spot out in the ocean. The other option, which companies like SpaceX have been pursuing, is to design the satellite to burn up entirely on reentry. The issue there is what effect all that vaporized metal might have on the atmosphere. Scientists don't yet know the answer, for the simple reason that there was never a reason to ask that question before. Now, the health of our planet may depend on it.

As space gets busier and busier, more and more will fall to us down here from up there. Up until now, the power of statistics has kept us safe. But eventually, a 1 in 10,000 chance is going to happen. Especially if some of those chances turn out to be riskier than intended.

#5693. Who Controls the Battery in Your Driveway?

Tesla brought home power backup to America. In Australia, an update is switching it off. North American owners just got Powershare with Powerwall. Australian owners of existing Teslas got a software update that appears to block the third-party gear they use to power their homes. It is a test case for who really controls the battery in your driveway.

Mark Purcell is an electrical engineer and energy advocate based in Noosa Heads, Queensland, Australia. He owns two Teslas and a bidirectional DC charger, and has been a member of the Australian Electric Vehicle Association since 2022. He has contributed content to CleanTechnica previously.

On 12 October, my Model Y ran my house. Through a Sigenergy bidirectional DC charger in my garage on Australia’s Sunshine Coast, it supplied about 25 kW to my home. The battery in my driveway holds several times the energy of a typical home battery, and I have already paid for it.

That may not last. Owners in several countries report that Tesla software from the 2026.38 branch, rolling out since October, cuts third-party discharge within minutes. On the Tesla Motors Club forum, owners describe power stopping after about three minutes with a battery management alert, or after 15 to 20 minutes whatever the load. The old Camp Mode and Service Mode workarounds no longer help. Drive Tesla Canada has covered the reports. EleJoy, Tlyard and Sigenergy users are all affected, and Tlyard now warns customers that Tesla’s 2026 software detects “simulated charging” and may cut the power link.

The release notes? “Security improvements” and minor fixes. Nothing about switching off a function owners use every day.

Here is the part that should interest readers everywhere. The same 2026.38 branch delivered Powershare with Powerwall home backup to owners in the US and Canada. That is a good thing. Tesla has finally joined Ford, GM, and Kia in letting the car back up the house.

Australia did not get it. Tesla Australia has said Powershare cannot be retrofitted to existing vehicles, and here Powershare is vehicle-to-load only. So, for every existing Tesla on Australian roads, third-party equipment is the only way to put the car to work for the home. If the software now blocks that equipment, Australian owners are left with nothing: not Tesla’s solution, and not anyone else’s.

The Tesla Australia owner’s manual says: “Do not use the Battery as a stationary power source. Doing so voids the warranty.” Tesla’s own Australian warranty page is narrower. It excludes damage caused by third-party adaptors or chargers, not the whole warranty.

Australian law is narrower again. Under the Australian Consumer Law, statutory consumer guarantees cannot be signed away by a line in a manual. Apple found this out when the Federal Court ordered A$9 million in penalties over the “Error 53” affair, after Apple told customers that third-party repairs had cost them their rights. American readers will recognise the shape of this argument from the right-to-repair fight.

Australia is a world leader in rooftop solar and is now subsidising home batteries at scale. The next step is obvious: the biggest battery most households will ever own is already parked outside. Bidirectional charging is how that capacity reaches the home and, in time, the grid.

That whole idea depends on interoperability. If one carmaker can switch off discharge overnight, through an over-the-air update the owner cannot roll back, and without saying so, then every bidirectional charger is a bet on that carmaker’s goodwill. Chargers bought in good faith become stranded. Competing suppliers lose access to the fleet. Grid operators lose flexibility they are counting on.

The ACCC, Australia’s competition and consumer regulator, has already named “denying interoperability” as conduct that can distort competition in digital platform markets. A car that decides which charger it will talk to is a platform in all but name.

I am deferring Tesla updates on both my cars, so I am also missing whatever genuine fixes they contain. I have asked Tesla in writing to hold updates until it confirms discharge will keep working. I have lodged a complaint with the ACCC under Australia’s competition and consumer laws. I have also asked the Australian Electric Vehicle Association, the national voice of EV users, to back it.

Tesla may have a real safety or engineering reason. If so, it should say what it is, and show why a less restrictive answer would not work: certified partner equipment, discharge limits, or a published interface that charger makers can build to.

Three things, and they apply well beyond Australia. Carmakers should disclose functional changes in plain language before they ship. Owners should be free to use the bidirectional charger of their choice. And regulators should set interoperability rules for vehicle discharge, as many already do for solar inverters. If we can make inverters speak a common language, we can stop cars locking out the chargers they plug into.

My car still powers my house. It does so only because I have stopped it updating. No owner, in any country, should have to choose between a current car and a working home battery.

“I am looking forward to the discussions around this topic,” David Waterworth, who helped get this article published, adds.

We publish a number of guest posts from experts in a large variety of fields. This is our contributor account for those special people, organizations, agencies, and companies.

#5692. Open Your Mind And The 2027 Mercedes-AMG GT 4-Door Coupe Will Blow It

Appealing to enthusiasts and buyers of performance cars is already hard enough with internal combustion engines, whether we're talking affordable hot hatchbacks or high-end supercars. As many automakers have been learning the hard way, it's orders of magnitude tougher to build and sell a good electric car to those same enthusiasts. They want their cars to feel real, with tactile sensations and character and emotion and all those other valid clichés, and few (if any) EVs have achieved that or even really gotten close.

Now, the wizards at Affalterbach have done it. The 2027 Mercedes-AMG GT 4-Door Coupe has unbelievable performance figures when it comes to power and speed as well as efficiency and charging, it has advanced technology features and F1-derived aerodynamics, and months after the reveal its design still has everybody talking, to say the least. Most importantly, it is absolute dynamite to drive – a grand slam, a home run, the automotive equivalent of an EGOT, however else you want to say it – and much of that is down to how it emulates a combustion powertrain, complete with V8 noises and shifts that will stretch your definition of "real."

Head of development Oliver Wiech told me that even the most staunch anti-EV car enthusiasts, from people on Mercedes' own engineering teams to its dealers and long-time AMG customers, have been completely enamored by the electric GT once they've experienced it for themselves. Regardless of how you feel about its styling or its powertrain or its perceived gimmicks, if you go into a drive in the new Mercedes-AMG GT 4-Door Coupe with an open mind, prepare to have your mind blown.

Full disclosure: Mercedes flew me to Málaga and put me up in a lovely hotel so I could spend two days driving the GT55 on the road and the GT63 on track at Ascari. I spilled a latte on my MacBook Pro on the first day of the trip, so if you see any typos in here, I blame the crappy PC I've had to write this on.

In many ways this car is the heir to the first-generation Mercedes CLS, particularly because of its sloping roofline that's the reason for the four-door coupe moniker, and thankfully the new GT is much easier to get in and out of than both the original CLS (which I own) and the first-gen GT 4-Door Coupe that this EV replaces. Even people much taller than my 5-foot-9 self won't really have to worry about smacking their head when getting in or fitting comfortably in the seat. Despite being almost two inches lower in height than the old GT 4-Door, its interior seems far more spacious, even in the back seats.

I settle into a sports car-like driving position with a low H-point and a great view out ahead; the rear window seems small at first but visibility isn't that bad through it, and the C-pillar blind spot is better than in my 20-year-old CLS. Progress! All of the cars I drive are equipped with the optional performance seats with integrated headrests, which look cool and are very supportive and comfortable, even after spending hours in the car. They have a heat function and adjustable bolsters and lumbar support, but unfortunately if you want ventilation and massage (and I do want them) you have to stick with the still-supportive base seats.

Aside from some flourishes like the center screen canted toward the driver and the surrounds of the air vents, the GT's interior feels much like any other new Mercedes EV, and that same feeling extends to how it drives – in Comfort mode, at least. This is an easy car to drive around the city, with standard six-degree rear-wheel steering giving it a tight turning radius. The cars we're driving have staggered-width 21-inch wheels wearing Continental SportContact summer tires, and even with that big rubber the optional Active Ride Control hydraulic suspension keeps the ride firm and sporty but never uncomfortable or rough. It's certainly much more comfortable than the last-gen GT, which had a horrible ride.

When still in Comfort, I try out the first of the three Race Engineer knobs on the center console, which adjusts the responsiveness of the throttle pedal. (More on the other two later.) The dial goes from 1 to 9, with 1 being the least-responsive and 9 being the most, and boy does turning it up all the way make a difference. In addition to adjusting the actual responsiveness of the motors, the physical feel of the pedal changes, giving you less resistance when you press it like when cycling through regen braking settings.

On the road we're driving GT55s, which have one electric motor on the front axle and two on the rear axle. Those motors are axial-flux units created by YASA, a British company that was acquired by Mercedes a few years ago. (YASA already has similar motors in plug-in-hybrid supercars like the Koenigsegg Regera and Ferrari 296.) The rear motors are combined together in a housing with planetary gearsets, an oil cooling system and two water-cooled silicon carbide inverters; the motors can spin to more than 13,000 rpm. The front motor, which also has an SiC inverter and a spur transmission, is activated when more power or traction are needed and can reach over 15,000 rpm. They're juiced up by an 800-volt battery pack with a usable capacity of 106 kWh, which has Formula 1-derived tech like skinny cylindrical cells and an electrically non-conductive cooling oil that flows between them all.

AMG's main goal with the GT's powertrain and the dedicated AMG.EA platform it rides on was sustained, repeatable performance in all aspects – especially important when there's this much power on tap. The GT55 has a peak output of 805 hp when using launch control or Boost mode (output is 577 hp continuous) and a massive 1,372 pound-feet of torque. Accelerating from 0 to 60 mph takes only 2.7 seconds (or 2.4 seconds with a 1-foot rollout included), and it'll reach 124 mph in 9.0 seconds (also three tenths quicker with the same rollout). It feels absurdly quick both from a stop and when accelerating at speed, even when in Comfort.

Switch the car into Race mode and the suspension hunkers down and tightens up, the front motor is permanently engaged, and special powertrain preconditioning is turned on. It's hard to think of a better point-to-point car than this, especially if your route includes spectacularly twisty mountain roads like the area around Ascari. The Active Ride suspension keeps the car extremely flat and stable in corners by using hydraulically interconnected dampers instead of mechanical anti-roll bars, and I promise you the car feels much lighter than its 5,501-pound curb weight suggests. Its steering doesn't have quite as much feedback as a Porsche Taycan, but it's sharp and direct, maybe the best-tuned setup that AMG currently offers.

The tri-motor setup allows for fully variable torque vectoring between the rear wheels, and with stability control in its regular on setting, there is an unstoppable amount of grip. Power out of a corner hard and the traction control light flashes, the car blasting ahead with zero drama. Put it into ESC Sport and the GT gets looser and more playful, the tail kicking out in easily controlled little slides without feeling like the computers are constantly reigning in the fun.

Very strong one-pedal regenerative braking can be dialed in using the steering wheel paddles; while I really enjoy driving fast EVs with just the throttle, and it's great to do so in the AMG, I prefer turning the regen to a milder setting and actually using the brake pedal. It's a hydraulic brake-by-wire system, with the GT coming with 16.5-inch carbon-ceramic brake discs up front and 14.9-inch steel discs in the rear. There's great initial bite and pedal feel, with seemingly no loss of performance after some hard driving. This setup is more than strong enough for most people, but I'd want to spec the optional ceramic high-performance compound braking system, partially just because it adds beefier carbon brakes to the rear that look a lot better than the base setup. Those stronger stoppers are part of a package that includes bronze calipers and a 186-mph top speed, instead of the normal 161 mph.

If that was all and the review ended there, I would say the AMG GT is one of the best EVs (or any sort of car) on the market. Once you try the AMGFORCE Sport+ mode with its V8 noises and shifts, though, you won't want to drive it in any other mode again. In fact, you probably won't want to ever stop driving the GT, and no other EV will scratch the same itch. It's hard to think of the right words to describe it. I definitely wouldn't call it "fake", and "simulated" doesn't feel right either. Saying the noises are "synthesized" is probably the way to go, but really it doesn't matter at all. Who cares that the sounds and shifts are not "real" when the end result is this absurdly good?

AMG recorded more than 1,600 sound files of the previous-gen GT R's twin-turbo 4.0-liter V8, capturing every situation from every possible angle, and they're mixed in real-time to match driver inputs and what the powertrain is doing. That means you're never hearing the same noises twice, and everything feels unique and organic to how you're driving the car. The same goes for how it "shifts" when you leave the car to its own devices, though you of course can and should use the paddles to shift, too. Put anyone into the GT as either a passenger or a driver without telling them what's powering the car, and they'll all think there's actually a V8 under the hood. It adds a ton of engagement and sensation to an already engaging drive, eliciting feelings of sheer joy and excitement.

First of all, it's loud, but not in a way that's obnoxious or too much. If you switch into AMGForce Sport+ when the car is stopped it'll burst to life sounding just like the real V8 on startup, but it's much funnier if you change the drive mode at speed, since the car will kick itself into a low gear with the revs up pretty high, resulting in a hilariously good sound. Keep the car in Sport+ around town and it emits wonderful burbles, while at cruising speeds it fades into the background and shifts smoothly like a V8 would. Drop a few gears and start driving more energetically, though, and it gets really gnarly. As my drive partner and friend of Jalopnik, Roberto Baldwin, points out, the placement of the speakers and the rumbling exciters in the seats make it sound like the car is mid-engined, or that there are big side-exit exhaust right underneath us. It roars under acceleration, utters pops and bangs on "overrun," barks when I shift. Nothing about the noises sound artificial, unnatural or repetitive.

It's just freakin' awesome, and after just a few minutes you might totally forget that you're in an EV at all. Except that even in this mode, with shifts that come with an authentic cut in torque, the GT's acceleration still gives the tunnel-vision feeling you'll only get from an EV. Engineers tell me that the GT is just as quick to accelerate and fast around a track with the shifts on as it would be with them turned off, and in fact the aural and physical feedback will probably help you post even better lap times than you otherwise would.

Crack off shifts with the paddles, and you'd swear there's a real DCT transmission in here. There's an urgency and gut punch quality to the upshifts, and downshifts can be quite forceful too. Using the vibrators in the seats, the car mimics the mechanical clunks and thumps you'd feel in an ICE car's drivetrain. When in S+ you can't mess with the regen, which is set to the minimum level, but downshifting does aid in deceleration, like strong engine braking. It will "rev" to 7,200 rpm, and the car will hold gears for pretty long and upshift right at redline.

You can hear the sounds outside the car as well, and it's loud enough that we can hear GTs driving on track from pretty far away. If you really want to be obnoxious you can park the car, put it in neutral and rev it, putting any nearby Dodge Charger Daytonas to shame. Keep your foot pinned to the floor and it will bounce off the redline seemingly indefinitely – we wouldn't know, because after about ten seconds of doing it for a TikTok, a few Germans walked over to ask us to please shut the hell up.

The GT's Boost function is also at its best in S+, though it's available in all drive modes. Pull both paddles at once and it instantly activates, providing maximum power for a long time. Like, a really long time. Most cars that offer a Boost do so for 10, 15, maybe 20 seconds, and sometimes you have to wait before activating it again. That's one of the big benefits of the GT's powertrain – in the GT55 the boost lasts for 55 seconds while in the GT63 it'll stay on for 63 seconds, and as soon as it finishes or you manually turn it off, you can immediately activate it again. One AMG representative told me the boost could theoretically last forever, and they needed to come up with an arbitrary time limit. It is actually nice to have it last so long, like if you're coming up on a particularly complex and lengthy set of switchbacks. Turning on the Boost always comes with louder sounds and a countdown timer in the gauge cluster, but with the V8 activated it's a lot more dramatic. The engine noises sound like they get 25% louder, and the shifts feel even more aggressive. It rules.

OK, sure, you might try the AMGFORCE mode and still come out hating the sounds and shifts, even though I can't imagine not loving it. At least you can just switch into one of the other drive modes and it all turns off. It is really nice to be able to go back into Comfort once I'm on the freeway or get stuck behind slow-moving traffic on a twisty road, the car immediately settling back down into a silent, swift electric cruiser. Our group of journalists was unanimous about one thing during dinner conversations with AMG execs and engineers, though: We want to be able to turn on all the AMGFORCE stuff in all modes from Comfort to Race, not just be restricted to Sport+. It really is that compelling, and that's something Mercedes could easily change with an over-the-air software update.

Good as the mountain roads are, AMG's real reason for bringing us to this part of Spain is so we can drive the GT around Circuito Ascari, a track you certainly recognize from "Top Gear" and racing games. Luckily I've been here once before, for the launch of the 992.2 Carrera GTS, so the track is a little less daunting. For this part of the day we swap into GT63s, which have the tri-motor setup boosted to produce a peak of 1,153 hp (711 hp continuous) and 1,475 lb-ft of torque. When accelerating to 60 mph the GT63 is 0.4 second quicker than the GT55, both when including or excluding that rollout, and it'll hit 124 mph a much more noticeable 2.3 seconds quicker than the GT55.

We complete our first two laps in Comfort mode (and at quite a fast pace immediately), with the car feeling fast and fun enough that you won't hate your sighting laps when first starting a track day, and on the second lap we play around with the responsiveness dial. For laps three and four AMGForce Sport+ gets activated, and our instructors talk about how nice the feedback is for executing cleaner and faster laps, and how much more fun it is to rip around a track with the V8 soundtrack turned on. After doing one lap with stability control on, we switch it to ESC Sport for the next lap to experience the difference in grip and slip that it allows.

Then we switch into Race mode to try out the other two Race Engineer dials. In the middle of the array is the agility control, which messes with the torque vectoring and chassis systems to simulate shortening the wheelbase for, well, increased agility, and to change the car's handling behavior from favoring a bit of understeer to a lot of oversteer. At the bottom is the traction dial, which adjusts the level of traction control intervention – at the loosest 9 setting, up to 90% of torque can be sent to the rear wheels. These two are only available to change yourself when stability control has been fully turned off; with it on, in Sport+ mode the car defaults to agility at 5 and traction at 2.

For the first lap, we crank all three dials down to 1, which means the powertrain is the least responsive, it's the least agile, and the traction control intervenes the most. Even set up like this the car is great to drive fast, but it's clear that the GT is being held back – traction control is butting in more prominently, turn in isn't super sharp, it favors a bit of understeer on corner entry and exit, and torque is obviously being deployed more sensitively.

The next lap we crank the responsiveness up to 9 and turn the agility and traction dials to 5, and the car's demeanor completely changes. It eagerly dives into corners and rotates like a sports car should, the rear end kicking out quite a bit as I accelerate out of the apex while giving it a dab of oppo, as so many British dudes have probably said to camera on this track. The GT feels so much more lively now, and still totally controllable. On the following lap we turn agility to 7, and the car feels even more precise. Sadly we don't get to try it out with everything turned all the way to 9, going back into Comfort for a cool-down lap, but if we were to do so, things would get quite lairy. There is a lot of video evidence out there of just how effortlessly the GT will drift, or pull off instant burnouts that would shame any muscle car.

Will buyers of this car take them to track days and actually mess with this stuff? Probably not, but they really should. It's fast as hell but fun too, an extremely competent car on track that can be perfectly adapted to anyone's driving skills and desires, allowing you to unlock more capability when you want.

Mercedes hasn't released U.S. range estimates for the GT yet, and neither has the EPA, but I do have some real-world data to give you. Depending on wheel and tire setup Mercedes says the GT55 has a range of between 371 miles and 435 miles on the European WLTP cycle; with a 91% charge at the start of our drive day, the GT55 shows an estimated range of about 300 miles, and that's with it calculating based on how the cars have been driven along the same routes in the hands of other journalists. At the start of my track session the GT63 has 80% charge, and after the eight laps the charge sits at 60%, which ain't bad. The range estimate only dropped by 30 miles, too.

In order to keep the baker's dozen of GTs juiced up for all our track sessions and routes to and from the hotel, AMG brought a bunch of fast chargers to Ascari, including one massive Alpitronic rig that is part of the charging company's partnership with Mercedes. This machine can dole out more than 1,000 kW of power, which the GTXX concept was able to handle and is a goal for future models. The production GT can "only" handle 600 kW of charging power, according to Mercedes. That's still more than nearly any station in the U.S. can provide, and it can take the GT from 10% to 80% in only 11 minutes. In a demo using that Alpitronic monster, we see a GT charge from 17% to 80% in exactly 10 minutes, reaching a peak of 647 kW, and that's with the charger experiencing infrastructure problems and not operating as well as it could.

Thanks to AMG's thermal management system, the harder you drive the more primed the car is for fast-charging. In one of the gauge cluster's many display options you can see the temperature of the battery and motors, and it'll show how much fast-charging power the car is ready for. Doing spirited driving in the canyons it easily shows well over 400 kW available, and when that demo GT63 came right off a track session to charge, it was receiving more than 560 kW in less than a second after being plugged in. As soon as a fast-charging session is finished, the car is ready to go right back on track and keep driving at maximum attack. There's no loss or delay in power delivery, energy and thermal efficiency, or anything else that could hold the car back.

Now I'm not going to try and change anyone's opinions when it comes to how the new AMG GT looks, but I do think it could really grow on you, especially once you start seeing them in the dozens and dozens of different paint colors that Mercedes offers through the Manufaktur program. The turbine wheel design you see above looks fantastic, and gets you more range. The interior is also offered in some great leather schemes too, like a classy full beige or bright blue or yellow, and you don't have to get carbon-fiber trim inside.

At the very least, the new GT's proportions and silhouette are a big improvement over the outgoing car. It's lower and longer, with a longer wheelbase and dash-to-axle ratio plus a more rakish, shark-like nose. With the 21-inch wheels its stance is pretty killer, and I genuinely do love a lot of the details, like the execution of the AMG grille and the trio of afterburner-style taillights set into that black panel. It's pretty practical too, with the liftback rear end opening to reveal 14.7 cubic feet of cargo space.

This may be the rare car where a passenger screen is something you'll actually want to use, at least if you're a bit of a data nerd like me and Roberto. When each of us sit shotgun while the other drives, we can't stop swiping through all of the performance data pages available on the 14-inch passenger touchscreen. (You can pull them up in the center screen, too, and there are a bunch of different designs for the gauge cluster that can also tell you performance info.)

These show the current rpm, torque and electrical output of the motors; pedal inputs, steering angle, suspension compression and g-forces; temperature of the motors and battery pack; the position of the various active dynamic elements such as the deploying rear diffuser; and an IWC stopwatch, among other things. The animations and graphics are all excellent, and looking through it all while the driver is really putting the hammer down must feel like how cats do when they watch birds at a feeder.

Somehow, this performance comes at a reasonable price, at least as far as this class of car is concerned. The GT55 will start at $145,000 before a $1,550 destination charge, putting it right between the Taycan 4S and GTS in terms of price. That also makes it about ten grand cheaper than the outgoing GT63 4-Door, the cheapest V8-powered one that made do with a meager 575 horsepower. For that price you get tons of standard active-safety features, a Burmester 3D surround sound system, fancy digital headlights, three-stage adjustable air springs, and the trio of screens. (A dual-motor GT53 with less power and equipment is coming later in 2027, but we don't have pricing details yet.)

The GT63 will start at $175,000 before a destination fee that Mercedes hasn't announced yet, making it about $25,000 cheaper than the old GT63 S E Performance PHEV and ten grand cheaper than a Taycan Turbo. That also undercuts a Lucid Air Sapphire by almost $100,000. It gets the Active Ride Control suspension, Race Engineer dials, Race mode, the Drift mode and AMG Track Pace features, all of which are available in the GT55's Dynamic Plus package. Other standard features on the GT63 include ventilated and massaging front seats, Nappa leather, a head-up display, and Magic Vision Control wipers.

Available on all GT 4-Door Coupes are a Sky Control panoramic sunroof with dimmable glass and illuminated AMG logos, soft-close doors, a three-person rear seat instead of the standard two, an even fancier Burmester sound system, and all sorts of styling options. An exterior lighting package adds a lightbar between the headlights, a light strip along the trunk edge, and illumination to the grille bars and surround; I would definitely get this, but lots of people prefer the front end without the light bar.

As awesome as it is, at the end of the day this is a niche sort of vehicle regardless of what's powering it. The GT 4-Door is never going to be a major seller for AMG, though the brand is very optimistic about its prospects around the globe, including here in the States. What makes the electric GT truly exciting is what it means for the future of AMG, and performance cars as a whole. Its axial-flux motors, advanced battery solutions, dynamic focus and spectacular sounds will spread across the AMG lineup – we've already seen its AMG GT SUV twin and the "entry-level" 671-hp CLA45, and models like the GLC and C-Class are coming with over 900 hp – and just think what other brands might dream up once they've driven one.

Like all the best magic acts and wonders of the world, the 2027 Mercedes-AMG GT 4-Door Coupe must be seen — or rather, heard and experienced — to be believed. This is a car that could truly win over even the most extreme internal combustion enthusiasts, as long as they'll open their minds and let it.

#5691. At $11,995, Could This 2013 Cadillac Escalade Hybrid Make You 'Slade In The Shade?

Today's Nice Price or No Dice Cadillac Escalade is a rare Hybrid model with two electric motors sandwiched between its V8 engine and 4WD. Once very expensive, we'll have to see if this Champagne-hued luxury SUV now fits our beer budget.

For the longest time, Bentley Motors and Rolls-Royce were intrinsically intertwined, with Bentley often getting the short shrift in the partnership. In the latter half of the 20th Century, Bentley's cars often felt like an afterthought compared to the Parthenon-grilled Rolls models. That's an unfortunate bit of history, as before Rolls-Royce bought Bentley in 1931, the latter company built entire automobiles, rather than just foisting chassis and drivetrains on commissioned coachbuilders like the former.

The 1997 Bentley Brooklands we looked at on Wednesday attempted to distinguish itself from its near-twin Rolls-Royce Silver Spirit by offering a tauter suspension, toned-down body-color grille surround, and a turbocharger bolted to its 6.75-liter V8 engine. Presented in excellent condition and, in the seller's words, "needing nothing," our Bentley came with an $18,000 asking price. That's about a tenth of what the car cost new, but when it came down to brass tacks, opinions were fairly evenly split on its value. Ultimately, the brave—or foolhardy—among us lost out, as the Bentley bombed in an excruciatingly narrow 52% 'No Dice' loss.

Regardless of outcome, yesterday's Bentley was a textbook example of what the ultimate in luxury travel was intended to be in the later decades of the 20th Century. By comparison, the 2013 Cadillac Escalade Hybrid that comes our way today is a more modern execution of that concept.

The Escalade, of course, is the vehicle that arguably saved Cadillac. Originally a slapped-together version of the GMC Denali SUV, the Escalade proved so successful that GM added additional versions and further differentiation with later iterations. Those included the comically weird ESV version based on the Chevy Avalanche pickup. One of the rarest Escalade models is the initial 4WD Hybrid, produced between 2009 and 2013.

The Hybrid Escalade's party piece is the dual-mode AHS2 (Advanced Hybrid System 2, Electric Boogaloo), which replaces the traditional automatic transmission. Co-developed by GM, Daimler-Chrysler, and BMW, the hybrid drive unit was used in several of GM's SUVs, along with Mercedes and BMW sedans and the Dodge Durango. Dual mode means the truck can be powered by the gasoline engine, one of the 60-kilowatt electric motors, or a combination of both. Another 60kW electric motor serves as a generator for the nickel-metal hydride battery pack. This was technology that all three partners in the development consortium thought would pave the way to greater efficiency, but ultimately proved overly complicated for the task. All three dropped the hybrid drive unit by the end of the 2013 model year.

This Escalade Hybrid is one result of that short-lived partnership and product run. According to the ad, it has done 140,000 miles (132k according to the text, 140k according to the sidebar listing details — we'll go with the larger number) and, aside from some minor wear and tear, presents admirably for those miles.

Naturally, the most expensive component of any hybrid or fully electric vehicle is the battery, and it's reassuring to know the pack in this Escalade was replaced at 90K. That gives it at least another 40K if the current pack has the same lifespan as the first.

On the gas side of things, there's a 6.0-liter LZ1 V8, making 332 horsepower and 367 pound-feet of torque all by its lonesome. Specs indicate that, combined with the electric motors, power jumps to 379 horses.

Per the seller, the HV battery isn't the only new component this truck has seen. It also has new shocks and suspension components, refreshed brake pads, and new tires on its chrome-plated factory alloys. The ad claims no issues with the truck's performance, saying that it has been "extremely well maintained with all the expensive items already taken care of."

Overall, the truck looks as nice as its description lets on. The exterior, appropriately enough in metallic Champagne, is said to only suffer from some minor scuffs on the rear bumper cap. Other than that, it still shines and is matched with clear, unclouded headlamp covers.

The interior looks lived-in but far from abused. The leather on the driver's seat has the patina of many posteriors, but seems fully intact. So too does the leather on the steering wheel, albeit with a glossy sheen expected given the truck's age and miles. The only other really glaring issue is the wear evident on the fan control in the automatic climate control panel. Geez, people, just leave it on auto!

This is a three-row SUV with room for seven, so it should be as versatile as it is efficient. It comes with built-in navigation, a tow package, and, most importantly, a clean title.

When new, this Escalade commanded over $77,000 to drive it off the dealership lot. That was a long time ago, with many miles and a long-expired warranty in the rearview, so naturally it should cost less now. We need to decide whether the seller's set price of $11,995 is low enough.

Since this one comes with the promise that all the expensive work is already done, it may be a safe bet to take ownership. Also, I think the less said about the AI-generated image of the truck in the ad as some sort of weird road boat, the better.

What do you say? Is this rare hybrid Escalade worth $11,995 as it sits? Or is that too much for a truck with an abandoned technology, no matter how fancy it is?

Seattle, Washington, Craigslist, or go here if the ad disappears.

#5690. Waystar touts bigger health system wins and growing AI pipeline

Waystar touts bigger health system wins and growing AI pipeline" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Healthcare payment software maker Waystar again outperformed analysts’ estimates in the third quarter as the company builds out new artificial intelligence capabilities and drives growth by adding new customers and selling more of its platform to existing clients.

Waystar brought in $325.6 million in Q3 revenue, up 21% from the same period a year ago, according to its Q3 financial results published Monday afternoon. It beat Wall Street analysts’ estimates by 0.46%.

During Q3, the company reported $181 million in subscription revenue, up 34%, while provider revenue grew 28% to reach $243 million. Patient revenue came in at $82 million, up 5% year-over-year, and volume-based revenue grew 8% to $143 million.

Waystar ended the quarter with 1,488 clients generating more than $100,000 of trailing 12-month revenue, up 14% year-over-year. Year-to-date bookings grew 25% year-over-year.

Waystar reported net income of $31 million and GAAP net income per share of 16 cents. It also reported adjusted EBITDA of $139.3 million and non-GAAP earnings per share of 44 cents.

Waystar provides healthcare payment and revenue cycle management tools to 30,000 clients, representing over 1.5 million distinct providers. Its platform processes over 8.5 billion healthcare payment transactions annually, representing more than $3 trillion in gross claims, according to CEO Matt Hawkins. Waystar says its clinical intelligence spans approximately one-third of U.S. hospital discharges. In 2026, Waystar added more than 100 direct connections to health plans, supporting nearly 50 million transactions annually, executives said.

Hawkins told investors and analysts during the Q3 earnings call that the quarter “reflects strong progress,” on three strategic priorities of “driving broader adoption of the Waystar platform, extending our reach through partners and integrations, and advancing AI and innovation.”

“Our near-term roadmap includes more than 20 planned AI capabilities, accelerating the autonomous revenue cycle vision to reduce manual work, automate increasingly complex tasks and improve financial and operational outcomes for our clients,” Hawkins said.

Waystar is focused on using AI to reshape the RCM process with a vision of building an "autonomous revenue cycle" that can reduce manual work, automate increasingly complex tasks and improve financial and operational outcomes for healthcare organizations, executives said.

In Q3, Waystar launched an autonomous claim resubmission capability that interprets payer responses, applies payer-specific intelligence to determine the next action and autonomously resubmits eligible rejected claims with minimal human intervention, Hawkins said.

"Based on early adopter results and the initial claim types supported, we estimate this capability could autonomously resubmit up to $5 billion in previously rejected claims annually with the potential to eliminate more than 400,000 hours of manual work each year," he said.

The company is also targeting mid-cycle processes. "We're combining Waystar's financial data, payer intelligence, workflows and connectivity with Iodine's clinical intelligence to bring greater automation earlier in the revenue cycle," Hawkins noted.

The company acquired AI-driven RCM company Iodine Software a year ago to add its clinical intelligence capabilities to Waystar's software. Iodine bookings exceeded management's year-to-date plan by 74% in Q3, Hawkins said. Iodine's CDI and pre-bill anomaly detection products generated nearly $30 million in bookings through Q3, including about $15 million during the quarter, and have a combined pipeline exceeding $100 million.

The company is winning bigger, broader deals in the healthcare market, Hawkins asserted. Large health care organizations increasingly look to Waystar to support more of the revenue cycle through a single connected platform, he said on the call. "Within our large client cohort, which we define as clients generating more than $100,000 in LTM revenue, the average client now uses approximately five Waystar product modules. With over 30 modules across six product families, we see significant opportunity to continue driving broader platform adoption within these relationships," he said.

Hawkins added that the company “secured the largest new client win in Waystar’s history” during Q3.

“In a competitive process, a major East Coast health system representing approximately $7 billion in annual net patient revenue selected Waystar's full platform across patient access, mid-cycle, and back-end revenue cycle operations,” he said. “The organization plans to replace more than 20 separate vendors with Waystar as it simplifies its technology infrastructure and streamlines operations.”

Moreover, Hawkins said the company is expanding its reach with “strategic channel relationships,” with an emphasis on the ambulatory market—noting an expanded partnership with a leading physical therapy practice management system that expands Waystar’s reach to “nearly 4,000 providers across more than 2,500 sites, representing approximately 17 million claims annually.”

“Decisions like these reflect the trust we've built with channel partners, the breadth of our platform, and our ability to deliver real ROI,” Hawkins said.

Alpana Wegner, who took over as Waystar’s chief financial officer in August, said that large client relationships “now represent approximately 75% of revenue,” adding the company is seeing momentum across growth in number of clients, strong bookings and implementation backlog expansion.

But larger, broader platform implementations have longer revenue conversion times, which can extend to 12 to 18 months, Wegner noted. This creates a longer period between booking and recognized revenue. The company reported that the backlog of larger deals, those in excess of $100,000 in annual sales, was up more than 50% year-over-year.

In response to a question from an analyst about the disconnect between bookings and revenue growth, Hawkins said, "We are seeing strong demand. We're not seeing a change in the competitive environment or our win rates, and we're pleased with that," adding that the company sees a "long-term double-digit opportunity to drive revenue."

For its full-year outlook, Waystar management forecasted revenue of $1.277 billion to $1.287 billion, with a midpoint of $1.282 billion. Adjusted EBITDA is expected to be between $543 million and $549 million for fiscal 2026.

The company expects slower, near-term revenue growth, forecasting fourth-quarter revenue of approximately $323 million, representing growth of about 6%.

Ryan Daniels, group head of healthcare technology and services at William Blair, wrote in an analyst note that Waystar delivered strong results on both the top and bottom line. "We continue to expect solid organic growth going forward. While investor focus may turn to the very modest (0.2%) reduction in sales guidance, we believe strong profitability, solid bookings performance, and robust free cash flows will continue to lead the stock higher over time; we maintain our Outperform rating," he wrote.

Daniels wrote that Waystar remains a "category leader in end-to-end RCM software... leveraging its competitive position and scale advantages to enhance the platform with innovations that drive client value. Moreover, we believe innovation momentum is driving an uptick in pipeline activity, size, and bookings performance, highlighted by a continuation of strong win rates and an uptick in larger deal sizes."

Daniels also noted that concerns over AI risks and "end-market noise," such as weaker healthcare volumes and Medicaid and ACA exchange lives moving to uninsured status, are "overblown."

Waystar is positioned to capitalize on the AI-enabled transformation of RCM via stronger pricing, an expanding total addressable market and increased value-add for clients, he said. "We continue to view the sales model as highly recurring (and visible) and do not anticipate any major AI-related competitive disruption as providers continue to turn toward trusted and fully integrated partners for RCM solutions," Daniels wrote.
