#5689. Elon Musk Threw Away $474 Million (Or More) … But May Benefit From Failing

Some people think Elon Musk has lost his mind. Others think he’s always been a charlatan and has just had an insane amount of luck. Some people think he’s a genius and that everything he touches will turn to gold. And then there’s also a decent portion of folks who think he’s an absolute idiot about some things but brilliant — or at least very clever — when it comes to others. Whatever you think of Elon Musk, though, there’s no denying he just threw away about half a billion dollars.

Musk reportedly spent at least $474 million on the midterm elections (because one individual is allowed to do that, apparently), and yet his picks — the key people he supported — got completely crushed. The politicians he spent all of that money to get elected did not get elected, and were actually not even close to getting elected. Apparently, voters in their jurisdictions thought they were horrible choices, sometimes historically so. Imagine if all of that money he spent had been spent on something good and useful instead! (Perhaps saving the lives of starving, poverty-stricken children and babies around the world? Perhaps stopping the spread of horrible diseases, since the US government has dropped such efforts on several threats? Perhaps to provide subsidies for electric vehicles, like Tesla sells, since Republicans in Congress and Donald Trump killed those? Perhaps to use solar power instead of fossil fuels to power AI data centers?)

Why did Elon Musk spend a whopping half a billion dollars (or more) on the 2026 midterm elections?

I know there are some people who don’t see this, but it’s been clear for a while that the following things are true about Elon Musk:

Musk largely targeted Texas with his political spending, and Texas had an epic, historic blue wave. Something that has been dreamt about for decades came true in dramatic fashion despite Elon Musk spending hundreds of millions of dollars to try to stop it. Ironically, Democratic politicians are the ones who support electric vehicles and solar power, key segments of Musk’s empire. It was California, led by Democrats, that birthed Tesla Motors and enabled it to grow and develop into an industrial behemoth. It was US policies under Democratic presidents and Congresses that also provided critical help for years upon years. So, despite Elon Musk’s worst instincts and biggest efforts politically, will his businesses actually do better under the newly elected Democratic leadership? Perhaps there are some corporate issues that need reigned in or need better regulation, and perhaps people Musk brazenly and often quite rudely campaigned against will squeeze down extra hard on his corporate actions, but policymakers who support cleantech over fossil fuels should, overall, mean more good news than bad news for Tesla and its broader mission, right?

Sure, Musk threw away $474 million and lost bigly, but is he going to be better off from failing in his efforts to pick the people running his current home state and representing it in the US government? What are the actual risks he and his companies face from the people he heavily campaigned against winning their elections? What are the benefits he and Tesla will get from fossil-loving, pollution-peddling Republican politicians no longer running the show in Texas and in Congress? One has to wonder.

By the way, one of the key people Musk campaigned against, James Talarico, has a message specifically for him. “Texas is not for sale,” Talarico said. Musk spent at least $150 million to try to get Talarico’s opponent elected. “The people of Texas delivered a crystal-clear message to the world’s first trillionaire: Texas is not for sale,” Talarico added. “The power in this state, in this country, belongs to the people, and we’ve got to make sure it stays that way.” What do the people want? Well, the people want clean air, clean and cheap energy, and less money in politics. Shouldn’t all of those things help Musk? On that last one, after all, if he wasn’t allowed to pour so much money into politics, he wouldn’t have thrown away half a billion dollars.

#5688. Kimi Antonelli Won The F1 Driver's Championship On A Cracked Oil Sump

Twenty-year-old Kimi Antonelli made history on Sunday becoming the youngest Formula 1 Drivers' Champion in the history of the sport and the first Italian driver to win it since Alberto Ascari in 1953. He clinched it finishing third at last weekend's Mexico Grand Prix, sharing the podium with fellow champs and legends in their own rights, Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton, who lifted Antonelli up onto their shoulders for an F1 photo op to end all F1 photo ops.

Mathematically, Antonelli's championship win was almost a foregone conclusion at that point, but his picture-perfect victory almost didn't happen that way because it's now been revealed that his final laps in Mexico City were done in a car that was very much on its last legs. Mercedes F1 deputy team principal Bradley Lord appeared on the High Performance Racing podcast after Sunday's race and said Antonelli won it all on a cracked oil sump.

"We got the car back after the race, took the floor off the bottom — covered in oil," Lord recalled. "Sump cracked, and Kimi said he thinks about four laps from the end, he could start to feel the engine just starting to struggle. So, right on the edge of retirement of that race and yet it held together." For what it's worth, non-catastrophic engine issues were a bit of a theme for Mercedes in Mexico as Antonelli's teammate George Russell, who qualified P2, suffered a power unit "deployment problem" right at the start of the race. He lost multiple places quickly and eventually finished sixth.

Cracked sump or not, it's unlikely Antonelli would've been going ham in those final stages of his race anyway as he apparently struggled to even see through his own tears before crossing the finish line as World Champion, according to Sky Sports. In the end, he finished a little over four seconds away from second-place Hamilton, who was eight-tenths off of race winner Verstappen. The Italian driver picked up 15 points, more than enough to secure the biggest trophy in motorsport earlier in life than anybody else who'd ever done it before.

#5687. Child Dies of Measles in Wisconsin's First Such Death Since 1990

— Four measles-associated deaths confirmed by CDC this year, but states report higher numbers

An infant in southwestern Wisconsin has died after contracting measles, the state's first death from the disease in 36 years, state officials announced Thursday.

The coroner listed the cause of death as measles, state health officials said.

"My heart is broken for the family," said Kirsten Johnson, MPH, secretary of the state health department. "Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease."

The U.S. stopped the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but they have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks of the viral disease.

The CDC has confirmed four measles-associated deaths in the U.S. this year, but state health departments have reported higher numbers. In Pennsylvania alone, health officials have reported five deaths this year and are investigating a possible sixth.

As of Thursday, Wisconsin reported 431 cases of measles, all but three in unvaccinated people. Nine people had been hospitalized.

#5686. What's The Worst Road Trip You've Ever Taken?

It might be getting colder outside, but road trips aren't over for the year yet. The busiest driving days are the days around Thanksgiving and Christmas, as people travel to visit loved ones. Some might be just heading across town. Others are driving around the state, while others are traveling across the country. And while the old adage that "it's not about the destination, it's about the journey" might be true, the journey can be crummy. What's the worst road trip you've ever taken?

Plenty of things can spoil a long drive. Snow is on the way in the next few months, and that's always something to look out for, but with hurricane season winding down, you can still get caught in a torrential downpour or an early winter storm with lots of non-frozen water. Never underestimate how dangerous precipitation can be out on the road. I learned that lesson the hard way while driving across Pennsylvania before the start of a fall semester in college. It was raining so hard that I couldn't see beyond my hood. The curtain of water made visibility so poor that I had to pull over beneath an underpass for shelter.

A big part of driving for hours at a time is staying comfortable behind the wheel. When it's scorching hot outside, a good climate control system is the only thing that can keep you cool inside a car because rolling down the windows will literally just blow hot air into your face. If an issue crops up with your car's air conditioning unit, it's never an easy fix. A road trip, especially a summer one, where your air conditioning breaks can be particularly brutal. You either have to suffer through oppressive temperatures, or stop somewhere unfamiliar to get a fix — potentially delaying your trip quite a bit.

A bad road trip could be well outside the bounds of one that's got expensive repairs or uncomfortable conditions. It could be an ultra-long trip that goes exclusively past boring, endless, flat terrain with no music to keep you entertained.

You tell us what your idea of a bad road trip is by leaving the story of your worst road trip in the comment section below. Include all the aggravating details along with the pertinent information, like when and where you were driving.

#5685. What Democratic control of Congress means for healthcare in 2027

What Democratic control of Congress means for healthcare in 2027" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Tuesday’s forecast-busting blue wave puts wind in the sails of Democrats who have promised a stark departure from Trump-era healthcare policy—though whether or not the shifts will be incremental or seismic hinges on intra-party debates and the president’s veto.

As of noon Wednesday, Democrats had flipped seven seats in the Senate and 21 in the House, setting the party up for comfortable majorities as unexpected battleground races continue to be tallied.

Healthcare issues were a major talking point through many midterm election campaigns. In battleground Senate races, for instance, Democrats spent $65 million on ads primarily focused on healthcare, more than twice that of their next-most prominent topic. Healthcare was overall the second-most prominent issue featured in ads (as measured by spend) across the two parties, behind a push on taxation topics from Republicans.

And within those ads: promises to deliver lower costs, greater coverage and federal oversight, starting Jan. 1, 2027.

The immediate legislative impact will be seen in the bills new chamber leaders bring to the floor.

A health policy agenda circulated in September by a working group under Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.)—the House’s current minority leader and likely speaker in the next Congress—outlined immediate, “First 100 Hours” goals that include repeal of the Medicaid coverage and funding cuts of 2025’s H.R. 1 (the One Big Beautiful Bill Act) as well as restoration of enhanced Affordable Care Act premium tax credits that expired at the top of 2026 and vastly increased marketplace plan premiums.

Other 100-hours priorities outlined in the document include medical debt protections, removal of visa program fees for healthcare workers, an end to an AI prior authorization program in Traditional Medicare, restoration of withheld National Institutes of Health funding, a block on immigration enforcement operations in hospitals and guaranteed no-cost coverage of recommended vaccines regardless of changes in federal recommendations.

Additionally, the new majorities would install key Democratic policy heads to congressional committees responsible for advancing healthcare legislation and conducting oversight into government and private sector conduct. Among those new chairs would be Vermont’s Bernie Sanders, a vocal opponent of corporate interests in healthcare and the country’s chief Medicare for All advocate, who would chair the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee; and Oregon’s Ron Wyden, who as Finance Committee ranking member recently pursued oversight of Medicaid stakeholders, endorsed Sanders’ Medicare for All bill, led calls to hold “Big Insurance” accountable for administrative roadblocks to care and summarized his midterms reaction with a single word: “Subpoenas.”

Underpinning the party’s legislative leaders are a slew of new-to-office healthcare advocates. Several of those elected to Congress have backgrounds as physicians or other COVID-era public health experience. Among the standouts are Ohio Governor-elect Amy Acton, a pediatrician who was director of the state’s Department of Health and resigned early in the pandemic in protest of state leadership; and Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and Detroit’s former health director, who has made progressive health policy goals like Medicare for All a cornerstone of his campaign.

For the public and the healthcare industry, the key question is how Democrats will pursue their healthcare agenda under a divided government and lame-duck president.

Molly Turco, who covers healthcare policy at TD Cowen Washington Research Group, wrote in a Wednesday policy note that “with Trump in the [White House], passage of major reforms are very unlikely and even medium-sized policies, like rollbacks of Medicaid [state-directed payment] cuts or restoring ACA subsidies, are an uphill battle. But the midterm results and catalysts like the debt ceiling give Ds leverage.”

Consultants at BRG, in a media roundtable late last week, generally agreed with the veto hurdle, but noted that a stymied Congress still has room to write and pass bills that could become new policy in a future majority, as was the case with Medicaid work requirements pushed by Republicans during the end of the Biden administration but ultimately codified last year.

There is still an avenue for dealmaking between the parties, analysts and advisors noted, such as on areas with general bipartisan agreement (think this year’s pharmacy benefit manager reforms, or other major pain points like physician pay or surprise billing arbitration reform) as part of must-pass spending packages slated for this December and the coming years. The president, for his part, told outlets late Tuesday night that he intends to work with Democrats to pass bills he believes will benefit the country—while also highlighting his willingness to veto.

PricewaterhouseCoopers, in a Wednesday policy note, said “targeted bipartisan legislation is most likely to move. Look for action on cybersecurity, AI, price transparency, modernizing drug development and prior authorization processes. Regardless of congressional gridlock, continued regulatory implementation will shape near-term business and compliance requirements.”

Turco’s note predicts a dual messaging strategy for congressional Democrats on affordability and accountability, with the latter involving “an aggressive corporate investigation and hearings strategy.”

The TD Cowen analyst also questioned whether Democrats’ midterm over-performance and gains by progressive candidates will embolden the party to pursue and campaign on “bold” healthcare reforms like Medicare for All ahead of 2028.

Wyden’s recent endorsement of Sanders’ reform bill “is a powerful signal that even long-tenured moderates are under pressure to have a vision that reimagines [healthcare],” Turco wrote, though “many other D members are worried about blowback from M4A support that has almost no chance of being a viable policy. These members are vocal about their concerns and want to work on more realistic policies like restoring the ACA and Medicaid, building on IRA negotiations, reducing premiums/ deductibles for employer-based coverage, adding more benefits to Medicare, etc.”

Investment banking firm William Blair’s equity research team, in an election day brief, noted that Democratic governorships bring immediate impact to the healthcare industry as states make strategic decisions on how to implement, or offset, the provisions of H.R. 1.

The limited avenues for swiftly rolling back that sweeping bill mean that industry players, including Medicare Advantage plans and margin-strapped hospitals, should begin preparing for its financial headwinds, consultants and health systems heads have said. But that doesn’t mean Democrats’ strong night has dashed all hopes for rollbacks or other tweaks to ease the pain.

“While the election has changed who controls Congress, it doesn't change the financial challenges hospitals will face in 2027,” Chris Van Gorder, president and CEO of nonprofit integrated health system Scripps Health, said in a statement reacting to midterm election results. “Democrats won't have the votes to simply reverse major federal health care cuts over a presidential veto. But Congress is far from powerless. Lawmakers can use their oversight and budget authority to press for changes in how those cuts are carried out, protect critical health care funding where possible and work across party lines to ease the growing financial pressures on hospitals and impact on patients."

Even if political gridlock takes hold, Tuesday’s results ensure that affordability will be center stage in Washington, analysts said, especially as consumers’ cost pressures will likely persist well through the 2028 election cycle.

“Even where legislation stalls, don’t dismiss the headlines,” PwC advised healthcare executives. “Democratic hearings, investigations and proposed bills offer insight into the policies taking shape for 2028, while growing pressure around affordability continues to push the healthcare market toward consumer expectations. Executives who look beyond near-term political conflict, plan for multiple policy scenarios and adapt to evolving consumer demands will be better positioned for potential healthcare reform after 2028.”

On the virtual care front, ATA Action, the advocacy-focused affiliate of the American Telemedicine Association, said the election presents an opportunity to build on strong bipartisan support for telehealth and virtual care at the federal and state levels. The group plans to continue working across party lines to make Medicare telehealth policies permanent, expand digital health access and remove regulatory barriers to virtual care, Kyle Zebley, CEO of the ATA and Executive Director of ATA Action, said in a statement.

#5684. Latin America EV Sales Report: With Over 200,000 Units Sold in Q3, EVs Now Stand at 12% Market Share!

Through 2026, EVs have gained significant momentum all over the world (safe for the US), and Latin America has been no exception. Sales grew by almost 140% in the third quarter, and clock in at a very healthy 120% growth through 2026, bringing the yearly total to more than half a million units. If this trend continues, it’s all but certain we will surpass 700,000 units by the end of the year, and perhaps even get to 800,000.

Another interesting bit of trivia is that sales reached 220,000 units in the third quarter, not too far behind the USA’s 266,000. In theory, this means it should be possible for LatAm to surpass total US EV sales as early as Q1 2027 … though, I would be much happier if the USA’s market starts growing strongly again and thus Latin America cannot get ahead.

Now, to be fair, the US is much more BEV-heavy (242,000 units sold, vs 127,000 in LatAm), whereas Latin America prefers PHEVs to a higher degree (93,000 units sold vs 44,000 in the US), but, still, these are impressive results for a region overall much poorer than the US, and with a vehicle market around a third of the size. For over a decade, it was the richest countries in the world that led EV adoption, but — as many of us predicted on this very site — that has now changed.

As mentioned earlier, total EV sales reached 220,000 units, surpassing for the first time the 200,000 mark and growing a healthy 140% YoY, and a strong 17% from Q2. BEVs grew faster than PHEVs (146% vs 130%), and thus now represent 57.5% of all EV sales in the region, slightly below the 58% result for Q2.

Market share grew to 12%, up from 10.7% in Q2 and 5.5% in Q3 last year, a pretty strong result. This brought market share above 10% through 2026, 5.9% BEV and 4.3% PHEV.

Latin America’s overall vehicle market is growing at rates of around 10% annually, but thanks to strong EV growth, combustion-based powertrains (HEV, MHEV and ICEV) are stagnant: they fell by 3.7% last quarter, and barely grew by 3.1% this one, meaning it’s very likely that we’re reaching “Peak Combustion” in Latin America and the market will only go down from 2027 onwards.

Sales wise, we have a pretty stable list, with Brazil being the unsurprising winner, followed by Mexico and Colombia, just as in Q2. Uruguay follows, but then we have a new rising star: Ecuador, which nearly reached 5,000 BEVs sold last quarter! Costa Rica, Chile, and Argentina close the top 8 and make up all the countries with over 1.000 quarterly BEV sales.

PHEV sales are much more varied, though. Brazil, of course, leads again, but following come Mexico and Argentina, with Colombia in 4th place and Ecuador in 5th.

Market share: again, we have a pretty constant list, with the first 8 positions unchanged. Uruguay, unsurprisingly, leads the region with a very strong 50.7% EV market share (45.7% BEV), followed by Costa Rica, Colombia, Ecuador, and Brazil. Notable mention to Paraguay, the sixth country in our region to reach 10% EV market share through a quarter, but in this case thanks to PHEVs.

This has been an eventful year due to Donald’s dubious defense decisions, but even as high oil prices have been driving massive EV adoption and/or massive ICEV crashes all over the world, I feel the situation in Latin America isn’t as clear cut.

In the US and Europe, fuel prices have gone up by around 40–50%, at least in the case of gasoline. Now, prices have gone up similarly in some countries in Latin America, including Panama, Paraguay and Perú, but in many others, like Brazil, Colombia and Mexico, it has barely moved, either because of significant subsidies — direct or indirect — to maintain prices, or because it was already expensive before the war and the government did not make any adjustments to its price.

One would think that the countries most affected by high fuel prices would be at the forefront of the EV transition, but no: the largest increases in EV sales only partially track gasoline prices. For example: Panama and Perú are still lagging behind the region despite having the highest increase in the region (>50% in both cases), whereas Colombia and Brazil are sprinting ahead despite relatively stable fuel prices. What gives?

The answer, I believe, is linked to EV prices and how they compare with their ICEV competition. Yes, I know the TCO is a very important metric, but evidence in our markets point to the sticker price being the main driver of adoption. The cases of Brazil and Colombia on one hand, and Peru and Panama on the other, exemplify this very well:

Brazil and Colombia have had pretty stable fuel prices, up around 10% or less since the war started, yet both have booming markets, up 160% and 190%, respectively, with EV market share getting close to 20%. Meanwhile, Panama and Peru have seen gasoline prices spike over 50% from their pre-war costs, yet the former only showed a meager 57% growth in September, and the latter, though clocking in at a more impressive 270% YoY, remains at a disappointing 1.3% market share.

The main difference has to do with the nature of the market. In Brazil and Colombia, combustion vehicles are relatively expensive — in no small part due to tariffs to protect local industry — and EVs have effectively reached price parity with their combustion counterparts. Meanwhile, in Panama and Per,u EVs are just as cheap if not cheaper than in Brazil or Colombia, but combustion cars are significantly cheaper, with some entry-level models at or below USD$10.,00. This makes customers hesitant to try the new technologies by the simple logic that even if the EV will save a lot of money in the long run, $6,000 will buy a lot of gas.

And in Peru, this is particularly relevant insofar as gas-mobiles from Chinese brands are very popular. Changan, Jetour, Geely, and JAC together account for 20% of the Peruvian market largely thanks to their hyper-affordable combustion cars, and since the Chinese gas-mobile market is collapsing, it’s likely these brands would rather keep it like this for a few more months so they can move some of the inventory they won’t be able to sell at home before betting it all on EVs.

In general, this tracks for most markets, where EV prices compared to traditional combustion cars are probably the most relevant factor to keep track of. And of course, fuel prices do have an influence, but it seems it’s rather limited compared to, for example, what we’re seeing in Europe.

But the lessons are clear: Want to improve EV sales? Either make them cheaper, or make gas-mobiles more expensive.

At the beginning of this year, I was hopeful we would see 10% market share in the fourth quarter, normally the highest in the year. We went past that in Q2, and at 12%, we’re sitting far beyond what I considered feasible only 10 months ago.

Yet, there’s still a long path ahead. Aside from the 5 leading markets, we’re yet to see a country getting consistent BEV market share above 5%, and several large markets — Chile, Argentina, and Mexico — are still lagging. PHEVs have raised the bar in several countries, Paraguay most important of all, but we would rather see more BEVs.

This is not to be overtly pessimistic. The results so far are great, much better than we would’ve expected even a year ago. But as things improve, the bar rises, and I’m now waiting to see the moment when we will see 20% market share (Q3 2027?) or when e-truck sales will start to ramp up (2027? 2028?).

Passionate for all things Latin American, I’ve been closely following the energy and mobility transitions since they started to become present south of the equator.

#5683. Here Are All The Cool Cars Elon Musk Could Have Bought Instead Of Spending $474,000,000 On Political Ads

The midterm elections are over. If you live in a swing state like I do, you've probably been inundated with political attack ads, texts, and phone calls for the last several months. This has been the most expensive election in U.S. history, and much of the blame for that can be laid on the shoulders of the richest man in the world, and one-time Jalopnik contributor, Elon Musk. After Joe Biden spurned him in 2021, the Tesla and SpaceX CEO has become the single largest political donor in history, spending hundreds of millions of dollars in support of Republican political campaigns. According to recent reports Musk spent an incredible 474 million American greenbacks nationwide, with some $200 million of that spent supporting Ken Paxton's campaign for U.S. Senate in his adopted home state of Texas.

Megadonor Musk's efforts were all in vain as every one of the political campaigns he supported in swing states failed. With economic inequality, an incredibly unpopular war, and AI data centers among the top concerns for American voters in this election, it certainly feels like these results are a referendum on Musk himself. Musk spent the weeks leading up to the election using his social media platform Twitter to call Texas Senator Elect James Talarico a "far left extremist" when he wasn't using it to promote his AI chatbot or retweet the thoughts of vile bigots.

So, after all that, it seems the world's only trillionaire decided to throw away half a billion dollars on unelectable candidates and an extremely unpopular agenda. $474 million is a small fraction of Elon's net worth, just under half a tenth of a percent, in fact. He probably won't even notice the money is gone, but the fact remains that he could have spent that money instead on something much cooler. He could have bought 6,423 brand new base model Corvettes, for example. He could have given each of the 500 people living in SpaceX company town Starbase, Texas, 12 Corvettes as a gift.

What if he had grander ambitions than Corvettes? Let's look into it.

Back in August, if Musk had found himself at Monterey Car Week instead of pumping money into his super pacs, he could have really cleaned house and built himself a really cool collection of some of the most important cars in history. As the CEO of the world's most valuable car company, Musk must have at least some interest in cars, right? He did own a McLaren F1 at one point, for example, so maybe there is still a car guy hiding in there. Auction house RM Sotheby's recently set a record for collector car auctions in Monterey, with more money changing hands that weekend than ever had in history. The wealthy car collectors are still flush with cash and willing to spend, it seems. The sale was led by the controversial $40 million Ferrari Luce charity auction, a rare $34.655 million McLaren F1 GTR sale, and an $18.7 million 1963 Corvette Grand Sport. In total the auction pushed 199 lots across the dais and nearly half of them were million-plus sales. What was that record breaking number? $380 million, meaning Musk could have used his political contribution slush fund to buy every single one of them and still have money left over for transportation, taxes, and registration.

If Musk really wants to be as popular as it seems he is desperate to be, he could have spent the summer driving around in his new Aston Martin Valkyrie Spider, Talbot-Lago T26 Record Cabriolet, Mercer Raceabout, or Lamborghini Miura P400. The point is, he could have bought whatever he wanted, but instead of something cool or useful, what he wanted was Ken Paxton.

What if he wanted to own the most expensive collector cars of all time? For just the money he spent in Texas he could easily have bought the one-of-two Mercedes-Benz 300 SLR "Uhlenhaut Coupe" which sold in 2022 for $142,000,000. In fact, for his 2026 political campaign contributions, Musk could have also purchased the Mercedes-Benz W 196 R Stromlinienwagen ($52,960,000), a Ferrari 330 LM/250 GTO ($51,705,000), another 250 GTO ($48,405,000), a Shelby Cobra Daytona Coupe ($42,905,000), the aforementioned Ferrari Luce, and yet two more Ferrari 250 GTOs ($38,500,000 and $38,115,000 respectively). That's the top eight most expensive cars ever sold in history. Or, you know, one feckless midterm election media buy blitz. Which would you rather have?

Let's say Elon woke up one day and felt like he wanted to do something magnanimous in an effort to repair his reputation with the American people. What could he have done with his $474,000,000 political contributions that would have instead helped the average American feel better about their country and place in it? Auto loan debt is pretty bad right now, reaching some $1.7 trillion. Obviously he couldn't clear the table on every car loan, and it would be absurd to expect him to. That said, Texas has been hit harder by auto loan debt than any other state with around 10% of borrowers in the state more than 30 days behind on their payments. How much goodwill could he garner for himself and Tesla if he were to forgive all Tesla loans in the state? That might be a good start.

Half a billion dollars buys a whole lot of goodwill for a man. Maybe he could start subsidizing grocery stores in poor Texas neighborhoods. Or pushing to fund the state's unreliable and undermaintained power grid. He could set up a fund to install EV chargers in apartment complexes or on the street, further growing Tesla's potential customer base in the state. Man, there are just so many better uses of that money than attack ads claiming James Talarico isn't manly enough to represent Texas.

My biggest takeaway from this election cycle is that America's wealthiest donor is spending his tremendous wealth trying to buy politicians. Thankfully, this time anyway, it seems that the voters have rebuked that effort. It certainly should be one of the priorities of this new crop of elected representatives to remove the ability for one man to wield this much potential political power, regardless of whether it was successful or not. It seems Americans are desperate for some kind of financial relief, whether that's reducing gas prices by ending the war in Iran, combating inflation, or making healthcare affordable, rather than fighting ridiculous culture wars. While those should be major priorities for the Democrats, campaign finance reform should probably be on the docket somewhere.

Elon seems to have made himself incredibly unpopular across the last half decade simply by aligning himself with MAGA Republicans. He's going to have a long uphill battle to revamp his image. Maybe he should just disappear from public life for a decade or so. Or buy a few hundred vintage collector cars at auction and simply give them to random American car enthusiasts. Either way, he should probably stop tweeting.

#5682. Patients Want 'Deep Plane' Facelifts. Are They Actually Better?

— Plastic surgeons weigh in on different rhytidectomy techniques

Welcome to Culture Clinic, MedPage Today's collaboration with Northwell Health to offer a healthcare professional's take on the latest viral medical topics.

As elective plastic surgery procedures, including facelifts, become more popular among everyday Americans, plastic surgeons say more people come in requesting "deep plane" facelifts.

Aviva Preminger, MD, a spokesperson for the American Society of Plastic Surgeons, has experienced this in her own practice in New York City. Whereas historically patients would come in asking for a facelift, now they ask for deep plane facelifts specifically.

"I think that the deep plane facelift is really having a moment right now, especially because of social media," Preminger told MedPage Today.

Indeed, there's been ample speculation online -- including from plastic surgeons -- about Kris Jenner, guessing that she's had a deep plane facelift.

While there's more awareness about deep plane facelifts, there's also some simmering misinformation, Preminger cautioned, noting that "social media can sometimes create the impression that one technique is universally superior for everyone," which isn't the case.

Deep plane facelifts aren't new; the procedure was first described by plastic surgeon Sam Hamra, MD, in 1990. Unlike traditional superficial facelifts, deep plane facelifts go below the superficial musculoaponeurotic system, which is the fibromuscular layer that supports the facial soft tissues.

"By releasing certain retaining ligaments, the surgeon can actually mobilize and reposition the deeper tissues of the cheeks, jawline, and the lower face, with the goal being to restore a more youthful facial contour without placing too much tension on the skin," Preminger said. Essentially, the intent of this procedure is "to address the deeper structural layers of the face rather than simply tightening the skin," she added.

Both traditional and deep plane facelifts involve incisions by the ears and at the hairline, but the exact position depends on skin laxity.

Lyle Leipziger, MD, chief of plastic surgery at Northwell Health's North Shore University Hospital in Manhasset, New York, and Long Island Jewish Medical Center in New Hyde Park, New York, told MedPage Today that deep plane facelifts are most appropriate for the mid-face, but there are a lot of considerations, like skin texture and tone, how a patient looked when they were younger, and how their face has sagged with age.

Because deep plane facelifts involve both tightening and repositioning, the results should be long-lasting. But Leipziger emphasized that one technique isn't superior to the other; it's a matter of choosing the appropriate strategy for a patient's facial structure and aesthetic goals.

Both traditional and deep plane facelifts should have longevity, he noted, but a consultation with an experienced surgeon is vital. That way, the surgeon can have an open conversation with the patient setting realistic expectations.

"You shouldn't choose a facelift based on the name of the technique alone," Leipziger said. "The technique really should be tailored to the face and not the other way around."

Depending on a patient's goals, Preminger said that it's not uncommon for surgeons to combine facelifts with other facial procedures. It used to be the case that patients were told to expect their facelift to last about 10 years, she added, but plastic surgery has improved greatly. Patients' genetics, sun exposure, and weight loss all impact the longevity of results, but patients now have access to non-surgical maintenance, like laser resurfacing, botulinum toxin (Botox), and filler, which add to the procedure's longevity.

Preminger said that facelifts aren't particularly painful, but innovation in the plastic surgery space still makes for better experiences. She noted that tranexamic acid can help reduce bruising, hemostatic nets can help reduce swelling and avoid the use of drains, and suzetrigine (Journavx) is a non-narcotic working well for post-op pain control.

More than anything, this trend reflects a broader cultural shift where plastic surgery is no longer thought of as a luxury only for the rich and famous but as an option for anyone willing to pay for it, surgeons said.

#5681. CommonSpirit Health signs definitive agreement to sell 3 more N.D. hospitals to Altru Health System

CommonSpirit Health signs definitive agreement to sell 3 more N.D. hospitals to Altru Health System" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

CommonSpirit Health has locked in a deal to sell three hospitals to Altru Health System, a rural North Dakota nonprofit.

The deal is contingent on regulatory review and other customary closing conditions, but is expected to close in early 2027. The pair's new definitive agreement, announced Wednesday, follows 10 months of due diligence following a letter of intent unveiled near the top of the year (see that story below). Financial details were not disclosed.

The to-be-sold facilities are CHI St. Alexius Health Bismarck, a multispecialty acute care medical center in the state’s capital, and two smaller critical access hospitals, CHI St. Alexius Health Turtle Lake and CHI St. Alexius Health Garrison.

They would join Altru's flagship acute care hospital, a critical access hospital it also purchased from CommonSpirit in March, a trauma center, a specialty hospital and 20 practices spread across northern North Dakota.

The organizations said there are no changes to patient care or day-to-day operations related to the deal. The hospitals will maintain their Catholic identity and mission.

"Through our work together over the years, we’ve developed tremendous confidence in Altru’s commitment to high-quality, compassionate care," Tim Bricker, president of CommonSpirit Health's Central Region, said in reference to prior partnerships with the health system. "We believe Altru is the right partner to build on St. Alexius’ proud legacy, honor its Catholic mission and continue serving patients and families for generations to come.”

CommonSpirit is in the midst of a sweeping operational overhaul as it looks to bolster its financial performance ahead of imminent Medicaid cuts. Those efforts have opened the $42.4 billion system to a string of hospital divestitures, including its four handoffs to Altru as well as the sale of a four-hospital Ohio system to UPMC in September.

CommonSpirit Health and Altru Health System are considering a deal to transfer three North Dakota hospitals to the latter, the organizations announced Thursday.

The pair’s signed letter of intent outlines plans to evaluate a potential deal for the facilities, a process they said would run “the next several months” before a potential definitive agreement might be struck.

In the balance are CHI St. Alexius Health Bismarck, a multispecialty acute care medical center in the state’s capital, and two smaller critical access hospitals, CHI St. Alexius Health Turtle Lake and CHI St. Alexius Health Garrison. All three are Catholic facilities within CommonSpirit’s regional healthcare system CHI St. Alexius Health.

Potential financial terms of any deal for the hospitals were not disclosed, nor were any details on whether other assets tied to the hospitals, such as clinics, would be included.

“This is a natural next step in exploring how we can continue to support strong, sustainable healthcare for the region,” Tim Bricker, president of CommonSpirit Health’s central region, which includes CHI St. Alexius Health, said in the announcement.

CommonSpirit is a $40 billion nonprofit that counted 137 hospitals in two dozen states. It’s in the midst of an operating performance turnaround initiative and, at this month’s J.P. Morgan Healthcare Conference, teased “a couple” of portfolio divestitures to be announced in the next quarter as part of the effort.

Grand Forks, North Dakota-based Altru Health System is a smaller nonprofit, with just over $700 million of revenue in 2024 from its sole acute care hospital, a specialty hospital and 20 practice locations in northeast North Dakota and northwest Minnesota. It opened a new $500 million hospital in January 2025.

The news comes hot on the heels of another deal between the systems for ownership of CHI St. Alexius Health Devils Lake, another critical access hospital. That handoff was unveiled in December and is set to close March 1.

Both deals have been described as a boon for rural communities and an opportunity for Altru to better coordinate its local care.

“Altru has a long history of serving communities across North Dakota and northwest Minnesota, and our organizations share a deep respect for the people we serve and the responsibility that comes with delivering local healthcare,” Todd Forkel, CEO of Altru, said in the announcement. “We look forward to working more closely with CommonSpirit to strengthen access to care for patients and families well into the future.”

#5680. The US Midterm Election Results Remind Us To Focus On The “Foundation Of Our Democracy”

The country feels different as the US midterm election results come rolling in. When all of the votes are counted, Democrats are set to win the national popular vote in all House races by about 13 percentage points. The voters have spoken in huge numbers: they want leaders who make everyday life a little bit easier.

Now the politicians must answer, and, essentially, they need to design policies that lower costs for ordinary people in the US. It’s not about revenge: revenge is too distinct from US consumers’ lived experiences.

Paul Krugman, the Nobel Prize-winning economist, says that one of the main things “Democrats need to do now is hold not just Trump’s officials, but also his enablers, accountable.” Representative Robert Garcia of California posted on social media in the same vein: “Lawyer Up” to the MAGA losers.

No, that’s playground antics. Instead, the next two years must demonstrate a willingness to listen to US citizens as each family struggles to make ends meet with groceries, household utilities, healthcare, and other daily costs.

Roy Cooper’s Senate campaign in North Carolina had a mantra that permeated every stop on his statewide tour: Make Stuff Cost Less.

James Talarico, Jon Ossoff, Roy Cooper, among others, grounded their campaigns in economic populist agendas. They harangued against President Trump’s economic record and called out corruption for what it is — self-promotion over the interest of US citizens.

Georgia’s Senator-elect Jon Ossoff made Trump’s assault on the rule of law practical. In everyday terms he pointed out to voters how democracy and economic distress depend on each other. He argued that “corruption is why nothing works for ordinary people.”

We are ready as a nation to reintroduce the importance of science to accomplish these goals.

In a recent commentary in the journal, Nature, a group of authors argue that “science is an essential backbone of democracy.” Science as a source of discovery, expertise, and innovation is intertwined, they continue, with democracy as a set of institutions, rules, and procedures. They put forward three pillars through which science enables democracy:

Citizens have legitimate concerns, the scientists agree, “about economic restructuring, regional inequities, how migration is governed, technological changes, ageing populations, climate risks and geopolitical instability.” Then again, “expertise strengthens democratic legitimacy when it is transparent, diverse, independent and open to scrutiny — as prescribed by the rules of science.”

Democracy — when it lives up to its responsibility as the rule of law — contributes to a decrease in CO2 emissions. Climate change, like voting in a democracy, is a collective action problem — a conflict between the individual interest and the group interest.

Congress can look ahead and back science-based clean energy in a variety of ways, from policies to investment, all of which will address the affordability crisis, improve public health, and protect the environment, says Gretchen Colman, president of the Union of Concerned Scientists. That will include renewables and clean transportation, modernizing the power grid, protecting our air and water, and more.

Science-based legislating, Colman continues, must be based “on facts and evidence, not political whims. We’ll petition Congress to restore funding for science, protect federal science agencies, and re-establish safeguards for federal scientists to carry out their work and communicate about it free from political interference.”

A national return to scientific reasoning is underway. Gina Hinojosa, elected as the first Texas Democratic governor, has called for an immediate moratorium on data center development. She has accused developers of “raising our utility rates and depleting our water.” As reported on Bloomberg Green, she’s vowed to halt approvals until “a legislative session that puts Texans first so that we don’t have any more communities in Texas who are powerless against these global corporations.”

Indeed, the output of data centers must also be questioned. Few AI-generated findings are peer-reviewed or tested in laboratories. Talk about mixed messages! We return to a nostalgic past by foregrounding large language models that are programmed to present particular, narrow, and self-serving points of view — generally by billionaires seeking to protect their wealth. It’s time to tax these rare individuals accordingly, eliminate any incentives for their built structures, and require them to provide major renewable energy contributions to communities that house them.

Yes, energy plays an increasingly important role in today’s world. Instead of treating electrification as an option to move us toward decarbonization, it’s time to see it is essential — we need to electrify everything quickly. In the US, more than 60 state and local governments are similarly in court to seek damages from oil companies. These are the lawsuits that Democrats in Congress should be pursuing as complements to transitioning virtually all building, transportation, and industrial systems to electric. This means subsidizing heat pumps and EVs and solar panels and home battery storage — subsidies are far cheaper than funding wars for oil.

The ground-breaking election events have hoisted non-traditional candidates to levels of power and influence, as the New York Times chronicles:

Political analyst Chris Armitrage suggests another important positive trend. “The thing that lasts past January 2027 is the voter who had never voted in a midterm, did it in 2026, and now has the habit,” he concludes.

The urgency of climate change has brought democracy to a critical moment in time. Whether longtime, non-traditional, or new voters, we must continue to argue for inclusive and participatory democracy to address climate change. Shaped by democratic governance, a robust civil society, and innovative advocacy strategies, collective climate action can be a force for the right to a healthy planet.

#5679. The Most Expensive Ford Fathom Will Still Cost Under $40,000

Good morning! It's Thursday, November 5, 2026, and this is The Morning Shift, your daily roundup of the top automotive headlines from around the world, in one place. This is where you'll find the most important stories that are shaping the way Americans drive and get around.

In this morning's edition, we get a better understanding of how much the upcoming Ford Fathom EV will cost, Canada is refusing to back down on its trade dispute with the U.S., Toyota is posting monster numbers and Stellantis is keeping Fiat 500 production paused for another week.

If you'd like a recap of the latest auto news sent to your inbox each weekday, you can sign up for Jalopnik's free Morning Shift newsletter here.

We've known the Ford Fathom's $29,945 starting price for some time now, but we're finally getting an idea of where the mid-size electric pickup will top out at, and it sounds like it could be a real value proposition. Ford is still on track to launch Fathom pre-orders in the first quarter of 2027, according to Andrew Frick, Ford Blue and Model e President. When those preorders do start, they'll top out in the "high $30,000 range," and there will be a "couple different offerings within that."

Frick says the Blue Oval has seen prices for new battery-electric vehicles in the U.S. rise by about 10% in the past couple of years, and that has pushed many new EVs outside of the "affordable" price point for a lot of shoppers. From the Detroit Free Press:

"It's not just the EV market, it's actually opening us op to a massive total addressable market," Frick said. "If you know that nearly 50% of the U.S. new vehicle industry transacts under $40,000, not only do we expect Fathom... to attract new and used EV buyers, but also (gasoline) and hybrid customers, especially because we're going to ahve much lower operating costs than even a mainstream hybrid vehicle."

He declined to add further details at the moment other than to say Ford would add an affordable advanced electrical architecture and offer a digital camera dashboard.

[Ford CEO Jim] Farley then said, "I won't go into all the detials Andrew said, but the digital suite, including the embedded Apple Maps, is really a game changer.... let alone at this price. For me personally, that is going to be the most exciting upset opportunity. It's really the long-term subscription and digital experieence for the customer."

Of course, there are now two things Ford must prove: 1) It can actually build the Fathom on time without having it recalled a million times a week. So far this year it has issued 84 separate recalls — 43 more than second-place Stellantis. 2) It can actually see the Fathom for the prices it has mentioned for at least some amount of time. As we all remember, the Maverick once started under $20,000. Now, a base 2027 May will set you back $29,990, including destination.

A senior Canadian cabinet minister said the results of Tuesday's midterm elections weren't going to change Ottawa's stance toward trade talks with the U.S., adding that he would soon be speaking with his American counterparts. The rising costs of goods brought on by President Trump's trade wars with various countries played a huge role in the thorough drubbing Republicans took earlier this week. From Reuters:

Dominic LeBlanc, the ​minister in charge of US trade ties, ​said "to a certain extent last night's results are interesting, but ‌they ⁠will not have any significant impact in terms of our government's focus and work."

LeBlanc told reporters that he planned to speak ​to US ​Commerce Secretary ⁠Howard Lutnick and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer over the next few ​days.

Trump said on Tuesday the ​United ⁠States was close to making a trade deal with Canada, but Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said ⁠work ​remained to be done ​and that Washington had dropped some demands.

It'll be interesting to see if the results of the election have changed Trump's tune on trade with Canada or if he'll now double down. After all, he's got literally nothing to lose at this point, so he could harden his position, taking us all down with him in the process. That's a fun thought, isn't it?

Toyota might have just posted its third-straight month of sales declines, but it's still raising its annual earnings forecast thanks to a weaker yen and cost cuts that boosted quarterly operating profits. CFO Yoichi Miyazaki gave more encouraging news — for shareholders, at least — saying there was further room for cost reduction, as well.

All of this is to say that operating profits climbed 34% to about $7.1 billion, and revenue was up 8.6% to about $85 billion. This good news comes despite everything going on in the Middle East right now. Toyota worked hard to mitigate those effects and others, even here in the U.S. From The Wall Street Journal:

The Japanese automaker has taken measures to mitigate the impact of disruptions caused by the Iran war, such as establishing alternative routes to shorten the time it takes to deliver vehicles to customers in the Middle East.

The carmaker has also implemented steps to expand production capacity in the U.S., after it announced a plan last November to invest up to $10 billion in the country over the next five years.

Toyota in July said it would spend $3.6 billion to bring production of its top-selling midsize pickup, the Tacoma, back to the U.S. by 2030. The company plans to build a second assembly line for the Tacoma at its San Antonio plant. Toyota currently builds the Tacoma in Mexico.

The Japanese carmaker, like many of its rivals, has been hit by the Trump administration's tariffs. Making more vehicles in the U.S. will help Toyota, the world's top-selling automaker, defray a hefty tariff bill in its largest market.

Because of the weaker yen, shipments have become more competitive abroad, according to WSJ. It also has the effect of boosting the value of profits earned overseas in yen terms. The currency has depreciated 28% against the dollar over the past five years, and it's not like the dollar is doing that hot itself.

Fiat's production is a mess right now. Its owner, Stellantis, is extending the current stoppage at its 500 plant in Turin, Italy, for the whole of next week because of a semiconductor chip shortage, according to both the automaker and the FIOM trade union. If it can't finish the engine control unit, it can't finish the car. It's more bad news for a company just looking to make money where it can at this point. From Reuters:

The November 9-13 ​extension marks the fourth consecutive week ⁠of no production at the historic ​Mirafiori plant.

Union officials have pointed at weak demand for the Fiat 500 city car as ​the continuing ​reason ⁠for the stoppage.

Gianni Mannori of the FIOM metalworkers' union said ​that blaming the shortage of ​components ⁠was "an alibi."

Last week Stellantis said the shortage in engine control units was causing "significant" ⁠disruption ​to the Italian production ​of the Fiat 500 and Fiat Pandina models.

The first two weeks of the shutdown apparently were not caused by this chip shortage. Instead, Stellantis blamed weak demand. It's certainly curious timing as to why this chip shortage would pop up all of a sudden. How convenient.

#5678. These Are The Recessionmobiles You Want Automakers To Build

Folks, it sure feels like we're trapped in the belly of a terrible machine and the machine is bleeding to death. The AI bubble threatens to pop and take the global economy with it, war with Iran is unending, we've heard it all before — the old world dying, the new one struggling to be born, yadda yadda. But even in the worst of times, we've all got to go to work and buy our groceries and take the kids to school, so we need cars that can ferry us through the time of monsters.

That's why, earlier this week, I asked you all what recessionmobiles automakers should build to get us through the next once-in-a-lifetime global financial crisis. Your answers took inspiration from all sorts of sections of the automotive world, from the oil embargo of the '70s to the very modern segment of electrically aided micro mobility. Let's dive in and see what you suggested.

Midsize sedans that start in the low $20s and end around $30 fully loaded. In a lot of trim levels, with manual transmissions and optional "big" engines that can be paired with those manuals as well. Wagon versions, coupe versions, AWD for those who want to pay an extra $1k. I miss the golden era of the family sedan from '00-'10.

We're already seeing it; e-bikes and e-scooters. Once we're all unemployed, and fuel goes to $8/gallon, it will be the only way we can afford to get around.

A recession coinciding with high fuel prices, or a possible physical shortage of fuel? The smallest and most efficient vehicles possible.

It's say just take the physically smaller half of every manufacturer's current lineup and add an actual base model trim that does away with the infotainment system, every ADAS feature, and leather/fake-leather seats, etc. Probably would've trim off much from the MSRP, but at least then there might be some new cars I'd actually consider buying.

"Automakers should sell me a Slate, but for more money" is certainly a unique take.

Chevy: Waving their hands around pointing at the Bolt which starts at 28k before incentives and seats four comfortably, with hatchback versatility and lifestyle-suggestive crossover styling, impervious to oil price swings caused by various international conflicts

I think that the rest of the world should be building cheap EVs, saving a ton of money on fuel, and being extremely demonstrative about it.

Every domestic manufacturer should offer basic subcompact 2-door and compact 4-door cars with a non-turbo 3 or 4 cylinder manual transmissions and a compact regular-cab 3 or 4-cylinder pickup truck and price them at $15,000 or below.

Imagine the possibilities if there was that much competition in the compact car and truck market. People say small cars and trucks don't sell in America, but they will if they're priced correctly.

2 words, Light and Cheap. Make something that doesn't weigh 2 tons to start. Bring back 4 cylinder non turbo cars that don't need 300+hp just to get up to highway speed. As others have said, the Maverick and Slate have shown there's a market for basic transportation. We need a modern Model T, not another Expedition.

Budget sub-brands. GM had Saturn, and Toyota had Scion. Toyota could take advantage of economies of scale to resurrect Scion as a budget-friendly, hybrid only brand. Use the Prius and Camry platforms and put quirky, boxy bodies on them for maximum utility.

#5677. Because Women: Rethinking What Freedom of Movement Can Feel Like

Most women know the unspoken checklist before getting into a car. They consider their surroundings, decide whether to chat or pretend to be on a phone call, and send a quick text to a friend with their live location, just in case. Getting from one place to another is rarely just a matter of distance; it comes with a quiet, constant layer of preparation and mental energy.

At Waymo, we believe women should get that energy back.

Our new film looks at what happens when the stress is taken out of the journey. Waymo allows our riders to take a work call, sit in total silence, or play music as loud as they want. We’re offering a space entirely on our riders’ own terms.

Riders are sharing that this shift matters. Our data shows that over half of women riders across established service markets reported that Waymo improves their sense of personal safety. Having a space where riders are in control of their environment makes a real difference.

To share this story, we were proud to partner with a women-led creative and production crew. The film was directed by Mollie Mills, with cinematography by Autumn Durald, and brought to life by executive producer Onye Anyanwu, editor Mah Ferraz, and music producer Shakari “Trakgirl” L.

How people move through the world is deeply personal. Women’s experiences and perspectives are an important part of how we think about the rider experience, including the value of having more choice, comfort and confidence when traveling.

Because having more choice in how we get around matters.

By Suzanne Philion, Chief Marketing Officer, Waymo

— News and commentary from the world of gastroenterology and hepatology

More than 264 million people globally had gallbladder and biliary diseases such as cholelithiasis, cholecystitis, or cholangitis in 2023, with the diseases together contributing to over 146,000 deaths. (Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology)

Are non-invasive tests in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease ready for prime time? (The Lancet)

A case study detailed the successful gene correction of a 66-year-old man with severe alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, a congenital metabolic disorder that leads to liver damage via accumulation of misfolded protein. (Journal of Hepatology)

Global liver societies including the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) issued consensus definitions for acute-on-chronic liver failure. (Hepatology)

Speaking of AASLD, Hepatology introduced the group's 78th president: Michael Ronan Lucey, MD, of the University of Wisconsin in Madison.

Less than a fourth of Medicaid beneficiaries with hepatitis C received treatment within 6 months of testing, an HHS Office of Inspector General report found.

Experts issued recommendations for managing small intestinal bacterial overgrowth in pediatric short bowel syndrome and reviewed the diagnosis and management of acute cholangitis and idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury. (JAMA Network Open, JAMA Surgery, JAMA)

Can certain gastrointestinal and psychological symptom profiles in irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) predict response to low-dose amitriptyline? (Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology)

Researchers from Norway linked inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) diagnoses with an increased risk of needing work disability benefits. (Inflammatory Bowel Diseases)

JAK inhibitors were associated with a higher risk of serious infections versus anti-interleukin (IL)-23 or -IL-12/23 blockers in older patients with immune-mediated diseases including IBD. (Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology)

Real-world data in ulcerative colitis showed higher clinical remission rates with ustekinumab (Stelara) as first- or second-line therapy compared with TNF inhibitors or vedolizumab (Entyvio), while upadacitinib (Rinvoq) had the highest rates in patients previously exposed to biologics. (Inflammatory Bowel Diseases)

In patients who underwent endoscopic mucosal resections for large colorectal polyps, rectal lesions were linked to a higher likelihood of invasive cancer and recurrence compared with colonic lesions, a retrospective cohort study from Poland found. (Gut)

Meanwhile, the level of risk for post-operative metachronous advanced colorectal neoplasia in early-onset colorectal cancer doesn't support increased surveillance efforts in this patient population, according to research in the American Journal of Gastroenterology.

#5675. Chutes & Ladders—UHC names individual MA leader; HATCo CEO steps down

Chutes & Ladders—UHC names individual MA leader; HATCo CEO steps down" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Welcome to this week's Chutes & Ladders, our roundup of hirings, firings and retirings throughout the industry. Please submit the good news—or the bad—from your shop, and we will feature it here each week.

> UnitedHealthcare has named Suha Assi as CEO of individual Medicare Advantage, per a LinkedIn post.

Assi previously spent nearly a decade as executive director for Medicare and Retirement in Tennessee, and she previously held roles based in the state for Cigna. She wrote in the post that the "relationships with our teams, providers and communities have shaped how I think about this business and, most importantly, the people we serve."

"As I step into this national role, I’m excited about what’s ahead for Medicare Advantage," she wrote. "I look forward to working alongside teams and provider partners across the country to modernize how we work together, strengthen relationships, and find new ways to deliver for our members."

> Daryl Tol, president and CEO of General Catalyst's Health Assurance Transformation Company (HATCo) is stepping down from the role, the venture capital firm's CEO Hemant Taneja shared Tuesday.

Tol had been with the firm for about four and a half years in the wake of his time as president and CEO of AdventHealth's Central Florida Division. During that time, he headed HATCo's partner and advisory network—helping grow it to nearly 40 providers, payers and other portfolio companies—and took the company's top spot partway through 2025. Of note, he helped HATCo close its acquisition of regional health system Summa Health and served as its interim CEO for much of the past year until the appointment of Jennifer Eslinger last month.

Tol is being succeeded by Reva Nohria, a founding member of the HATCo team who has been with General Catalyst since 2018. Taneja, in his announcement, said her work at both organizations has encompassed investment, company creation and strategic partnership, and that she will continue as an investor at the venture capital firm alongside her new appointment.

Tol will support a smooth leadership transition and remain in an advisory role, a representative of General Catalyst told Fierce Healthcare.

> Jennifer Shuford, M.D., is leaving her post as deputy director and chief medical officer of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Nov. 12, just four months after joining, according to a Washington Post report that was confirmed by the agency on Tuesday.

The agency told press in a statement that Shuford was departing "to spend more time with family." Her appointment was announced by President Donald Trump in April, and she joined in June.

Shuford is an infectious disease specialist who came to the federal stage from a role as commissioner of the Texas Department of State Health Services and before that, served as the state's chief epidemiologist. Notably, she was credited with heading Texas' response to a measles outbreak last year. Her departure comes as the CDC clashes with state health departments and other public health leaders over its response to a growing national measles outbreak.

Satish Pillai, M.D., is slated to fill the role in the interim as the agency seeks a replacement, the CDC said.

> Johns Hopkins Health System CEO Kevin Sowers is set to retire at the end of 2027.

Sowers has served as president and CEO of the Johns Hopkins system since 2018. He also previously spent more than 32 years as a leader within the Duke University Health System, including eight as CEO of Duke University Hospital.

The early announcement of his retirement plans gives Johns Hopkins significant time to conduct a search for a successor, with Theodore DeWeese, dean of the medical faculty and CEO of Johns Hopkins Medicine, leading the charge. Sowers will become a strategic adviser to Johns Hopkins to support the transition, the health system said.

"When I joined Johns Hopkins Medicine in 2018, I made a commitment to the organization and to myself to give 10 years of everything I had to this extraordinary place—to the talented, dedicated people who work here, and the people and communities we serve. And I intend to keep that commitment," Sowers said in a video message.

> Calley Means, a prominent senior advisor to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. closely aligned with the Make America Healthy Again Movement, resigned from his role on Thursday.

The resignation was reported by the Wall Street Journal and confirmed by Means on social media.

Media reports from the past several months described Means' frustrations seeing MAHA policy priorities delayed or blunted by others in the administration, with the journal citing sources describing him as "disillusioned." Still, his time advising the secretary notched several wins for the movement, including overhauled dietary guidelines, steps toward greater food ingredient transparency and loosened restrictions on psychedelics as potential medical treatments.

Means wrote in his confirmation post that he still holds "tremendous respect for President Trump and Bobby Kennedy" in their battles against "the entrenched, dark forces in D.C. that profit from Americans getting sick."

"More policy and cultural change has happened around these goals in the past two years than any time in history—and I know this movement is just getting started," he wrote.

> Premier Health, a five-hospital nonprofit academic system in Southwest Ohio, has appointed Rosanna Morris as its upcoming president and CEO, effective in the first quarter of 2027.

Morris is currently executive vice president and chief clinical operating officer at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, and was previously president of Beaumont Hospital-Royal Oak. She is a registered nurse by training and has more than 27 years of health leadership.

She takes over for the retiring Michael Riordan, who has led Premier Health for about half a decade. During that period, he's credited, by the system's board, with stabilizing the system's finances.

> Centivo has added two leaders to its C-suite, the health plan announced.

Lisa Bielamowicz, M.D., will join the company as chief health officer, while James Parr will step into the role of chief commercial officer. Both are veteran healthcare leaders, Centivo said.

Bielamowicz has a long career as a physician and health system consultant, and will take on the chief health officer title after advising Centivo's board of directors.

Parr has previously served as a senior adviser to employers at Lockton as well as senior vice president and head of sales at Collective Health. Parr has also held leadership roles at Cigna, per the announcement.

"There are few leaders in healthcare who have the health benefits strategy knowledge and have built the strong relationships that Lisa and James bring to Centivo," said Ashok Subramanian, co-founder and CEO of Centivo, in the announcement. "These new leaders put Centivo in a strong position as we launch in new markets and help more employers across the country tackle rising healthcare costs and restore affordability by rethinking their healthcare benefits strategy."

> Inspira Health CEO Amy Mansue will be retiring at the end of the year, and will be succeeded by current President and Chief Operating Officer Warren Moore, the four-hospital South Jersey system announced this week.

Mansue will have been at the helm for six years, and is credited by the organization for expanding local care access and championing a culture of wellness among its 7,800-person workforce.

Moore has led Inspira's operations since 2021 and was promoted to president at the top of this year. He has 35 years of industry experience and will most immediately prioritize the opening of a new hospital tower and building upon the system's recent Epic launch.

“Leading Inspira has been one of the great privileges of my career,” Mansue said in the announcement. “I’m proud of what our team has accomplished and grateful for the trust of our communities. After working alongside Warren for many years, I know his ability to bring people together, navigate complex challenges and understand what our patients and neighbors count on us to deliver. I have every confidence in his leadership of Inspira’s next chapter.”

> Joint Commission has named Ken Grubbs as its chief operating officer, effective Jan. 1.

Grubbs is the first nurse to serve as COO of Joint Commission Enterprise in organization’s history, according to the Oct. 13 announcement. He currently serves as the organization's chief nursing executive and executive vice president of Accreditation and Certification Operations.

He will succeed James Merlino, M.D., who will take over as the organization's president and CEO this coming January.

> Beth Israel Lahey Health's national leadership search has yielded Peter Shorett as its next president and CEO. His appointment takes effect this coming January.

Shorett is currently the system's senior executive vice president and chief operating officer, and played a role bringing together its Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute for an upcoming strategic collaboration for cancer care. Prior to joining in 2019, he was a senior partner at Chartis.

He'll be taking over for Kevin Tabb, M.D., who in March gave notice to the system's board that he plans to step down after this year. He'd the role at Beth Israel Deaconess since 2011 and guided the organization through its 2019 merger with Lahey Health.

> WellSpan's Board of Directors has named Laureen Driscoll as the Pennsylvania-based system's new president and CEO.

The executive and registered nurse's appointment will go into effect Jan. 4, 2027. She takes over for Roxanna Gapstur, Ph.D., who announced plans to retire this past spring.

Driscoll is joining the 12-hospital, $4.7 billion nonprofit from Providence, where she currently serves as chief executive for its south division and oversees 17 hospitals with $10.3 billion of net operating revenue. Prior to that she held roles at MultiCare Health System, Swedish Health System, Le Bonheur Children's Medical Center and Maine Medical Center.

“She has led complex health systems through transformation while strengthening quality, culture, access and performance," Board Chair Joe Crosswhite said in the announcement. "Just as important, she leads with purpose and understands that listening to team members, clinicians and communities is essential. The Board is confident Laureen is the right leader for WellSpan’s next chapter.”

> UnitedHealthcare has elevated Bobby Hunter to the role of president at the insurer.

Hunter wrote in a LinkedIn post that in the new position he will be tasked with leading the charge on the company's modernization efforts, including investments in technology and other initiatives to simplify the healthcare experience for its members.

Hunter most recently served as CEO of Government Programs at UnitedHealthcare, and has held multiple leadership roles at the insurer dating back to 2011.

"The future we're working toward is one where plans and providers work together more seamlessly, information flows instantly, trust is earned through transparency and accountability, and care teams are able to spend more time focused on patients," he wrote in the post. "To get there, we must continue to deliver on the commitments we make to the people, providers, customers, and communities who count on us every day."

> Jonathan B. Perlin, M.D., Ph.D., will retire from his roles as president and CEO of accrediting organization Joint Commission on Dec. 31. Current Chief Operating Officer James I. Merlino, M.D., is slated to succeed him.

Perlin boasted three decades of healthcare executive leadership across his career, which included five at the top of Joint Commission. During that period he oversaw a substantial reduction on Joint Commission standards deemed to be burdensome or obsolete, and programs to support healthcare safety issues in low- and middle-income countries. Titles preceding his time at the organization included president of clinical operations and chief medical officer for HCA Healthcare, and the U.S. Department of Veteran's Affairs' under secretary for health.

Perlin will remain a strategic advisor to the group following his retirement, holding the title of president emeritus.

Merlino's career included leadership roles at Cleveland Clinic such as chief clinical transformation officer and chief experience officer, as well as at healthcare performance improvement company Press Ganey.

> Robert C. Garrett, CEO of Hackensack Meridian Health, will retire next year after decades with the organization, including its formative 2016 merger.

Garrett is set to step down on June 30, upon which time he'll hold the role of CEO emeritus for a year to help ease the transition. The 18-hospital, nearly $10 billion nonprofit said it plans to announce his successor before the year's end.

Garrett began his career in the early 1980s at Hackensack University Medical Center, and in 2009 was named president and CEO of Hackensack University Health Network. When the organization merged with Meridian Health in 2016 to form New Jersey's largest health system, he served as co-CEO for two years before taking on the solo mantle.

Alongside the organization's growth to more than 500 patient care locations, Garrett's tenure also marked the opening of the Hackensack Meridian School of Medicine, New Jersey's first new medical school in decades.

"Bob has been the driving force behind HMH's unprecedented growth and transformation, its superior quality, innovation and commitment to building an exceptional workforce," Board Chair Keith Banks said in a statement. "At the heart of Bob's legacy is his unwavering belief that we must deliver the most innovative and compassionate care to all patients. HMH is solidly positioned for continued growth, and we are profoundly grateful to Bob and extend our warmest wishes to him for this well-deserved next chapter."

> The Pharmaceutical Care Management Association, the leading lobbying group for the pharmacy benefit management industry, has named CVS Health executive Ed DeVaney as its board chair.

DeVaney currently serves as president of CVS Caremark, one of the PBM industry's "Big Three" firms. He succeeds Adam Kautzner, president of Express Scripts and Evernorth Health Services, representing one of the other "Big Three" companies.

“The role PBMs play in lowering costs and improving access to prescription drugs for Americans is critically important,” DeVaney said in the announcement. “As Board Chair, I’m committed to ensuring PCMA shares our story with policymakers, consumers and employers so they have a full understanding of the work we do to fulfill our commitment to lower drug costs.”

> UnitedHealth Group has elevated Dan Kueter to serve as the company's chief commercial officer, per a LinkedIn post.

Kueter previously served as the CEO of UnitedHealthcare's commercial business for four years. UHC is the health insurance arm of UnitedHealth Group.

In the new role, Kueter will be tasked with working across both UnitedHealthcare and Optum to support coordination in product development and innovation, he wrote in the post. He said he will also collaborate closely with other senior leaders at the UnitedHealth Group level.

"I'm looking forward to working across the company with colleagues at Optum and UnitedHealthcare to help drive our next chapter of growth and innovation, focused on helping make healthcare work better for everyone," Kueter wrote.
