> Highmark Health has tapped former UnitedHealth Group executive Heather Cianfrocco as its new chief operating officer.

In her time at UHG, Cianfrocco held multiple key leadership positions, including serving as CEO of Optum where she helmed its three core business lines: Optum Rx, Optum Health and Optum Insight. She was most recently the healthcare giant's executive vice president of governance, compliance and information security.

She announced her departure from UnitedHealth in March.

"We have boldly said that we want to be one of the organizations that solves the complex and fragmented health care system," said David Holmberg, Highmark Health CEO, in the announcement. "Heather is a seasoned, innovative health care leader who has a broad national lens, and her skills will be critical as we strive to further expand the reach of our mission and accelerate the work we are doing to transform our industry."

Highmark President Karen Hanlon will continue to lead the company's Living Health initiative, per the announcement.

> Emad Rizk will join Premier, Inc. as its new president and CEO, the company announced.

Rizk, M.D., comes to Premier from healthcare analytics company Cotiviti, where he also served as president and CEO. In the new role, Rizk will be tasked with continuing to drive Premier forward as it seeks to support better patient outcomes at a lower cost.

“I’ve seen healthcare from every angle, and I know what is at stake for Premier’s members,” said Rizk in the announcement. “Providers are being asked to do more with less in an environment that is only getting more complex. Premier has the scale, the data and the relationships to help providers make better decisions and deliver better outcomes. This is where we can make the greatest impact.”

> Alexander Billioux, M.D., is joining the executive team at Cityblock as chief health officer.

Billioux spent the last five years at UnitedHealthcare, where he most recently served as chief medical officer for government programs. He also held leadership roles at the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation and the Louisiana Office of Public Health.

In his new role, Billioux will spearhead Cityblock's clinical strategy and care operations as the company looks to continue advancing its care model.

"I've always been passionate about ensuring that the opportunity for quality healthcare is accessible for all populations. For a large part of my career, that has meant supporting members who face increasing financial and social challenges," Billioux said in the announcement. "Joining Cityblock allows me the opportunity to leverage ground-breaking technology to empower teams to deliver high-quality, comprehensive care that improves the health of vulnerable members."

> Blue Shield of California has named Hayley Park as its new senior vice president and chief pharmacy officer.

In the role, Park will lead the charge on Blue Shield's Pharmacy Care Reimagined initiative, which eschews traditional pharmacy benefit management models for an "unbundled" approach that leans on multiple solutions to offer different elements of the benefit.

Blue Shield said Park brings more than 25 years of experience to the position, and that she served most recently at Kaiser Permanente Northern California as president of pharmacy operations and services.

“What drew me to Blue Shield is that it’s a mission-driven nonprofit health plan that’s committed to improving member health and their lives—not just lowering costs for medications,” Park said. “As pharmacy care shifts to support individuals in a more connected and personalized way, I am excited to join an organization that is transforming healthcare to make it more accessible for everyone.”

Janice Nevin, M.D., will end her 12-year run as president and CEO of ChristianaCare on Sept. 1, the system's board announced.

She retires after 23 years at the organization, initially joining as its chair of family and community medicine. The physician executive is credited by the board with expanding the system's physical footprint, shepherding "significant investment in historically under-resourced areas" and strengthening its academic partnerships.

Taking up the mantle will be Jenn Schwartz, who was named executive vice president and chief strategy officer at the top of 2026. She came to ChristianaCare in 2018 to initially serve as chief legal officer. Prior to that she spent over a decade at Lourdes Health System, where she was vice president of legal affairs & general counsel as well as its executive director.

> Maui Health CEO Lynn Fulton will be stepping down on May 3 after a little over two years in the Hawaiian health system's top role. She plans to return to central Illinois to be closer to her family, according to the announcement that promises a leadership transition plan "in the coming days."

Fulton is credited with overseeing improved quality and financial stabilization during her time at the three-hospital nonprofit system.

> Tenet Healthcare Chief Information Officer Paola Arbour plans to retire at the end of this year, according to a recent regulatory filing from the for-profit hospital and ambulatory surgical center chain. She's been in the role since 2018, and plans to stick with the organization in a part-time, non-executive role through April 1, 2028 "to provide continuing transition services and support."

> Samuel Marchio was named senior vice president, chief government relations and policy officer at Ascension, per a social media post. He comes off a 15-year stint at Elevance Health (initially Anthem), where most recently served as regional vice president of federal government affairs.

> Stephen Taluja was named chief mission officer of Providence, a role that tasks him with aligning the Catholic nonprofit system's charity and service aims with ongoing strategic and organizational transformation. The appointment takes effect on June 29.

Taluja comes to the organization from a Bon Secours Mercy Health, where he is currently chief sponsorship and formation officer. He's been there in various roles since 2014, and before that led multicultural parish ministries.

> Addiction treatment provider Birches Health has added former Cigna Chief Medical Officer Doug Nemecek, M.D., to its advisory board as a senior adviser. As a senior adviser, Nemecek will work closely with the leadership team at Birches as it evolves its clinical and payer engagement strategies.

Nemecek's experience in the payer market will be key to informing this work, according to an announcement.

> Oraida Roman has been named as Aledade's new chief commercial officer, the company revealed on Wednesday. In the role, she will be tasked with leading the team's strategy around national health plan partnerships.

Roman brings 25 years of experience to the role, and will spearhead work around 200 contracts including Medicare Advantage, Medicaid and commercial plans.

> WellSpan Health President and CEO Roxanna Gapstur, Ph.D, is calling it a career after more than eight years at the nonprofit system's helm.

WellSpan's board announced the plans April 6, sharing that Gapstur will continue in the role until the transition to a replacement is complete. No specific or expected timeline was given, other than sharing that a national search for that new executive has begun.

The system, which employs 23,000 people, has grown under her tenure from eight hospitals to 12, and from $2.5 billion of revenue to $4.7 billion. Its footprint has also expanded from five counties to 12 across Pennsylvania and northern Maryland, now reaching more than 1 million patients.

The announcement credits Gapstur with bringing "clear strategic direction" that focused on quality, safety, patient experience and employee engagement. That approach brough national recognitions and designations to its facilities, plus new developments like a genomic program bringing precision medicine into patient care.

> Centene Corporation has created two new positions to lead key segments of its insurance business.

The company said in an announcement that it has named Daniel Finke as group president for markets and commercial and Michael Carson as its group president for Medicare and specialty. Both executives will report to CEO Sarah London, per Centene.

Finke is an experienced insurance executive and will be tasked with overseeing and scaling the company's Medicaid and commercial segments. He joins the insurer from Convey Health Solutions, where he was CEO, and has also previously served as president of Aetna at CVS Health.

Carson, meanwhile, will take on an expanded role in overseeing Centene's Medicare Advantage, Part D, dual-eligible and specialty populations. He joined the company as CEO of WellCare in 2024, and previously held leadership roles at Bright Healthcare and Harvard Pilgrim Health Care.

London said in the announcement that the shift recognizes Carson's significant contributions to the company and the experience that Finke brings to the table in driving operations forward.

"Their collective experience will be instrumental as we continue to strengthen performance across the portfolio and deliver sustainable, profitable growth," she said.

Elevance said the new leaders will help expand and scale Carelon, which reaches over 90 million healthcare consumers. The Health Benefits segment provides coordinated solutions to more than 45 million Elevance members.

Small is currently president of Medicaid at Elevance Health, where he has been for nearly seven years. He has over 25 years of healthcare leadership experience, including roles at Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Minnesota, Highmark and Aetna.

At Elevance, he oversaw a Medicaid business with about 8.5 million members. CareFirst, meanwhile, is a nonprofit with 3.5 million members primarily living in the District of Columbia, Maryland and Northern Virginia. It has been without a permanent top executive since last September, with Ja'Ron Bridges serving as interim president and CEO.

On deck is Winjie Miao, who is currently senior executive vice president and chief operating officer. In the role, Crittenden will the lead the insurer's clinical operations, and will be tasked with partnering with other key leaders across the company to support the central goals of improving access and simplifying the healthcare journey for both patients and providers.

Crittenden brings years of experience in managed care, value-based care and population health to the role, Cigna said in an announcement. He most recently served as CMO at Quantum Health, and also held leadership roles at Evergreen Nephrology, Anthem and Humana.

Crittenden is also board certified in internal medicine and nephrology, Cigna said.

“I’m honored to join Cigna Healthcare at this important moment in its transformation toward making health care simpler, more personalized and more affordable,” said Crittenden in the announcement. “I am committed to fostering a collaborative and supportive environment, doing everything we can to improve the experience and outcomes of all those we serve.”

Haupert will stick around through 2027 in an advisory role to soften the transition, support philanthropic and capital fundraising and provide strategic guidance on a new $1+ billion medical campus the nonprofit also announced this week.

#5674. 1968 Ford Mustang For Sale Is A Clean, Green V8 Cruiser Begging To Be Driven Daily

When you hear "green 1968 Ford Mustang," you likely picture one very specific car. You know the one: a verdant, tire-killing fastback driven by mercurial automotive and Hollywood legend Steve McQueen in the 1968 film "Bullitt." Today, a first-generation Ford Mustang Fastback similar to the one from the 58-year-old action-crime thriller could demand six figures, especially in that oh-so coveted color: Highland Green. For first-gen Mustang fans who can't afford to spend fixer-upper-home money on a car, there are alternatives. Alternatives like this green 1968 Ford Mustang.

At a glance and on paper, it ticks boxes. A V8 under the hood? Of course. That classic facelifted first-generation Mustang look? Thankfully, it's intact. Mostly. See, someone thought this one was deserving of a cool restomod treatment, and it got just that. Instead of being a numbers-matching carbureted survivor, this one benefits from a myriad of modern and aftermarket updates, like electronic fuel injection, electric fans, power locks, keyless entry, and Vintage Air air-conditioning and heat. This is a daily-driver-ready take on a classic. It's up for grabs, too. As of this writing, the restomod-ed Mustang is for sale just north of Dallas. Purists need not apply.

No, it's not finished in Highland Green. Not even close, really. The 1968 Ford Mustang restomod currently for sale by PC Classic Cars in Sherman, Texas is a much lighter hue. The headlights have been replaced with an integrated LED lamp-and-signal set and the tail lights are sequential like an aftermarket set you'd find on a much newer Mustang. It also rides on a set of staggered two-tone Halibrand-style alloy wheels that complement the paintwork, wrapped up in Nitto rubber. The builder also swapped in a Mustang II front end, complete with a sway bar and tubular control arms.

Under the hood, the '68 Mustang gets a familiar engine option: a 289-cubic-inch V8. It's far from stock, though. The parts list continues with a set of aluminum AFR cylinder heads, a Holley Sniper EFI setup, a Fi-Tech electronic ignition, an aftermarket serpentine system, an aluminum radiator in place of the tired old stock unit, and dual electric fans, to name a few things. The whole thing hooks up to a four-speed automatic gearbox with overdrive. Sorry, no manual here.

There are more modern touches beyond the engine bay, including power locks with keyless entry via an aftermarket fob, a stereo system with an amplifier and subwoofers, and that Vintage Air climate control. The restomod treatment continues inside the classic Mustang's cabin. It's a full brown leather TMI interior with black accents on the folding bucket seats and dash paneling. The brown leather even extends into the trunk.

It's not perfect. A glance at the driver's side door reveals a little misalignment. The car was once red. There are blemishes here and there. In short, this is more of a driver, less of a concours condition car meant to be kept out of the rain or prolonged direct sunlight. That doesn't mean the modified pony car loses the aesthetic charm that landed the 1968 model on the list of your favorite Ford Mustangs. Well, the fastback did, at least.

So just how much does PC Classic Cars want for this one? It's currently on sale for $46,950. That's quite a bit steeper than the average $25,310 price of 1968 Ford Mustang coupé sales over the last year. Then again, not every '68 Mustang on the market has had this much work done.

Get this: Its clock shows just 119 miles. Though, as you might expect, that's not exactly accurate. It's likely that this build's underpinnings have a much higher mileage. Frankly, a 1968 Ford Mustang with a 289-cubic-inch V8 and an true odometer reading anywhere near 119 would demand a much, much higher price. Still, with the modern tweaks already on this 58-year-old 'Stang, it seriously needs a driver to take it on as a daily and run that odometer up. After all, what would McQueen do? He'd almost certainly drive it — and so should the next owner.

#5673. Oracle rethinks the lakehouse as AI agents become data consumers

A shared semantic layer is fast becoming the dividing line between lakehouses built for reporting and those built for artificial intelligence.

As AI agents join human analysts in querying corporate data, enterprises need platforms that make sense of information scattered across clouds, formats and rival systems. Oracle Corp. has spent the past year rebuilding its data stack around that shift, part of a broader database modernization push. The company now pitches its Autonomous AI Lakehouse as an open layer that sits across an enterprise’s existing data estate rather than replacing it, according to Nipun Agarwal (pictured), senior vice president of software engineering, Oracle Database, at Oracle.

“Lakehouses were the platform which customers use for running analytics,” Agarwal said. “Now, lakehouses have become the decision backbone for AI.”

Agarwal spoke with theCUBE’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Oracle’s Autonomous AI Lakehouse combines a shared semantic layer with fast, real-time access to data across platforms to support AI agents. (* Disclosure below.)

Oracle’s approach rests on a catalog that can mount other catalogs, such as Databricks Inc.’s Unity Catalog, along with Postgres and MySQL databases, so data is queried in place rather than copied. The company announced a business semantic layer and broader Apache Iceberg support at the October event, with table and column descriptions the system generates applying to non-Oracle sources as well, according to Agarwal. Crucially, Oracle does not see the offering as competing with other lakehouses, he added.

“We really believe that for any enterprise, they’re gonna have a choice,” he said. “They’re gonna be using multiple data sources. They’ll have multiple lakehouses.”

Oracle’s Lake Cache speeds up queries by moving the most-used Iceberg tables into Exadata’s flash cache. Real-time access is also becoming essential as software agents become the main consumers of the data: Scheduled refreshes of copied data can fall short when agents request it on demand, according to Agarwal.

“With AI that’s no longer the case, because for AI, the consumer is not a human necessarily,” Agarwal said. “The need for real-time access is a lot more with AI.”

#5672. Electric Buses Need a Plan for the Next Operating Contract

Greater Manchester is entering a new stage of bus franchising. In September 2026, Go-Ahead announced that Go North West had won two Bee Network operating contracts covering 38 routes and approximately 60 buses, with service beginning in March 2027. Eighteen of those routes will operate from a new depot in Leigh. The award is a reminder that operating companies can change while the depots, charging infrastructure and grid connections supporting the passenger network remain in place for decades.

Electric-bus procurement adds a long-lived physical commitment to contracts that are often much shorter. An operating agreement may run for five to seven years. A depot building, substation or multi-megawatt electricity connection can remain useful through several such contracts. Buses can sometimes be transferred between operators, but land, cable routes, electrical capacity and installed charging equipment are tied to particular sites. Those assets need to support the passenger service even when the company responsible for driving the buses changes.

Consider an authority retendering electric-bus routes. The incumbent has used a convenient depot and financed chargers and a substantial grid connection. A competing operator submits an attractive price and a credible operating plan, but has no assured right to use the depot and electricity infrastructure. It might need to negotiate with the incumbent, find alternative premises or secure another grid connection, potentially adding years of work and substantial costs. A nominally competitive tender can become much less contestable once those obligations are included.

South Yorkshire has taken a deliberate approach to this problem. In March 2026, the South Yorkshire Mayoral Combined Authority announced the purchase of five major depots, adding them to the publicly owned Leger Way depot in Doncaster. First Bus and Stagecoach will lease the acquired premises back during the transition. The authority intends to use the estate for franchised operations and electric-bus infrastructure, with its first franchised services scheduled for September 2027. Six operators reached the next procurement stage for the initial packages at Olive Grove and Leger Way.

This does not establish that every city should own every depot. London has long maintained a publicly specified, competitively operated bus network while many garages remain outside direct Transport for London ownership. Secure leases, access rights, assignable contracts and specialist infrastructure providers may preserve the same continuity, depending on the local market. The practical test is whether a qualified successor operator can obtain the depot, buses, charging capacity and operational information required to take over on the contracted date.

Remaining asset value is central to that test. If an operator finances twenty-year charging infrastructure under a five-year contract, it needs to know what happens to the investment if another operator wins the routes. The authority must also avoid paying for a useful electrical connection and then finding it cannot make that capacity available to the next contractor. Depreciation, compensation, asset transfer, warranties, software access and grid-connection permissions need to be settled before the first contract ends, ideally before it starts.

England’s January 2026 bus-franchising guidance recognizes the importance of depots, charging infrastructure, transfer arrangements and competition in subsequent procurements. The engineering of electric buses has advanced considerably. Public authorities now need procurement structures that keep the fleet and its supporting infrastructure useful as routes, contractors and technologies evolve.

My TFIE Strategy Briefing article examines the second-contract test through Greater Manchester and South Yorkshire, including asset access, residual values and operating continuity. It draws on my open report, The Bus Is Not the System, comparing metropolitan bus governance and electrification across Britain and Ireland.

#5671. Ayrton Senna's Honda NSX Sells For Record $1.1 Million At Auction

One of the original NSX's biggest selling points was that Honda recruited three-time Formula 1 champion Ayrton Senna to help develop the sports car. While the legendary Brazilian wasn't impressed with the NSX at first, it evolved into a mass-produced machine he eventually praised. Senna's personal 1991 Honda NSX sold for $1.17 million at RM Sotheby's auction in London last week. The sale made the late champion's car the most expensive first-generation NSX ever sold at auction, surpassing a $1.06 million mark set for a 2003 NSX-R last year.

Honda was contractually obligated to provide Senna with an NSX for his personal use. The Japanese automaker supplied three examples of the sports car, a pair in black and one in Formula Red. The red NSX, the auctioned car, was stored in Portugal and delivered to Senna when he visited the country. It's the same car that the Brazilian was photographed washing with a garden hose. The 1992 documentary "Ayrton Senna: Racing Is In My Blood" also features Senna spinning the wheels on this NSX. After Senna's death in 1994, the sports car stayed with the Portuguese dealership that owned it until 1997.

Senna's most successful period in F1 came with McLaren from 1988 until 1993. The Brazilian won three F1 world championships and 35 races over the six seasons with the British team. Honda supplied engines to McLaren, ending the partnership after the 1992 season. If by fate, McLaren conducted a preseason test at Suzuka Circuit in February 1989, just as Honda's R&D department was wrapping up its month-long NSX testing program. The engineers let Senna run laps in the sports car. According to Road & Track, Senna wasn't pleased, stating, "I'm not sure I can really give you appropriate advice on a mass-production car, but I feel it's a little fragile."

Honda went back to the drawing board and increased the NSX's chassis stiffness by 50%. The automaker even invited Senna back to test the sports car at the Nürburgring and help tune the suspension. The expert input played a significant role in the NSX's success, from marketing to the sports car's critical success. While most of us didn't have the budget to bid on Senna's NSX, Honda is doing its part to help other NSX owners keep their cars just as pristine. The Japanese automaker's heritage program now produces over 3,000 official reproduction parts to keep first-generation NSXs on the road and running smoothly.

#5670. Amwell bets AI boom will boost demand for its unified care platform

Amwell bets AI boom will boost demand for its unified care platform" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

As health plans and employers contend with a growing array of virtual care and AI-enabled tools, Amwell is positioning its digital health platform as the infrastructure layer for AI-enabled care.

Executives at Amwell, formerly known as American Well, touted the company's platform strategy, government contracts and higher-value clinical services as the main drivers of future growth during the company's third-quarter earnings call Tuesday.

Rising healthcare costs are pushing health plans and employers to adopt tech-enabled care solutions, but they are looking for measurable engagement and outcomes from digital health vendors, not just access, according to Ido Schoenberg, M.D., Amwell chairperson and CEO.

The proliferation of point solutions, accelerated by AI, is creating more vendor sprawl and member confusion, Schoenberg told investors and analysts during the call.

There's also a lack of proof with many digital health tools, he noted. "It is hard to see which programs work and harder still to replace one without disrupting members. That sprawl is accelerating. AI has made it faster and cheaper to build a clinical program. Investors have backed hundreds of new digital health companies this year, many of them built on AI. Our customers feel pressure to offer these programs, but each one brings its own cost, its own integration, and its own front door. The opportunity is real. So is the complexity," he said.

More patients are turning to AI for health guidance, but those interactions don’t necessarily lead them to appropriate, covered care, creating the risk of poor clinical decisions and unnecessary costs for health plans, Schoenberg said.

"This is the problem Amwell is determined to solve for our customers. We help them improve clinical and financial outcomes. We do it through activation, getting more of their members into technology-enabled care in place of conventional care that often costs more. We give our customers one platform under their brand with one integration. It provides reliable, scalable rails to bring in a program, exchange data with it, and tests whether it works. The member's experience stays consistent, simple, and engaging. A common data structure proves the outcomes and improves performance over time," he said.

As AI adoption grows, a unified care platform becomes more valuable, Schoenberg asserted.

"We are not selling an AI feature. We are the trusted platform where AI-powered care runs with clinicians in the loop," he said during the Q3 call.

Amwell's customers represent more than 90 million covered lives, and the company also serves 9.6 million beneficiaries of the Military Health System.

Amwell's platform can help drive member engagement and utilization of digital health tools, executives said.

"Most of the health plans we talk to still see engagement in the single digits. We address that with always-on engagement, outreach to members through our customers' own channels within the rules they set. When a customer switches it fully on, members use the platform at more than three times the rate we see when it's off," Schoenberg said.

The platform runs on a common data structure, he noted. "It sends a member into a program with the right information. It collects outcomes back, and it reports value in the customer's own terms, whether that customer is a health plan or an employer that the plan serves. That is how a program proves its return on investment and how it gets better over time," he said.

In response to a question from an analyst, Schoenberg suggested pricing for the solution could evolve from fixed Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) fees toward outcomes-based arrangements in which Amwell shares in the savings it produces for health plans.

Amwell executives view that platform strategy as key to the company's growth.

In Q3, Amwell reported revenue that was slightly above Wall Street's consensus and a narrower adjusted loss than analysts expected. Amwell executives also reiterated confidence in reaching positive operating cash flow and breakeven to positive adjusted EBITDA in the fourth quarter.

Amwell brought in $49 million in Q3 revenue, according to financial results published Tuesday afternoon. Revenue was down approximately 12.9% year-over-year, but $1 million above the high end of management's guidance range, according to Chief Financial Officer Mark Hirschhorn.

Subscription revenue was $23.9 million, down approximately 22.5% year-over-year and 6.8% sequentially, Hirschhorn said. “The year-over-year decline continues to reflect the previously disclosed churn we've discussed on prior earnings calls,” he added.

Amwell Medical Group (AMG) visit revenue was $23.7 million, up approximately 11.7% year over year, while AMG paid visits totaled approximately 301,000 visits, essentially flat year over year, Hirschhorn said.

Virtual primary care visits were up 41% year over year, continuing that segment's strong growth trajectory. Total platform visits were approximately 760,000 visits, down approximately 30.5% year over year—though Hirschhorn noted the decline is consistent with previously discussed portfolio changes.

The telehealth platform reported a net loss of $11.7 million during the quarter, compared to a loss of $29.3 million for the same period a year ago, Hirschhorn said. Adjusted EBITDA loss narrowed to $3.6 million from a loss of $12.7 million a year earlier.

Amwell executives are bullish on revenue growth from its own clinical services, including virtual primary care and behavioral health.

Executives also highlighted the company's government business as it delivered solid third-quarter financial performance. Amwell announced in September that the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) issued a letter of intent to deploy its platform enterprise-wide.

"I want to be precise about what this is," Schoenberg said. "The letter is not a binding contract. A definitive agreement still has to be negotiated and executed under federal procurement rules, and that work is underway."

Schoenberg noted the letter followed a "comprehensive evaluation."

"It cited scalable video consultations, interoperability, cybersecurity compliance and support for integrated care delivery," he said. "In plain terms, the capabilities the department evaluated are the ones we already run at scale for the military health system, and the department's own scale is considerable."

Amwell executives are optimistic the company will sign a contract with the VA "over the next couple of months," Hirschhorn said, with implementation beginning in 2027, but no definitive agreement exists yet.

Moreover, Schoenberg said the platform is continuing to negotiate a "direct, longer-term contract" with the Defense Health Agency (DHA).

The DHA, which oversees services for the Military Health System, renewed its contract with the telehealth platform in August 2025. In June, it called for sole contracts with Amwell and four other vendors.

DHA discontinued its payment for behavioral health and automated care services with Amwell last year. Schoenberg said the cessation was due to the Department of Defense’s cost-cutting measures—not the department’s satisfaction with the services.

Hirschhorn said that Amwell is raising its full-year revenue guidance to between $204 million to $206 million, up from $195 million to $205 million. The company now expects full-year adjusted EBITDA to be a loss in the range of $6.9 million to $7.9 million, a meaningful improvement from its prior range of a loss of $12 million to $16 million.

Amwell forecasts full-year AMG visits between 1.32 million to 1.37 million visits.

“In summary, during the third quarter, we exceeded our revenue guidance with stronger visit volumes, a stable subscription base, and a leaner cost structure that positions us to finish the year on a strong note,” Hirschhorn said.

#5668. U.S. Acura Dealers Are Now Selling 3,000 Factory Reproduction Parts For Your OG NSX

News about Honda making and selling new reproduction parts for the first-generation NSX has been brewing for more than a year now, but it's finally, actually here. The Honda Heritage Parts program launched in Japan back in April but is now making its way stateside. The automaker announced Monday that more than 3,000 Genuine Honda Reproduction Parts for its first-ever supercar are now available for purchase at Acura dealerships across the U.S. and via the online Honda DreamShop. There are apparently plans for "future expansion" of the program, as well.

The American Honda Motor Co. hasn't released a master list of all 3,000 parts being offered, but taking a quick gander at the program's Japanese webpage shows a wide range of stuff available. You can get a camshaft for the yen equivalent of about $850, an accelerator pedal assembly costs $340, and the car's entire V6 cylinder block can be had for around $6,300. If you're a fan looking for some merch-type items, a little armrest emblem that says "NSX DOHC VTEC" on it and the Japanese NSX owner's manual go for about $40 and $60, respectively.

The O.G. NSX (known to Honda nerds as the NA1 and NA2) was branded in America as an Acura and was sold from model years 1991 to 2005, and the newly produced parts apply to NSXs across that entire production run. The program is called Honda Heritage Parts, by the way, not Honda NSX Heritage Parts, which means reproduced parts for other classic Hondas are almost certainly coming in the future.

From Acura's press release: "Honda Heritage Parts was created to help our customers enjoy their classic Acura and Honda performance models, and it's appropriate that we begin with an iconic model like the first-generation Acura NSX," said American Honda executive vice president Mamadou Diallo (though the emphasis is mine). As the owner of a 2004 S2000 that could definitely use some rejuvenation here and there, hopefully that's the next Honda to get the Heritage Parts treatment.

#5667. CMS finalizes steeper Medicare physician pay cuts for 2027, moves ahead with RPM vendor restrictions

CMS finalizes steeper Medicare physician pay cuts for 2027, moves ahead with RPM vendor restrictions" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services finalized sweeping Medicare payment reforms it says will shift the program from volume-based "sick care" toward prevention, primary care and accountable care.

The 2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule rule includes a roughly 2% reduction in baseline physician payment rates with targeted increases and new payment opportunities for accountable care, primary and chronic care and behavioral health. CMS finalized steeper physician payment cuts than it had proposed in July.

An unpublished PDF version of the 2,468-page final rule can be found here.

In a press release, CMS said it is "prioritizing prevention, strengthening primary care, cracking down on duplicate billing and reinforcing fiscal stewardship across Medicare."

The final rule modernizes physician payment structures to "reward health maintenance and coordinated primary care rather than disjointed, volume-based intervention," CMS said.

"Medicare should reward clinicians for keeping people healthy," HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. said in a statement. "Under President Trump’s leadership, we are putting prevention and primary care at the center of Medicare, closing payment loopholes, and cracking down on waste. This rule directs resources toward coordinated care that puts patients first. We are changing what Medicare pays for to change what our health system delivers."

Under the final rule, CMS will officially sunset the traditional Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) reporting option beginning with the CY 2031 performance period. Clinicians will have through CY 2030 to transition to the MIPS Value Pathways (MVPs), which already cover approximately 98% of clinicians, or Advanced Alternative Payment Models. This reflects two additional years of transition time compared to the proposed rule. The rule also finalizes three new MVPs focused on diabetes, hypertension and hospitalists, and requires clinicians to report at least one specialty-specific "Core Measure" starting in CY 2027.

The final 2027 PFS rule also establishes new 340B reporting requirements. Covered entities will have to report certain Medicare Part D claims involving drugs purchased through the 340B Drug Pricing Program to the Medicare Part D Claims Data 340B Repository beginning with claims with a date of service on or after Jan.1, 2027. The deadline for the first quarterly submission is delayed until Sept. 30, 2027.

For physicians, while the proposed rule includes statutory payment increases, Medicare payment rates face an overall baseline decrease for 2027 due to the expiration of a temporary 2.5% legislative increase from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) in 2026.

Under the Medicare Access and CHIP Reauthorization Act (MACRA), the CY2027 conversion factors reflect statutory updates of +0.75% for qualifying Alternative Payment Model (APM) participants and +0.25% for non-qualifying participants. The changes to the PFS conversion factors for CY 2027 include these updates as required by statute and an estimated -0.12% adjustment necessary to account for proposed changes in work RVUs for some services, according to CMS in a fact sheet.

For clinicians who don't qualify through an advanced alternative payment model, the conversion factor drops from $33.40 to $32.63, a 2.31% reduction. For qualifying APM participants, the conversion factor drops 1.83% from $33.57 to $32.95. In the draft rule issued in July, CMS projected cuts of 1.68% and 1.19%, respectively.

CMS is also addressing what it sees as overpayment and duplicate reimbursement when multiple services are delivered during the same patient encounter. Under the final rule, when an office visit and minor procedure occur on the same day, CMS will reduce payment by 20% for the lower-cost service, reducing duplication in payment by patients and the Medicare program for clinical work already covered in the procedure’s valuation.

CMS had initially proposed paying the higher-cost service in full and reducing payment for the other service by 50%.

Physician groups were quick to criticize CMS' payment changes in the final rule.

"Notwithstanding modest policy improvements to enhance value-based care through MSSP, MGMA is disappointed by CMS’s decision to finalize several destabilizing policies in the 2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule," Anders Gilberg, senior vice president of government affairs at the Medical Group Management Association, said in a statement.

"Conversion factor cuts of 1.83% for qualifying APM participants and 2.31% for all other clinicians further degrade an already fragile payment system and amplify severe financial challenges caused by years of inadequate Medicare reimbursement," Gilberg said.

Compounding this ongoing reimbursement decline, CMS will cut payments by 20% when office visits billed with modifier 25 are performed on the same day as certain procedures, "interfering with physician practices’ ability to offer same-day care," he noted.

MGMA is urging Congress to intervene by immediately fixing cuts to the conversion factor, along with changes to modifier 25. "To prevent annual disruption, Congress should prioritize comprehensive MACRA reform by passing the Patients First Act," Gilberg said.

The agency is overhauling the office/outpatient evaluation and management visit complexity add-on code, HCPCS code G2211. CMS is transitioning HCPCS code G2211 from a flat add-on payment to a modifier that would increase the payment of the associated E/M code by 16%. That would maintain an equal percentage increase across all levels of E/M codes, CMS said.

The agency also finalized a new modifier that would offset the costs incurred by practitioners in accountable care organizations (ACOs) when providing longitudinal care and care coordination. The modifier would only be available for practitioners participating in a Shared Savings Program ACO or participant providers in a Long-term Enhanced ACO Design (LEAD) Model ACO and would increase payment of the associated E/M visit by 32%, CMS said.

In the final rule, CMS tightened remote patient monitoring and remote therapeutic monitoring requirements, following through on a controversial ban of third-party RPM vendors. However, CMS delayed that restriction for two years.

Beginning in 2027, as CMS outlined in the proposed rule, RTM services can only be furnished to established patients, and providers must provide a separately reportable initiating visit before billing for RPM or RTM services.

Despite intense industry pushback, CMS completed a proposal that will prevent providers from using third-party vendors or contractors for RPM services. For the purposes of billing, RPM services must be performed by clinical staff employed by the practice, according to the PFS rule. But the agency provided a two-year reprieve on that requirement as it goes into effect Jan. 1, 2029, "giving practices that rely on contractors two additional years to adapt," CMS said.

Health tech companies, providers and lawmakers pushed back on the proposal to restrict third-party vendors, urging CMS to reconsider the proposed changes to preserve patients' access to these tech-enabled services. Many rural, small, and independent practices, as well as both urban and rural health systems, rely on specialized clinical and technology partners to make remote monitoring services available to their patients.

CMS finalized changes to the Medicare Shared Savings Program, the nation’s largest value-based payment program, to "accelerate accountable care service delivery, further CMS' goal of aligning spending and value in Original Medicare, and support achieving other related strategic objectives," the agency said in a fact sheet.

The overhaul to the MSSP program aims to make ACO participation more financially attractive, encourage organizations to take on risk, expand beneficiary participation and ease some quality-reporting requirements.

The agency says the changes are projected to grow the program by adding up to 1 million assigned beneficiaries in an average year and produce $5.5 billion in net federal savings over 10 years. CMS also projects the changes will generate an overall increase in shared savings net of losses to ACOs by $1.1 billion over a decade.

The final rule changes the Shared Savings Program’s benchmarking and financial methodology to balance incentives between Level E of the BASIC track and the ENHANCED track. Under the final rule, the shared savings rate for Level E of the BASIC track increases from 50% to 60%, and it reduces the maximum weight used in calculating the positive regional adjustment for lower-spending ACOs participating under the ENHANCED track from 50% to 35%.

The agency is increasing the prior savings adjustment's scaling factor from 50% to 75%, allowing more of an ACO's previous savings to be reflected in future benchmarks.

Under the final rule, CMS will risk-adjust the 5% cap on benchmark increases, potentially allowing ACOs that care for sicker, higher-cost patients to receive larger upward adjustments.

Data shows patients aligned with an ACO are less likely to experience uncontrolled diabetes or hypertension and are more likely to receive recommended preventive care, according to CMS. In performance year 2024, 75% of the 476 participating ACOs earned shared savings totaling $4.1 billion, while generating net savings for the Medicare Trust Funds of approximately $2.5 billion compared to projected spending benchmarks.

Under the final 2027 PFS rule, approved ACOs may reduce or eliminate Part B cost-sharing for many items and services for assigned beneficiaries, directly lowering out-of-pocket costs for essential care. That change goes into effect April 1, 2027.

The rule also increases shared savings rates for eligible ACOs, provides novel incentives for first-time participants and sets more predictable spending targets. The rule also simplifies electronic health record reporting requirements, streamlines patient notice mandates and removes outdated administrative hurdles, CMS said.

#5666. A State Law Targeted Fentanyl Dealers. Prosecutors Are Using It to Charge Users Too.

— More than 30 people in Idaho have been charged with fentanyl trafficking without proof of sales

When two Idaho lawmakers pitched harsher penalties for people caught with fentanyl, they said the new law would target drug dealers -- not those struggling with addiction.

But 2 years after the law was implemented, prosecutors have charged at least 30 people with fentanyl trafficking without presenting evidence that they were dealing or distributing the drug.

The law, which went into effect on July 1, 2024, does not differentiate between those using and those selling the drug, and it doesn't require prosecutors to find evidence of trafficking. Instead, prosecutors can charge people with fentanyl trafficking if they possess at least 4 grams or 100 pills that contain fentanyl. InvestigateWest reviewed court records for all fentanyl trafficking charges filed through June 30 of this year. Among the 90 cases that included arrest reports, one-third of them lacked evidence such as scales, ledgers, and small bags, which when found together are commonly considered proof that someone sold or intended to sell drugs. But court records show those people were charged with trafficking and face the law's mandatory minimum prison terms based on the amount of fentanyl police said they had.

A sheriff deputy in western Idaho's Nez Perce County arrested a man for drug possession after he dropped a bag of blue pills that the deputy identified as fentanyl on the floor of a casino, according to the police report. After counting 111 pills, "I changed the charge from possession, to trafficking fentanyl," the deputy wrote in the report.

One county north, Isaac Berger was charged with fentanyl trafficking by the Latah County Prosecutor's Office after an emergency room nurse who was treating him for an overdose reported Berger to police. Less than 3 months later, Berger died of fentanyl poisoning. The detective who investigated Berger's death said there was no evidence that he was planning to sell or distribute the drugs, which Berger's mother brought to the hospital in an effort to help healthcare workers save her son.

Prosecutors who supported the law during legislative debates continue to defend it, saying it deters drug dealers from bringing fentanyl into the state, though none provided evidence to support the claim. Fifteen people charged with trafficking fentanyl were accused by police of selling drugs to an informant or admitting they sold drugs. Seven of them were convicted and are serving time in prison.

"Treatment is not the right outcome for every case," Bonneville County Prosecuting Attorney Randy Neal said. "Accountability is just as important. And if you're looking at somebody who's distributing, who's delivering, if you don't have the accountability, I promise you, probation is a joke."

Neal, who has been a vocal advocate of the law, pointed to a graphic originating from the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration widely shared by prosecutors and law enforcement showing a No. 2 pencil with 2 mg of fentanyl powder on the tip, which can be lethal. Neal said "it's highly unlikely" that someone caught with the state threshold of at least 4 grams -- about four sugar packets -- of fentanyl is not planning to distribute it "because the numbers are so insane."

Opponents of Idaho's law disagree. Kellen Russoniello, MPH, director of public health for the Drug Policy Alliance, which advocates for drug treatment instead of criminalization, said it would not be unusual for someone with a severe addiction and a higher tolerance, or someone who made a bulk purchase on payday, to acquire the state's 4-gram threshold.

Russoniello said state lawmakers could save lives by diverting more people to treatment. InvestigateWest's analysis revealed that 13 people charged with trafficking received substance use treatment instead of prison. (All of them accepted plea deals for a different charge. The law's mandatory minimum prison terms do not allow for alternative sentences.) Forty people have served time in prison after being convicted of the trafficking charge or pleading guilty to an alternative charge.

"This law is ensnaring people who are possessing for personal use," Russoniello said. "Prosecuting or imprisoning people instead of providing necessary health services is counterproductive, ultimately making recovery more difficult by compounding trauma and saddling people with criminal records that will make accessing housing, employment, and services more difficult."

Republican state legislators Rep. Ted Hill and Sen. Todd Lakey introduced the law at a January 2024 hearing. Fentanyl possession and intent to deliver were already felonies with the possibility of prison -- a decision that was typically made by judges.

But House Bill 406 added a new trafficking offense that allows people in possession of threshold amounts of fentanyl to be charged as traffickers and imposes mandatory prison terms of 3, 5, or 10 years depending on the amount. The lawmakers, who represent constituents in and near Ada County, the state's most populated county, said the change was needed to "shut down the cartels" and prevent rising overdose deaths. Fentanyl-related deaths spiked in Idaho in 2021 and reached their highest point in 2023, when the drug killed 197 people, according to data from the state Department of Health and Welfare. Each year, fentanyl was responsible for more overdose deaths than any other drug, the data show.

By the time the fentanyl trafficking law went into effect in 2024, deaths had begun to decline. Last year saw the same number of fatalities as 2024, according to the data. (Lakey and Hill did not respond to calls and messages from InvestigateWest for this article.)

Idaho is one of nine states that allows people to be charged as traffickers based on possession above a certain threshold, according to a 2025 report by the Legislative Analysis and Public Policy Association summarizing fentanyl criminal statutes by state. Idaho's threshold is similar to other states, but it is the only state allowing pill counts to be used instead of grams. Seven of those states, including Idaho, have mandatory minimum prison terms.

Two years after Idaho's law took effect, prosecutors across the state have charged 134 people with fentanyl trafficking, InvestigateWest's analysis of court records found. Thirty-one of those cases are still pending.

Of the completed cases, 30% were dismissed and nearly half resulted in plea deals for other charges, such as possession of a controlled substance or possession with intent to deliver. Twenty-two people were convicted of fentanyl trafficking and are serving time in prison.

When attorney Mike French opposed the law on behalf of the Idaho Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers during a legislative debate, she said it's drug users, not traffickers, who are getting caught up in the state's mandatory minimum laws for marijuana, cocaine, and heroin trafficking. Laws like this do not effectively deter people struggling with addiction, she said, because they're typically unaware of the potential criminal penalties or are unable to stop using without help.

"This is a sledge hammer when we need a scalpel," French said.

Idaho's fentanyl trafficking law continued a decades-long trend where state lawmakers have sought to curb drug use by sharpening criminal penalties, despite national research showing those penalties do not deter drug use. A 10-year-old U.S. Department of Justice report found that "increasing the severity of punishment does little to deter crime."

The most effective response combines law enforcement efforts that target traffickers and alternatives to prison for people who are using but not selling drugs, according to a 2018 Pew Center report titled "More Imprisonment Does Not Reduce State Drug Problems." Drug courts, community supervision, and reduced prison sentences for drug offenders in Oklahoma, Mississippi, Alaska, and other states decreased prison populations and the cost to taxpayers in those states, the Pew Center found.

Russoniello, public health director at the Drug Policy Alliance, said lawmakers across the country are in "a moment where the pendulum is swinging back towards tough-on-crime and the war-on-drugs mentality."

Policies like Idaho's, which allow prosecutors to charge crimes like trafficking without any evidence of trafficking or intent to sell, circumvent well-established rights granted to people entangled in the criminal justice system, Russoniello said.

Families Against Mandatory Minimums, whose founder launched the nonprofit after her brother was sentenced to 5 years in prison for a drug crime, calls the practice "unjust, irrational, or counterproductive." Katrina Baugh, the nonprofit's national policy director, said mandatory incarceration allows increased political influence in courtrooms, by letting lawmakers and prosecutors rather than courts dictate criminal punishments. Mandatory minimum prison terms strip judges of discretion in sentencing, shifting the decision "away from the impartial adjudicator," she said, giving the power instead to "the party that has a self-interest of pursuing harsher punishments in every case."

Latah County Prosecuting Attorney Bill Thompson, who charged Berger after his nurse called police, said limiting judicial discretion was necessary because some judges were not coming down hard enough on drug dealers.

"Historically, in our part of the state, our judges have not been particularly strong on what we consider to be appropriate punishments for people who actually are dealing the drugs, not just users," Thompson said. "So the trafficking statutes have been a really important tool in trying to get around that reluctance that we encounter on occasion with some members of the courts."

Berger was the first person in Latah County to be charged under the new law. He was arrested at a hospital in the university town of Moscow in May 2025 and taken to jail. Berger and his attorney were working on a treatment plan they hoped would result in reduced charges. But Berger's health rapidly declined, and he died at home 2 months later from fentanyl poisoning – one of two Idahoans who fatally overdosed while their case was pending.

Fentanyl trafficking charges have been filed by prosecutors in 18 of Idaho's 44 counties. Six counties account for more than 75% of the charges.

In eastern Idaho near the Wyoming border, prosecutor Neal's office in Bonneville County has filed 28 charges -- more than any other county. One person was convicted of the charge. Sixteen others accepted plea deals for other charges including possession and delivering a controlled substance. Interstate 15, which runs from northern Montana to Southern California, cuts through the county and is a known drug pipeline, Neal said. He also credits a drug task force that's a collaboration between the county sheriff's department and Idaho Falls police with successful arrests and prosecutions.

"The effectiveness of the law enforcement is what you're seeing the numbers reflect," Neal said when presented with InvestigateWest's findings. "So, if our folks in Idaho Falls have a special drug task force, and a place like Rigby doesn't have a task force or doesn't have a specialized unit, well, that's going to skew the numbers because it's going to look like Bonneville has a hell of a lot bigger drug problem than Jefferson County. It's just that Jefferson's making less arrests."

Major thoroughfares that are known routes for transporting drugs between states also cut through Bannock, Kootenai, and Shoshone counties, accounting for some of the charges filed by prosecutors there. At least seven of those arrests originated from traffic stops, court records show. Meanwhile, in Ada and Canyon counties, which have the state's densest populations, more crime resulted in more charges.

Charges in Ada County, which encompasses Boise, resulted in more fentanyl trafficking convictions than anywhere else. The Ada County Prosecutor's Office, run by Jan Bennetts, who was elected to the position in 2016, declined requests for an interview. Alyson Outen, a spokesperson for the office, said in an email that the law "was a needed change."

Multiple overdoses had been reported at Andrea Forbini's home in Boise by the time police showed up with a search warrant in May 2025, according to court documents. They found nearly 400 pills containing fentanyl and arrested Forbini and two of her roommates, police records show. Only Forbini was charged with trafficking fentanyl.

Forbini's daughter, Halle Lillquist, said her mother struggled with addiction for most of her life, leaning on drugs to treat the pain she experienced from autoimmune conditions. She had recovered from an overdose weeks before being arrested last year. Over Lillquist's objections, Forbini's boyfriend bailed her mom out of jail, Lillquist said.

"Jail was just detox," Lillquist said. "She wasn't getting treatment there but at least she was sober."

Lillquist said she understands the need to punish people like her mom, who have committed a crime. But in states like Idaho that increase penalties without addressing the addiction, nothing will change.

Jail kept Forbini sober for about 3 months, but without addiction treatment she relapsed after her release, Lillquist said. One week later, her mom died from fentanyl poisoning.

"They shouldn't have let her go so freely like that without any help," Lillquist said. "Something should have been done."

#5665. Suzuki GSX-10R And SV-7S Put New Twists On Old Classics

Suzuki has long been, for better and for worse, a motorcycle maker that keeps its old assembly lines running. While the company comes up with something truly new every once in a while, it's more likely to figure out a new combination of parts it already has laying around. So, for EICMA, we shouldn't be surprised that Suzuki's big announcements are based around engines old enough to drink. We also shouldn't be surprised that those engines are inside what look to be some damn good bikes.

Suzuki's big reveals this year are the SV-7S and GSX-10R, bikes built around the 27-year-old SV650 engine and 21-year-old K5 GSX-R1000 engines, respectively. The former looks to be a mild update to the outgoing SV650, with new lighting, emissions equipment, a quickshifter, and a ride-by-wire throttle wrapped around the prior bike's frame and engine. Most importantly, the SV-7S is available in Europe, meaning that the 645 cc V-twin lives on under Euro 5+ emissions. Suzuki's site doesn't list power claims for the new bike, but it's likely to make the same 73 horses it has since time immemorial.

While the SV-7S is an update and a name change for the SV650, the GSX-10R (above) is ostensibly an entirely new bike — admittedly a bike that's largely just a faired version of the GSX-S1000, the company's naked literbike. Despite the similar displacement, the GSX-10R is nothing like the top-tier GSX-R1000. Instead, it's closer to a revival of the beloved K5 GSX-R1000 of the mid-aughts.

Yet, no matter what Reddit says, the GSX-10R is more than just a reheated leftover K5. Its name points to the difference, putting the bike in line with the GSX-8R — Suzuki intends the new 10R to be more streetable than the highest-test Gixxer, with lower footpegs, USB power, and a torque-rich engine for those times you can't sit at redline. There's also a full suite of electronics, to assist everything from traction to braking, launches, engine braking, hill starts, and cruising.

If the GSX-10R turns out to be what Suzuki says — a four-cylinder GSX-8R, a literbike with K5 reliability and daily-rider comfort — it could be the EICMA release I'm most excited to swing a leg over. To know for sure, though, I'll have to figure out how to get my hands on one.

Avanlee Care, a platform to engage family caregivers, has clinched $3.5 million in seed funding, Fierce Healthcare has learned.

The round was led by BEA Venture Fund, with participation from angel investor Esther Dyson, who is Avanlee’s board chair, Chrysalis Ventures and FairBridge VC. Avanlee will use the capital, which brings its total raised to $6 million, to expand across the Medicare Advantage market.

Avanlee Care helps MA plans and other organizations engage caregivers within their member populations, enabling caregivers to take action and organizations to measure the impact. On the Avanlee platform, caregivers can schedule appointments, manage medications, connect with retailers, communicate with their plan and provider, get vaccination reminders and search for providers. Meanwhile, payers get insight into caregiver burnout and member health trend data.

“Avanlee Care is addressing an enormous and underutilized resource within healthcare,” Melissa Bradley, founder and managing partner of BEA Venture Fund, said in a comment. “As healthcare organizations look for more effective ways to improve engagement and outcomes, Avanlee is offering the infrastructure to make caregivers part of that strategy. We believe that creates a significant opportunity to improve both the caregiver experience and healthcare outcomes at scale.”

Founded in 2020, Avanlee began as a direct-to-consumer app, since transitioning into the enterprise space. It is fully integrated with Mark Cuban Cost Plus Drugs as its lead pharmacy partner for discounted medications, and is in discussions with a national, undisclosed MA plan to bring its platform to members with an assigned caregiver. As part of an initial potential pilot with this plan, thousands of members with an assigned caregiver would participate in Avanlee, with a broader expansion planned for mid-2027. Additionally, Avanlee is working toward a separate unnamed integration with a national pharmacy partner for delivering medications.

“We are excited to work with Avanlee Care. We share a common mission: to provide lower costs on prescribed medications, saving money for the unpaid family caregiver and their loved one, the care-receiver,” Mark Cuban, co-founder of Cost Plus Drug Company, told Fierce Healthcare.

Nearly 1 in 4 Americans provide ongoing care for an adult or child with a complex medical condition or a disability, coordinating medications, appointments, transportation, food and other needs. Yet by overlooking the person managing a member’s care and day-to-day living, plans’ efforts to engage MA members are less effective, Avanlee executives argue.

“Caregivers spend an astronomical amount of time having to juggle their career, their families, and suddenly now I’m thrust into this role of I’m a caregiver for my mom … so saving time is huge,” Avanlee Christine, co-founder and CEO of Avanlee Care, told Fierce Healthcare exclusively. Christine, who grew up with a grandfather with Parkinson’s and dementia, was inspired to build the platform that could have supported her mom when she was caregiving.

Avanlee offers caregiver wellness tools on its platform, which 59% of past users have engaged with. Over half of consistent users also reported a decrease in overall stress. In its DTC days, Avanlee supported thousands of families, claiming it saved their caregivers thousands of hours. The wellness tools include a weekly questionnaire on stress and educational resources on topics such as estate planning, life planning and legal services. Caregivers can add other relatives to the platform for extra visibility or support, and Avanlee also facilitates grocery delivery through an integration with Walmart (their pricing applies). “If the caregiver fails, the one ultimately receiving care fails,” Christine said.

This stress survey becomes a key data stream for Avanlee plan partners, allowing them to evaluate caregiver burnout. Avanlee's platform also provides payers with insights about appointment bookings, home health services and medication adherence.

There’s a reason Avanlee is targeting MA to start. Nearly two-thirds of caregivers say MA makes caregiving duties easier to manage than traditional Medicare, according to one survey. Avanlee is also interested in eventually expanding to dual-eligibles. "There's a lot of tailwinds in caregiving for both Medicare and Medicaid and those dually eligible populations,” Eric Scott, Avanlee’s chief growth officer, said.

In order to streamline scheduling, Avanlee is seeking MA partners that allow it to also tap into their provider networks. Avanlee can automatically schedule appointments when prompted by a health plan, such as annual wellness visits or cancer screenings. Caregivers can also manually add their existing appointments to get reminders. In the near future, Avanlee plans to let caregivers book ad hoc appointments for needs beyond those specifically requested by the health plan.

Avanlee charges payers per-member-per-month and is available at no direct cost to the caregiver. It behooves plans to support this population, Christine argues, not only because of their influence over member outcomes but also because they could become a loyal future customer base. “You want to build a relationship with that adult daughter or son because you take such good care of their mom,” Christine said.

Avanlee is incorporating AI to reduce friction for caregivers, like summarizing caregiver notes recorded via audio, recommending providers based on caregiver preferences and matching users’ questions with curated resources. It also makes recommendations to caregivers based on a number of insights, including what medications a member is taking, what conditions they have and what their social needs are. These AI features are powered by AWS Bedrock, with requests handled within Avanlee’s cloud environment rather than being sent to a third-party model provider.

“How do we make it the new norm in healthcare that these people are part of healthcare for mom or dad on day one,” Christine said.

#5662. As AI takes over coding, Oracle rethinks how applications are built

As vibe coding moves from novelty to everyday practice, enterprises face a new problem: Machine-generated software still has to be maintained, governed and understood by people.

Low-code platforms were built to speed up application development, and AI is now rewriting that mission. Oracle Corp. previewed its answer ahead of its annual conference, and the tipping point for software development has already arrived, according to Mike Hichwa (pictured), senior vice president of software engineering at Oracle.

“In 2025, the majority of code was human-authored, and in 2026 and forever afterwards, the majority of code is going to be machine-generated,” Hichwa said. “We’re probably not going back. What we’ve done to address this change is we invented our own language. We call it APEXlang.”

Hichwa spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed vibe coding and the need to maintain and govern AI-generated code. (* Disclosure below.)

APEXlang is a highly abstracted application definition language that captures intent rather than implementation. Oracle introduced it with the APEX AI Application Generator and is publishing its grammar, skills and documentation in the public domain so coding agents such as Anthropic PBC’s Claude and OpenAI Group PBC’s Codex can generate it. Oracle is also working with OpenAI to train models to generate the language more efficiently, Hichwa explained.

“What you’re generating actually matters, because once you generate it, and you generate it 100 times or 1,000 times within your enterprise, then you’re going to need to maintain it. You’re going to need to look after it,” Hichwa said. “What people want with their portfolio of applications, they want consistency, they want governance, they want ease of understanding.”

Governance comes from the runtime, too. Generated APEXlang is interpreted by the APEX engine, which Oracle patches and updates monthly, so customers don’t have to revisit what they built. The same design is meant to curb AI slop, since a compact definition is easier to read than sprawling generated code, according to Hichwa.

“What we’re generating is much, much smaller, much more human understandable, so it is less sloppy because it is more abstracted,” Hichwa said. “It’s like a CliffsNotes. It’s not the full book.”

#5661. 'Forever Chemicals' Linked to Aggressive Breast Cancers

— Findings have "important public health implications," researchers say

Two common "forever chemicals" were associated with a higher risk of estrogen receptor (ER)-negative breast cancer, a prospective case-cohort study suggested.

The highest exposure quartile of perfluoro-n-octanoic acid (PFOA) was associated with a higher risk of ER-negative breast cancer compared with the lowest quartile (HR 1.67, 95% CI 1.10-2.53), and the same was true for perfluorooctane-1-sulfonic acid (PFOS; HR 1.93, 95% CI 1.15-3.22), reported Alexandra J. White, PhD, of the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences, and colleagues.

A meta-analysis of seven studies further supported an association for PFOA (relative risk [RR] 1.30, 95% CI 1.05-1.62), and less so for PFOS (RR 1.20, 95% CI 0.91-1.58), they noted in the Journal of Clinical Oncology.

"Our positive findings were generally concentrated among hormone receptor-negative tumors," White and team wrote, adding that this suggests that per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) "may act through nonhormonal mechanisms, consistent with the evidence that many PFAS are only weak endocrine disrupting chemicals and that other relevant mechanisms, such as epigenetic alterations and immunosuppression, may underlie these associations."

"These findings have important public health implications given the limited established risk factors for ER-negative tumors, which are generally more aggressive," they concluded.

White told MedPage Today that "there are a lot of factors related to a woman's risk of developing breast cancer. Our findings suggest these chemicals may be one contributor to ER-negative breast cancer risk specifically, and if women have concerns about their PFAS exposure, reducing exposure to sources such as contaminated water would be a very reasonable step."

She pointed out that the compounds assessed here "have been phased out from industry and largely replaced by other PFAS compounds. Most of us still have measurable levels of these compounds in our bodies and it is important to document the different health outcomes or cancer tumor sites that are related to exposure to these compounds."

"From a public health perspective, we probably want to start shifting our focus to the health effects of these replacement PFAS compounds that are being used more today," she added.

There have been several other studies that have demonstrated positive associations between PFOS and PFOA and ER-negative tumors, including an analysis of the Prostate, Lung, Colorectal, and Ovarian Cancer Screening Trial and a French study.

For this analysis, the authors used the Sister Study, a prospective cohort of 50,884 breast cancer-free women ages 35 to 74, each of whom had a full or half-sister diagnosed with breast cancer, enrolled in the U.S. and Puerto Rico between 2003 and 2009.

The researchers included 1,609 women who developed breast cancer and a comparison sample of 2,269 women. They were followed for a median of 5.9 and 9.7 years, and had a median baseline age of 57.2 and 55.6 years, respectively.

White observed that she and her team oversampled women with ER-negative tumors to improve the study's statistical power. "These tumors are less frequently diagnosed and so they've been harder to study," she said.

White and her team quantified 17 PFAS in prediagnostic plasma using liquid chromatography-high-resolution mass spectrometry.

They also observed a potential link between n-methylperfluoro-1-octanesulfonamidoacetic acid and ER-negative breast cancer, although that association did not reach statistical significance (HR 1.42, 95% CI 0.99-2.04).

On the other hand, perfluoro-n-tridecanoic acid was inversely associated with ER-negative tumors (HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.41-0.97).

Perfluorooctane sulfonamide (PFOSA), which was not commonly detected (6.9%), was positively associated with ER-positive tumors (HR 1.36, 95% CI 1.03-1.81).

Regarding overall breast cancer incidence, White and colleagues found that PFOSA showed a trend toward higher risk among patients with detectable versus non-detectable concentrations (HR 1.29, 95% CI 0.99-1.67), while perfluoro-n-decanoic acid showed a "suggestive" positive association (HR 1.17, 95% CI 0.95-1.44).

There were "negligible" associations between the rest of the PFAS and overall breast cancer incidence.

#5659. Infant Bleeding Rises as Newborn Vitamin K Shots Have Fallen

— Brain bleed risk more than doubled in infants who missed routine vitamin K shots

Newborns who missed routine vitamin K shots had higher bleeding risks and more than double the risk of intracranial hemorrhage, a nationwide study of over 5 million infants showed.

Infants who did not receive prophylactic vitamin K shots, the share of which increased from 3.1% in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025, had a 47% higher bleeding risk by 6 months (288.0 vs 185.9 per 10,000; adjusted risk ratio [RR] 1.47, 95% CI 1.43-1.51), reported Heather Burris, MD, MPH, of the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, and colleagues in JAMA.

They also had more than twice the risks of intracranial bleeding (33.0 vs 13.2 per 10,000; adjusted RR 2.43, 95% CI 2.26-2.62) and death with concurrent bleeding during the birth hospitalization (2.9 vs 1.1 per 10,000; adjusted RR 2.69, 95% CI 2.09-3.47).

Diagnosed vitamin K deficiency tripled in infants and vitamin K deficiency bleeding more than quadrupled during this period, noted Elizabeth Wolf, MD, MPH, of Virginia Commonwealth University in Richmond, and co-authors in a related JAMA Pediatrics research letter.

Among children ages 0 to 6 months, the rate of vitamin K deficiency climbed from 11.8 to 37.3 per 100,000 from 2017 to 2025, while vitamin K deficiency bleeding rose from 24.0 to 107.4 per 100,000.

Brain hemorrhages occurred in 6.9% of infants diagnosed with vitamin K deficiency and 2.4% of those with vitamin K-deficient bleeding.

Both studies leveraged electronic health record data from January 2017 through December 2025 using the Epic Cosmos research platform to evaluate infants born at 35 weeks' gestation or later. The JAMA study followed 5.24 million newborns for the first 6 months of life. The JAMA Pediatrics study evaluated 11 million U.S. infants ages 0 to 6 months who received care from 2017 through 2025.

Vitamin K is required to activate clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, Wolf and co-authors noted. Newborns can be deficient in vitamin K due to low transplacental transfer, limited gut synthesis, low breast milk concentration, and poor gastrointestinal absorption, they said.

The American Academy of Pediatrics has recommended vitamin K shots since 1961. However, parental rejection of prophylactic vitamin K has increased in recent years, placing more infants at risk for vitamin K deficiency bleeding, Wolf and colleagues observed.

"This study shows the real-world consequences of vitamin K refusal," Wolf told MedPage Today. "Vitamin K-deficient bleeding can be very serious in babies. When the bleeding occurs in the brain, it can result in permanent neurologic damage or even death."

Classical vitamin K deficiency occurs between 2 days and 1 week after birth and leads to umbilical bleeding and bruising. Late vitamin K deficiency occurs between ages 1 week and 6 months and has a 30% to 60% risk of intracranial hemorrhage. Studies have shown that infants without vitamin K shots were 81 times more likely to develop late vitamin K deficiency bleeding.

Temporal trends in the JAMA study showed year-over-year increases in the number of infants with bleeding and these trends differed significantly by vitamin K receipt, noted Laura Kair, MD, MAS, of the University of California Davis School of Medicine in Sacramento, and colleagues in an accompanying editorial.

"While the causes underlying these trends remain uncertain, the authors speculate that maternal-infant dyads may have had more severe medical comorbidities in recent years, and they emphasize that bleeding rates rose significantly faster among those with vitamin K nonreceipt," Kair and colleagues wrote.

"As with all serious but rare outcomes, vitamin K deficiency bleeding risk is a difficult concept to communicate, and when presented as a percentage may seem purely theoretical," the editorialists noted.

"Based on the authors' calculation of number needed to harm, one additional infant would have a bleeding event if just 114 infants did not receive vitamin K," Kair and co-authors pointed out. "This number needed to harm provides a powerful narrative that may be more readily accessible to parents, supporting more effective counseling and decision-making."

Study limitations included reliance on Epic Cosmos data, which excludes infants treated at facilities using other electronic health record systems.

"In countries such as France, Germany, the Netherlands, Switzerland, and Canada, oral vitamin K is offered either routinely or alternatively to intramuscular vitamin K," wrote Wolf and colleagues. "Although the oral form can be less effective in preventing late vitamin K deficiency, a harm-reduction approach that offers oral vitamin K as a second-line alternative may be warranted in the U.S. if rejection of injectable vitamin K continues."
