#5657. CMS’ final 2027 outpatient pay rule brings hospitals little relief on 340B, site-neutral changes

CMS’ final 2027 outpatient pay rule brings hospitals little relief on 340B, site-neutral changes" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services on Tuesday finalized its annual outpatient hospital payments rule with a lower-than-proposed rate bump and its major, industry-opposed policy shifts moderated, but largely intact.

The 2027 Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment (OPPS) and Ambulatory Surgical Center (ASC) Payment Systems rule outlines a 2.3% reimbursement increase for those meeting applicable quality reporting requirements. That’s below the proposed 2.4% increase and reflects a 3.2% projected hospital market basket increase and a 0.9 percentage point productivity adjustment.

The agency is also moving forward with a substantial and controversial cut in 340B drug reimbursements, though not quite to the extent that it initially proposed.

The final rule adjusts these drug payments down from the current bar of average sales price (ASP) plus 6% to ASP minus 28%, as opposed to the proposed 33.4% below ASP. To make the reimbursement change budget neutral as required by statute, OPPS payments for non-drug services will be boosted by 7.5%.

CMS said it tweaked the proposed 340B reimbursement cut based on 340B ceiling price data from the Health Resources and Services Administration, with the baseline reductions informed by a drug acquisition cost survey it conducted earlier this year. Those changes will reduce Original Medicare drug payments by $4.35 billion and the drug payments from beneficiaries by $1.1 billion (or $900 on average per beneficiary who receives an affected drug from a hospital outpatient department) in the policy’s first year, CMS said.

The rate adjustment did little to calm hospital industry groups who’d railed against the 340B reimbursement changes as a threat to safety-net care and a gift to for-profit hospitals that do not participate in the subsidy program but would benefit from the budget-neutral offset. The American Hospital Association, the Association of American Medical Colleges and America’s Essential Hospitals each condemned the finalized policy in reaction statements, with the latter two issuing more forceful rebukes.

“CMS has based its reimbursement to 340B hospitals on the results of a hasty and faulty survey, failing to follow the clear requirements of the Medicare statute,” AAMC Chief Health Care Officer Jonathan Jaffery, M.D., said. “The drug payment cuts disproportionately affect and target non-profit and public hospitals serving low-income patients, while redistributing billions of dollars to hospitals that do not share the same safety-net and academic missions. These cuts threaten access to critical services made possible by the 340B program and will lead to worse health outcomes for patients.”

“Rather than strengthening and preserving safety net funding, CMS is instead prioritizing hospitals that do not serve the safety net and nodding to the pharmaceutical industry's interests,” AEH’s statement reads. “These cuts are landing at a time when essential hospitals and their mission are more important than ever, as millions of people risk losing their Medicaid coverage in the coming months.”

The Federation of American Hospitals, which represents for-profit hospitals that do not participate in 340B, struck a different tone, calling the rulemaking “a win for patients, taxpayers and the hospitals that communities depend on.”

“By bringing Medicare drug payments more in line with actual costs, this reform will lower seniors’ out-of-pocket expenses and redirect billions in Medicare dollars where they’re needed most—supporting access to care for patients served by small and rural hospitals across the country,” Charlene MacDonald, the group’s president and CEO, said in a statement. “We applaud the Administration for advancing a smarter, fairer approach to Medicare payment.”

Additionally, CMS finalized an increase in an annual OPPS conversion factor to non-drug items and services, speeding up the agency’s effort to offset a prior $7.8 billion recoupment to 340B hospitals it was forced to make after previously reducing 340B rates contrary to law. But while this accelerated payback—often described by non-340B hospitals as a clawback—was proposed as an increase from 0.5% to 3%, the final rule brings the conversion factor to 2%.

AHA Senior Vice President of Public Policy Analysis and Development Ashley Thompson described both 340B policy changes together as a “continued assault” on the subsidy program that “will further stress hospitals’ ability to care for their patients.” AAMC’s Jaffery said the combined policies’ impact “will be devastating to patients,” and that his group “remains committed to pursuing all available avenues to reverse these payment cuts.”

Further rankling the hospital industry was the final rule’s continued push toward site-neutral payment policy and a phase-out of the inpatient-only list.

For the former, the agency will apply Physician Fee Schedule payment rates for some imaging services to off-campus provider-based departments. In line with the proposed rule, CMS said it expects the plan to trigger first-year reductions in Medicare Part B expenditures and beneficiary cost-sharing obligations of $260 million and $70 million, while also reducing a market incentive for provider consolidation.

Meanwhile, CMS finalized its proposal to remove 647 services from the inpatient-only list, allowing them to be delivered and paid for in the lower-cost outpatient setting.

“Both policies are misguided,” AHA’s Thompson said, “and overlook the unique role hospital outpatient departments play in delivering care to patients in communities nationwide. Hospital outpatient departments treat sicker and more complex groups of patients than independent physician practices, including those with higher rates of disability and who are more likely to come from low-income and rural communities.”

CMS’ fact sheet on the 1,270-page annual rule also noted various changes to quality reporting programs for hospital outpatient departments and ASCs, a proposal to require prior authorization for eight botulinum toxin injection codes CMS said it has seen a jump in claim volume, and new permission for accreditation organizations to assess hospitals’ compliance with EMTALA (the Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act of 1986).

“CMS is committed to spending taxpayer funds wisely and efficiently, so [that] America’s seniors can continue getting the care they need,” CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., said in a release. “By right-sizing payments and rooting out waste, today’s reforms will drive affordability in Medicare for current beneficiaries while ensuring it will still be there to serve their children and grandchildren.”

#5656. DUOTAP Trial: Postdilation Sets Up TAVR for Success

— Extra step optimizes transcatheter heart valve geometry for better downstream hemodynamics

Routine postdilation conferred several upsides in transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) with a balloon-expandable platform, according to emerging trial evidence.

In the DUOTAP trial, routine postdilation largely corrected any Sapien device asymmetry, with transcatheter heart valve (THV) asymmetry index on fluoroscopy reduced by 70% compared to TAVR without postdilation, in the optimization of THV geometry, according to Maximilian Autherith, MD, of the Medical University of Vienna.

This was associated with downstream benefits, such as a 67% reduction in more-than-mild paravalvular leak (PVL) on pre-discharge echocardiography after TAVR, and a 63% reduction in hypo-attenuated leaflet thickening (HALT) per cardiac CT at 3 months, he reported at the Transcatheter Cardiovascular Therapeutics annual conference hosted by the Cardiovascular Research Foundation, with study results simultaneously published in JAMA Cardiology.

"However, what we don't know to date is if this also translates into longer valve durability and ultimately better clinical long-term outcomes. This remains to be investigated," Autherith cautioned during a press conference.

Even so, the "really impressive" lowering of HALT in particular was highlighted by Adnan Chhatriwalla, MD, of Saint Luke's Mid America Heart Institute in Kansas City, Missouri. Considering the lower PVL as well, "these data suggest that we should routinely do [postdilation]," Chhatriwalla commented during the press conference.

In TAVR, postdilation is the controversial step of reinflating the balloon a second time inside the newly deployed THV, giving it a so-called "double tap" that in theory covers the operator's bases for optimizing THV geometry in the absence of a good way to gauge device expansion. If left alone, asymmetric device expansion may be associated with higher residual gradients, PVL, and impaired THV performance.

Safety is a major concern with postdilation, however, especially when it comes to possible annulus rupture, valve migration, and conduction system disruption.

"So you don't want to take it for no reason," said Susheel Kodali, MD, of NYU Langone Health in New York City, another panelist at TCT.

Kodali said that echocardiographic and fluoroscopic characteristics will be key to defining who gets TAVR with postdilation. He also cited predilation and longer balloon inflation as other strategies for optimizing THV valve expansion -- which is really the ultimate goal for the patient.

"It's valve expansion to the maximum that's needed for that patient, and that's where AI [artificial intelligence], echo, fluoro, all of these things are going to help us understand who to do [postdilation] in," Kodali commented. Currently, "we just inflate, deflate, and don't assess how is the valve expanded. I think we need to be better at that."

Reassuringly, DUOTAP reported a favorable safety trend for routine postdilation, albeit without reaching a statistical difference. Procedural or early clinical adverse events at 30 days reached 24.3% with postdilation versus 31.1% with controls. A new conduction system disorder requiring pacemaker implantation was logged in 20.3% and 21.6% of patients, respectively.

"Certainly yes, there may be some consequences to universally doing a double tap. But having said that, we very clearly often will see asymmetric expansion," said Sammy Elmariah, MD, of UCSF Health in San Francisco. "Some individuals don't pursue it and don't postdilate. And so at least this gives us more motivation to at least, in a selective fashion, to start postdilating those valves and to really aim for symmetric expansion of the valve."

The single-blind, single-center trial enrolled people with severe aortic stenosis undergoing transfemoral TAVR with a Sapien balloon-expandable platform. Participants had to have no high-risk features on CT, no bicuspid aortic valves, and no valve-in-valve procedures, among other exclusion criteria.

Investigators randomized 148 TAVR patients 1:1 to postdilation or no postdilation.

Autherith noted that this was a typical TAVR cohort with a median age of 81 years, 47% women, and a EuroScore-II of 2.3%. The THV sizes chosen were a mix of 23 mm (29.0%), 26 mm (48.7%), and 29 mm (22.3%). A Sapien device with Resilia tissue was given to 42.6% of the group.

Fluoroscopic analysis indicated that postdilation corrects THV asymmetry by inducing valve height reduction on the outer curve of the device.

Postdilation consistently corrected asymmetry across prespecified subgroups including those by sex, THV size, and aortic valve calcification. Only on a post hoc exploratory analysis did a signal emerge that possibly people who got predilation did not have the same benefit of postdilation, according to Autherith.

"Regarding the subgroup analysis, these were only 11 patients receiving predilation, so confidence intervals were quite wide. I think it's difficult to interpret, but of course this is also an important consideration," he said during the press conference.

Other findings include postdilation being tied to increased Doppler velocity index and reduced residual trans-prosthetic gradients on echocardiography. Cardiac CTs also linked the intervention to valves with larger inflow and midframe areas, plus an increase in outflow area, at 3 months.

#5655. Oracle connects AI-driven testing with a new approach to database security

Frontier AI models that uncover software flaws by the hundreds are forcing database providers into larger, faster patch cycles, and real application testing is becoming the safeguard that keeps those fixes from breaking production systems. The same AI wave is also undermining security rules written into applications.

Oracle Corp. has responded on two fronts, hardening its code against outside attackers while moving agent controls down to the data layer. The first effort began when the company turned an early-access frontier model on its own software, according to Juan Loaiza (pictured), executive vice president of Oracle Database Technologies at Oracle.

“Back in March, we got early access to the Mythos model and we ran it against our code and it started finding all these security vulnerabilities,” Loaiza said. “It’s turning up some very serious security issues. And so we said, ‘Hey, this is a code red moment. The house is on fire.'”

Loaiza spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed why AI-discovered vulnerabilities, AI-generated code and AI agents require enterprises to treat security as a data problem. (* Disclosure below.)

Most of Oracle’s response to AI-discovered vulnerabilities is landing in its regular quarterly patches, which have grown much larger as a result, Loaiza explained. Customers must automate patching and stay current, but every large patch raises fears of regression in systems that cannot fail.

“We have something called Real Application Testing where we can capture real workload and run it to make sure that your workload is not affected by these patches,” Loaiza said. “It’s not quite as simple as just apply because the applications that people run are extraordinarily complex. They run entire countries, entire industries.”

Patching handles outside attackers. Internal AI use is a separate threat, because applications have traditionally enforced end-user security, and AI now writes much of that code or goes straight to the data. Oracle’s answer is Deep Data Security, which began shipping in April and passes an authenticated user’s identity as an encrypted token through to the database. The company has since extended those authorization controls across remote databases, lakehouse data and related tables.

“The new world as I see it is all these end-user security rules have to be enforced where AI can’t bypass them, which means all the way down in the data,” Loaiza said. “The AI agent has to get your identity. It’s acting on behalf of you. It can’t leak the data if it can’t see the data.”

Business rules follow the same logic. Application code has always blocked a credit card charge above the customer’s limit, but an AI agent told to enforce that rule may not comply, Loaiza noted. Oracle is providing declarative ways to define such rules, along with SQL Assertions that check whether changes made through SQL are valid.

“There’s credit limits, there’s all sorts of things that are business rules that can’t be violated. And again, if we move those all the way down into the data, then no matter how you access the data, what mechanism you use, how AI is used, it cannot violate those rules,” Loaiza said.

Cigna offers investors a look at its new Lead to One strategy" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Cigna offered investors additional color on its new healthcare transformation strategy on Thursday morning.

First unveiled at the company's investor day on Sept. 30, the Lead to One initiative aims to bring together the array of assets under the Cigna Group's umbrella—from medical and pharmacy benefits to behavioral health to specialty care—to address the individual needs of members and patients.

CEO Brian Evanko said during Cigna's earnings call that the program aims to lean on data analytics and technology to identify risks more quickly and deliver personalized supports. The goal, he said, is to drive better outcomes while lowering healthcare costs in tandem.

"Our Lead to One vision will benefit all customers, and we see a particular opportunity with the most clinically complex patient needs, where healthcare costs are increasingly concentrated and represent over 50% of total healthcare spending," he said.

Evanko said that the approach helps to establish "clear strategic growth framework for creating long-term value."

"It is an exciting time here at The Cigna Group as our company unifies around a single vision, Lead to One, and begins to compound the distinctive capabilities we have developed to capture the opportunity set in front of us," he said.

In addition, the company is undertaking an initiative called Accelerate to One, which aims to support operational efficiency for its workforce while supporting greater accountability and better decision-making. Evanko said that program is set to drive $3 billion in run rate savings for the company by 2030.

Evanko said the company expects to see those savings opportunities materialize across the company.

Cigna is the latest health insurance company to boost its guidance for the year on the back of its Q3 results.

The company released its earnings report Thursday morning, posting $1.4 billion in profit. That's down year over year from the $1.9 billion haul the company reported in the third quarter of 2025.

Through the first three quarters of the year, the company has earned $4.8 billion in profit, on par with the $4.7 billion posted for the first nine months of 2025. Total revenue at the end of Q3 was $213.8 billion, growing from $202.4 billion through three quarters in 2025.

CEO Brian Evanko said in the release that the company's current financial strategy is rooted in three key principles, including "driving core growth, leveraging our distinct capabilities and executing with discipline."

"As we put our strategy in action, our strong third quarter results demonstrate how we are building on this momentum by making health care more affordable and personalized, while advancing Accelerate to One to drive productivity, reduce costs, and support sustained long-term earnings growth," he said.

The company reported a medical loss ratio in the quarter of 85%, up slightly from 84.8% in Q3 2025. Cigna attributed the uptick to higher costs in its employer plans, while lower costs in the individual market segment did partially offset this trend.

Cigna Healthcare, the company's core insurance business, reported 18.45 million members as of Q3. By comparison, the insurer had 18.1 million members at the end of 2025.

Pharmacy benefit membership, meanwhile, was 117.7 million, down 123.6 million as of Dec. 31, 2025. Cigna said the decrease reflects "expected client transitions" as well as lower membership at its health plan clients.

Its Evernorth unit reported $63.8 billion in adjusted revenue for the quarter, up from $61.5 billion a year ago. Highlights include ongoing organic growth in its specialty pharmacy business, the company said.

Cigna Healthcare reported $11.7 billion in adjusted revenue for Q3, up from $10.7 billion in the prior-year quarter. The company said this largely reflects higher premium revenue as it adapts to higher medical costs.

#5651. This mysterious mushroom makes people see hundreds of tiny humans

People living thousands of miles apart have reported an extraordinarily strange experience after eating certain wild mushrooms. They begin seeing tiny human figures that appear to move through the real world, walking around objects, climbing over surfaces, and interacting with their surroundings.

These visions are known as Lilliputian hallucinations, named after the miniature inhabitants of "Gulliver's Travels," who stand just 6 inches tall. For decades, researchers suspected that cultural beliefs and folklore might explain why people in different regions described such similar experiences.

Now, a new study provides evidence that the phenomenon has a biological explanation.

Researchers at the University of Utah (U) used DNA sequencing to identify Lanmaoa asiatica as the mushroom responsible for these unusual hallucinations in Southwest China and the northern Philippines. Surprisingly, their investigation found no evidence of any known psychoactive mushroom compounds, including psilocybin.

The findings suggest that the mushroom may produce an entirely unfamiliar hallucinogenic substance. Identifying that chemical could help scientists better understand neurological disorders, unusual visual experiences, and the processes through which the brain creates our perception of reality.

The research was conducted by Colin Domnauer, a doctoral student at the U, and Bryn Dentinger, a mycologist affiliated with the university and the Natural History Museum of Utah. Their findings were published in the journal Mycologia.

In an interview with @theU, Domnauer explained how researchers traced the mushroom's identity, what makes its effects so unusual, and why the discovery could have implications far beyond the study of fungi.

A Century-Old Mystery of Tiny Human Hallucinations

The scientific mystery dates back to 1934, when Western researchers learned that people in Papua New Guinea sometimes experienced vivid visions of miniature humans after eating wild mushrooms. The bizarre effect became known as "mushroom madness."

During the 1950s and 1960s, anthropologists and mushroom specialists traveled to Papua New Guinea to investigate. Their work pointed toward several possible species belonging to the Boletaceae (bolete) family.

However, chemical testing failed to reveal any substances that could explain the hallucinations. Samples were even examined by Albert Hofmann, the scientist who first isolated psilocybin and discovered LSD. He, too, was unable to identify an active ingredient.

With no chemical explanation available, some researchers began questioning whether the mushrooms were responsible at all. They suggested that the visions might instead arise from cultural expectations or traditional beliefs. By the end of the 1960s, scientific investigation of the phenomenon had largely stopped.

The mystery resurfaced during the 1990s, when people in Yunnan, Southwest China, reported similar hallucinations after eating bolete mushrooms. Although the precise species remained uncertain, researchers suspected a recently described mushroom called Lanmaoa asiatica.

Scientists Identify the Mushroom Behind the Strange Visions

Another important clue appeared in 2024, when Domnauer learned of comparable experiences among an Indigenous community in the remote Northern Cordillera region of the Philippines.

Community members described a wild edible mushroom called "Sedesdem" that could sometimes cause people to see miniature human figures. Similar mushrooms were known locally as "Nonda" in Papua New Guinea and "Jian shou qing" in Yunnan.

These mushrooms have an important place in local food traditions, but consuming them without thoroughly cooking them can trigger the unusual hallucinations.

The Philippine accounts represented a third independent report of wild mushrooms causing remarkably similar visions of tiny people.

To investigate, Domnauer traveled to Yunnan and the Philippines, interviewed local residents, and collected specimens of L. asiatica along with other mushrooms belonging to the Lanmaoa genus.

The fieldwork included the first scientific survey of fungi in the northern Philippines. Researchers then analyzed DNA from the collected mushrooms to establish their identities and evolutionary relationships.

The results revealed that the mushrooms called Jian shou qing in China and Sedesdem in the Philippines were both L. asiatica.

This was an unexpected finding because scientists had previously believed the species occurred only in China.

Dentinger also visited Papua New Guinea in hopes of collecting specimens from the location where the mystery originally began. Unfortunately, unusually dry weather made it impossible to obtain samples for genetic comparison.

Although the Papua New Guinea mushroom remains unverified, the evidence from China and the Philippines provides a compelling connection. Three geographically separated cultures have described the same highly specific hallucinations, and DNA testing has linked two of those cases to a single mushroom species.

That consistency strongly suggests a shared chemical and neurological explanation rather than unrelated cultural influences.

Hallucinations of Tiny Humans That Seem Remarkably Real

What makes these hallucinations especially unusual is their striking similarity across different accounts.

People typically describe seeing dozens or even hundreds of miniature figures, generally measuring between 3 and 30 centimeters tall. The figures appear with extraordinary clarity, often seeming as solid and convincing as actual people.

According to Domnauer, approximately 90% of those experiencing the visions describe figures resembling elves, clowns, or other fairy-like characters, often wearing brightly colored clothing.

Even more surprising is the way these imaginary figures seem to behave.

Rather than floating through walls or ignoring their surroundings, they appear to follow familiar physical rules. They walk around obstacles, move across ordinary objects, and sometimes tumble from the edges of tables.

Domnauer recalled one particularly unusual account involving someone eating soup. The person reported seeing tiny humans leap from a spoon into the bowl, where they began swimming. When the person took another spoonful, the miniature figures reportedly remained visible inside their mouth.

Such detailed interactions distinguish these visions from many other forms of drug-induced hallucination.

A Mysterious Psychedelic Compound Unlike Any Known Drug

Scientists also investigated whether L. asiatica contains any of the chemicals already known to cause psychedelic experiences.

Using both chemical testing and genetic analysis, the researchers searched for established psychoactive compounds found in other mushroom species.

The absence of familiar hallucinogens was particularly intriguing because the mushroom's effects differ so dramatically from those associated with known psychedelic drugs.

Researchers now suspect that L. asiatica produces an unidentified psychoactive substance responsible for the tiny human hallucinations.

The compound has not yet been isolated or chemically identified, so its exact nature and mechanism remain unknown.

Discovering it could open an entirely new avenue of research into how certain chemicals alter visual perception.

What the Mushroom Could Reveal About the Human Brain

Although L. asiatica provides an unusually consistent trigger for Lilliputian hallucinations, the phenomenon is not limited to mushroom consumption.

Stories involving miniature humanlike beings appear throughout folklore around the world. Similar hallucinations have also been documented in people experiencing alcohol withdrawal, dementia, macular degeneration, and other neurological conditions.

These connections suggest that the visions may arise from a fundamental feature of the way the human brain processes visual information.

However, scientists still do not fully understand the neurological mechanisms responsible for these experiences or how best to treat them when they occur in medical settings.

This is where the mysterious mushroom could become especially valuable.

Unlike the neurological and medical conditions in which Lilliputian hallucinations occur relatively rarely, L. asiatica can produce the phenomenon in a more consistent and recognizable way.

If researchers can isolate the chemical responsible, they may gain a useful tool for investigating the brain circuits and processes that create these unusually detailed visual experiences.

Such research could eventually improve scientific understanding of hallucinations associated with neurological diseases.

The research team's next major objective is to isolate and identify the suspected psychedelic compound.

DNA Sequencing Reveals Four Previously Unknown Mushroom Species

The investigation also produced important discoveries about fungal biodiversity.

Rather than studying L. asiatica alone, Domnauer and Dentinger conducted the first comprehensive genomic analysis of the Lanmaoa genus.

They examined 53 mushroom specimens collected from natural habitats and preserved in fungarium collections around the world.

Genetic sequencing revealed 17 species within the group, including four species previously unknown to science.

Remarkably, two of those newly identified species had already been preserved in existing collections in the United States. Their distinct identities had gone unrecognized until researchers examined their DNA.

The analysis also indicated that L. asiatica is the only species in the genus currently known to produce psychoactive effects.

Scientists are now working to reconstruct the group's evolutionary history. They hope to determine how the unusual chemical trait developed and whether closely related mushrooms might produce comparable substances.

The findings also demonstrate the scientific value of museum collections. Specimens preserved for years can contain biological discoveries that become apparent only when newer analytical techniques are applied.

For Domnauer, the hidden diversity found in these collections is a reminder that many species and potentially important biological characteristics remain undiscovered, even among organisms that scientists have already collected.

Exploring Fungi Could Lead to New Medicines and Discoveries

The broader implications extend well beyond unusual hallucinations.

Fungi remain one of the least thoroughly explored groups of organisms, and researchers believe their chemical diversity could provide valuable clues about biology, medicine, and the nervous system.

One of the most famous examples is penicillin, the antibiotic originally obtained from a fungus that transformed the treatment of bacterial infections and became one of the most consequential medical discoveries of the last century.

Scientists hope continued exploration of fungal biodiversity could reveal other medically useful compounds and previously unknown biological processes.

The mysterious effects of L. asiatica illustrate just how much remains to be learned about the fungal kingdom. A mushroom long consumed by communities in Asia may contain a substance capable of revealing new information about the human brain and how it creates conscious experience.

The research received funding from the National Science Foundation (award #DEB-2114785).

#5650. Physician Groups Give Mixed Reviews on Medicare Fee Schedule Final Rule

— Pay cut, modifier-25 rule are panned, but payment expansion for primary care gets good marks

Physician groups had mixed opinions on the final Medicare Physician Fee Schedule rule for 2027, which included slightly increased pay cuts for doctors who treat Medicare beneficiaries, compared to a proposed rule released in July.

The rule issued Wednesday by CMS includes a 2.31% decrease in the conversion factor -- the multiplier used to determine payment for each service or procedure performed -- for physicians who don't participate in an advanced payment model (APM). There is also a smaller decrease of 1.83% for physicians participating in APMs. The decreases in the proposed rule issued in July were 1.68% and 1.19%, respectively, for the two groups.

"Medicare should reward clinicians for keeping people healthy," HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said in a press release. "We are putting prevention and primary care at the center of Medicare, closing payment loopholes, and cracking down on waste. This rule directs resources toward coordinated care that puts patients first. We are changing what Medicare pays for to change what our health system delivers."

Not surprisingly, physician groups were unhappy with the pay cut.

"The American Academy of Neurology (AAN) is deeply concerned with year-over-year cuts to physician payments and is committed to working with Congress to avert this cut before it goes into effect for 2027," the organization said in a statement. "The AAN will continue to work with legislators in support of payment reform efforts to promote a sustainable payment system, such as ensuring physicians receive an inflationary adjustment tied to the Medicare Economic Index."

"The continued erosion of Medicare physician payments, combined with policies that fail to recognize the complexity of care provided by rheumatologists, threatens the stability of physician practices and patients' access to essential care," William Harvey, MD, MSc, president of the American College of Rheumatology (ACR), said in a statement. "The ACR urges Congress and CMS to pursue meaningful, long-term payment reforms that account for the real cost of practicing medicine and protect access to specialty care, particularly for patients in rural and underserved communities."

Physician organizations also panned CMS's decision to implement the proposed "modifier-25" rule, which says that if two or more services are performed on the same day, the most expensive service (either surgical or evaluation and management [E/M] visits) would be paid at 100%, and all other surgical procedure(s) or E/M visit(s) would be paid at 50%.

"Congress must intervene to prevent further harm by immediately fixing cuts to the conversion factor, along with changes to modifier 25," Anders Gilberg, senior vice president for government affairs at the Medical Group Management Association, said in a statement.

However, other clinicians -- such as those who work in accountable care organizations (ACOs) -- were pleased with several of the changes. In a statement from Accountable for Health, which represents ACOs, CEO Mara McDermott said her group "welcomes CMS's continued efforts to move Medicare away from a broken fee-for-service system that rewards volume and toward one that holds providers accountable for quality and spending."

The fee schedule "takes several meaningful steps in that direction. It establishes a 32% payment increase for qualifying visits by clinicians in the Medicare Shared Savings Program and LEAD Model [two Medicare ACO models], increases from 50% to 75% the credit ACOs receive for savings achieved in prior years, and allows eligible ACOs to reduce or eliminate Medicare Part B cost-sharing for beneficiaries," McDermott noted.

The American Academy of Family Physicians (AAFP) praised the rule's expansion of the Primary Care Exception, which allows qualifying residents to provide more complex office and outpatient care without a teaching physician in the room. "This change will give residents additional experience caring for complex Medicare patients as they prepare for independent practice," the AAFP said in a statement.

The academy also applauded the rule's expansion of payment for more comprehensive primary care services, including shared medical appointments, maternity care, tobacco cessation, and advance care planning.

The Primary Care Collaborative echoed those comments, noting that the rule also included reimbursement for health coaching and more resources to integrate behavioral healthcare. "These changes -- especially when paired with an effort to more accurately price primary care -- are important steps toward a more effective system focused on better health," President and CEO Ann Greiner said in a statement.

ATA Action, the lobbying affiliate of the American Telemedicine Association, praised CMS for delaying by 2 years a rule requiring that only clinical staff directly employed by the billing practice may furnish remote physiologic or therapeutic monitoring services. "CMS listened," said Kyle Zebley, CEO of the ATA and executive director of ATA Action, in a statement. "By delaying this requirement, the agency has given patients, practices, and health systems time to keep remote monitoring programs running while we work toward a lasting solution."

Even with all the applause, the reimbursement cuts remained top of mind for many groups.

"These cuts are not happening in isolation," Jerry Penso, MD, president and CEO of the American Medical Group Association, said in a statement. "Our members are absorbing reductions to physician and clinician reimbursement and outpatient drug reimbursement at the same time they face a trillion dollars in pending Medicaid cuts. Each one makes it harder to sustain the staff, technology, and care models patients depend on. Congress must enact lasting reforms now, before access to care suffers."

#5649. Measles update: Wisconsin reports first measles-associated death since 1990

Measles update: Wisconsin reports first measles-associated death since 1990" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Wisconsin Department of Health Services on Thursday reported its first measles-outbreak associated death since 1990.

The deceased was an infant whose case was among many in the southwestern part of the state, for whom the coroner listed measles as immediate cause of death. As of Nov. 3, the department has reported 431 cases across 13 counties in 2026, the highest number of cases in over 35 years. All but three of those are among individuals who were not vaccinated, and nine have involved hospitalizations.

"Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease," Kirsten Johnson, secretary of the Wisconsin Department of Health Services, said in the announcement. "Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is important for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family."

As of Oct. 29, the Centers for Disease Control reports 4,852 confirmed cases of measles this year across the country, far outpacing 2025's total of 2,289. Of these, 511 have been hospitalized (versus 244 in 2025) and three deaths have been recognized—though health officials in Pennsylvania alone said they have confirmed five measles-associated deaths. The CDC has said its death count may change after it completes work to develop a new standardized case definition for "deaths due to measles."

The New York State Department of Health on Monday afternoon reported its first measles-associated death in 30 years.

The state has counted 210 total cases this year as of Nov. 3. The reported death was a child in the northern Lewis County, according to the department. No information was given about the child's specific illness or the role measles infection may have played in their death.

Sixteen confirmed cases of measles have been reported in Lewis County as of Tuesday, the department said. Many of New York's cases are located among upstate counties, and just eight are in New York City, according to the department.

In a statement, New York Governor Kathy Hochul—who on Oct. 5 declared a Disaster Emergency in response to rising measles case rates—expressed her sympathies to the child's family and told residents that "vaccination remains our best protection against this dangerous disease."

"This is New York’s first measles-related death in 30 years, a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses," the statement reads, echoing criticisms of federal health leadership voiced by Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro regarding measles-associated deaths in his own state.

As of Oct. 29, the Centers for Disease Control reports 4,852 confirmed cases of measles this year across the country, far outpacing 2025's total of 2,289. Of these, 511 have been hospitalized (versus 244 in 2025) and three deaths have been recognized—though health officials in Pennsylvania alone said they have confirmed five measles-associated deaths. The CDC has said its death count may change after it completes work to develop a new standardized case definition for "deaths due to measles."

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services told Fierce Healthcare that it had deployed epidemiologists and other experts to New York after receiving a formal request for support. The support is currently scheduled to run through Nov. 13, and includes on-the-ground "surveillance, data analysis, strategic planning and other outbreak response support," they said.

Of the roughly $100 million in additional measles and vaccine-preventable diseases funding the department has provided via the CDC since August, nearly $2.4 million has gone directly to New York State and $2.1 million to New York City, they said.

"Secretary Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz continue to make clear that the MMR vaccine is the most effective way to prevent measles," they added.

The U.S. is in the midst of its worst measles outbreak in decades, with more than 4,000 cases reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention as of early October and a sixth measles-associated death disclosed by local Pennsylvania officials on Monday.

The vaccine-preventable disease was declared eliminated in the U.S. back in 2000—meaning that there was no endemic spread of the disease—but has resurfaced in force during recent years as declining childhood vaccination rates have pushed most states below the 95% coverage bar for school-age herd immunity.

The CDC had counted 2,289 cases across the entirety of 2025, which had been the country’s highest total since 1990, and several public health officials have warned for months that number would likely be surpassed based on the scale and frequency of early-year cases.

Measles-associated deaths have also accompanied the higher case counts, though just how many is a subject of dispute. While three deaths were confirmed in all of 2025, this year logged its first in late August with Pennsylvania, which hosts more than a quarter of the total cases, now reporting six measles-associated deaths as of Oct. 13. The CDC, however, lists two deaths alongside a note that its count is subject to change, and has promised more broadly to develop a new, standardized case definition to be used across all reporting states.

That discrepancy is an example of friction between federal health leadership and the broader public health community that experts say has contributed to this year’s outbreaks.

Pennsylvania’s initial death announcements in August were contested by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who accused Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro of withholding sufficient information for the CDC to confirm the deaths and using his press conference announcing them as “gaslighting the public” for political purposes.

During an ensuing social media feud, the governor and the secretary described a heated phone call in which Shapiro (at the time) rejected federal assistance and accused Kennedy of fueling the outbreaks with only lukewarm endorsement of the MMR vaccine and a broader concurrent campaign to scale back other routine childhood vaccinations.

Numerous state public health officials and experts have lobbed similar criticisms of Kennedy, who is affiliated with anti-vaccine groups, and federal health agencies under his purview.

The CDC, for its part, has reportedly infused at least $100 million of extra public health funding to states for immunization programs and surveillance, and leading officials including Kennedy and new CDC Director Erica Schwartz, M.D., have described the MMR vaccine as safe and effective when asked directly. Still, the agency has not launched the type of broader vaccine messaging and awareness campaigns that it would have in years past, critics are quick to note.

Pennsylvania isn’t alone in raising alarms over rising measles cases. New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a State Disaster Emergency in early October, the first such declaration in recent years.

#5648. Low-dose aspirin linked to 70% lower dementia risk, but there's a catch

A new analysis from Monash University suggests that low-dose aspirin may be linked to a dramatically lower risk of dementia in older adults with certain genetic characteristics. Researchers found that people with a specific genetic profile who took aspirin had a 70 percent lower relative risk of developing dementia, raising the possibility that genetic testing could eventually help identify people who might benefit from preventive treatments.

The findings, published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association, were based on genetic data from more than 13,500 participants in the landmark ASPREE Trial (Aspirin in Reducing Events in the Elderly). Scientists examined whether differences in participants' genes could help explain why aspirin might affect dementia risk differently from one person to another.

Aspirin Linked to 70% Lower Dementia Risk in Certain People

The most striking results involved genes associated with platelet count. Platelets are small components of the blood that help form clots, and researchers wanted to determine whether genetic variations related to platelet levels could influence aspirin's potential effects on dementia.

After assigning participants genetic scores associated with platelet count, the team compared dementia rates among those who received aspirin and those given a placebo.

Among people in the highest 20 percent of platelet count genetic scores, just 1 percent of aspirin users developed dementia, compared with 3.3 percent of participants taking a placebo. That difference translates to approximately a 70 percent lower relative risk of dementia among those receiving aspirin.

However, the apparent benefit was accompanied by a significant safety concern. In the same genetic group, 4.4 percent of aspirin users experienced major bleeding, compared with 2.1 percent of those receiving a placebo.

A Genetic Clue Could Change Dementia Prevention

Lead author Dr. Peter Fransquet, a Research Fellow at Monash's School of Public Health and Preventive Medicine, said the results suggest that a person's genetic makeup could eventually play an important role in determining which dementia prevention strategies are most appropriate.

"Previous trials found aspirin didn't prevent dementia when everyone was considered together," Dr. Fransquet said.

"Our findings suggest there may be more to the story.

"In people with this particular genetic profile, we saw substantially fewer cases of dementia among those taking aspirin.

"It raises the possibility that genetics could one day help us identify who may benefit from a preventive treatment, rather than taking a one-size-fits-all approach."

The possibility of more targeted prevention is especially important as dementia becomes increasingly common. Dementia Australia estimates that approximately 446,500 people in Australia are living with the condition in 2026. That number is expected to exceed one million by 2065.

Blood Platelets Reveal an Unexpected Dementia Connection

Previous research has connected dementia with platelet activation and aggregation, the processes through which platelets become active and stick together. However, scientists have had a less complete understanding of how a person's overall platelet count might relate to dementia.

The new findings point toward platelet biology as a potentially important area of investigation. Notably, the genetic association identified by researchers did not involve the well-established genetic risk factors typically linked to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia.

"What's particularly interesting is that the signal wasn't linked to the established genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's disease and dementia," Dr. Fransquet said.

"Instead, it's pointing us towards platelet biology and gives us a new avenue to investigate."

Why More Research Is Needed Before Taking Aspirin

Although the findings suggest that aspirin could have different effects depending on a person's genes, researchers emphasize that the results must be confirmed before they can guide medical recommendations.

The next step is to investigate whether the association appears in other populations. Scientists would then need to conduct a clinical trial specifically involving people with the genetic profile identified in the analysis.

"We now need to confirm the finding in other studies and ultimately test it in a trial designed specifically for people with this genetic profile.

"People shouldn't start taking aspirin to prevent dementia on the basis of this study without consulting with their doctor, particularly given the increased risk of serious bleeding.

"If it holds up, the fact that aspirin is already cheap and widely available could make personalized dementia prevention a real possibility."

Materials provided by Monash University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5646. Court blocks CMS' moratorium on new ACA broker registrations

Court blocks CMS' moratorium on new ACA broker registrations" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

A federal court has granted a preliminary injunction to two key groups representing insurance brokers over the Trump administration's moratorium on new broker enrollments.

The District Court of Maryland issued the injunction after determining that the National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals and Health Agents for America "have shown that they are likely to succeed on the merits of their claims under the Administrative Procedure Act."

The court also said that the organizations made clear they would likely suffer significant harm if the moratorium stays in place.

NABIP said that the ruling means that it will restart training for new brokers beginning on Nov. 6.

"Today’s ruling is a significant victory for licensed agents and brokers and the consumers who rely on their expertise," said NABIP President Mychal Walker in an announcement (PDF). "With Open Enrollment already underway, every day matters."

"Lifting the moratorium immediately and beginning training tomorrow will help affected professionals get to work assisting individuals and families in finding coverage that fits their needs and budgets," said Walker.

NABIP initially sued on Oct. 15 to challenge the moratorium. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services instituted the moratorium in late September as part of its broader push to combat fraud on the Affordable Care Act's exchanges.

The National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals is suing the Trump administration over its moratorium on new brokers entering the Affordable Care Act marketplaces.

The organization, the leading trade group for insurance brokers and agents, said the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services' moratorium impacts close to 19,000 brokers and agents who will be barred from registering ahead of open enrollment.

CMS unveiled the moratorium in late September as part of its ongoing push to root out fraud, waste and abuse. In addition, the agency said it would terminate more than 200 agents and brokers that failed to comply with marketplace standards.

The agency said new brokers and agents were disproportionately responsible for submitting inappropriate enrollments and engaging in behaviors at high risk for fraud.

In an announcement (PDF), NABIP says that it supports the broader effort to combat fraud, but that CMS' moratorium "threatens the livelihoods of thousands of legitimate, licensed professionals who have not been accused of fraud and limits consumers’ access to professional assistance as they navigate Open Enrollment."

The organization argues in the lawsuit that the rule instituting the moratorium violates both the Administrative Procedure Act and the Affordable Care Act. The regulation is unlawful as it is "arbitrary, capricious, and unsupported by sufficient evidence," NABIP said.

The 19,000 agents who would be barred from participating under the rule are part of a critical network of professionals who help consumers find coverage that meets their needs, the organization said.

NABIP President Mychal Walker said that CMS should look elsewhere in its fraud efforts.

"The existence of fraud is not in dispute. NABIP has raised these concerns with CMS repeatedly and has offered concrete solutions to address them," Walker said in the announcement. "What is in dispute is whether the appropriate response is to exclude thousands of legitimate agents based solely on whether they registered last year, without any individualized evidence about them."

"There is a better approach: target fraud where it occurs, strengthen the system’s security and hold bad actors accountable while preserving consumers’ access to trusted professionals," Walker continued.

CMS has taken steps to crack down on brokers as the agency views improper ACA enrollments as a key target in its fight against fraud. CMS officials have repeatedly raised concerns that people are enrolled in ACA plans without their knowledge, or despite being deceased.

Earlier this week, the agency revealed it will purge 189,000 enrollees who are currently listed as enrolled in both ACA plans and other coverage, such as Medicaid or Medicare.

#5645. Research prediction: Shift from digital banking to AI-driven finance will transform financial services in 2027

The coming year will signal an abrupt transition from digital banking to intelligent finance, as AI agents and operating models reshape the ways that financial firms acquire customers and provide advice.

This is the central thesis of a new Forrester Research report, “Predictions 2027: Banking and Investing.” The findings were summarized from data involving 915 respondents in the U.S., U.K., and Canada.

Forrester identified several key points of transition. These included fundamental changes through automation in financial discovery and guidance journeys, as well as a belief that although one-third of banks will announce an AI transformation program, only 5% will succeed.

“In 2027, financial services will enter a new phase in which intelligence becomes the primary source of value creation,” said Forrester researchers in the report. “AI assistants are reshaping how customers discover, evaluate and act on financial products; investment participation is expanding despite persistent economic anxiety; and banks are racing to determine whether AI will merely enhance existing operations or fundamentally transform them.”

Forrester’s prediction of a 5% success rate is based on a belief that many banks will rebrand existing AI initiatives as AI-native without significant changes in operational infrastructure. Retention of legacy processes and operating models will prevent an ability to scale AI deployment, a fundamental requirement that AI technology providers such as Dell Technologies Inc. are emphasizing to their clients in the financial services world.

“Ultimately, I think we’ve enough proof points now that AI works and it works really well and it gives you speed and efficiency in your company,” according to David Kennedy, chief financial officer of Dell, during a recent interview with theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. “The question is, can you do that at scale?”

One way that financial institutions will pursue scale is through mergers and acquisitions. Forrester predicts that AI banking technology M&A will increase by 50% in 2027. Acquisition of proprietary data assets, governance capabilities, and AI-native orchestration will require an ability to navigate hybrid computing environments, a need that compute providers such as Advanced Micro Devices Inc. has seen among its own customers.

“As a provider of AI compute, we want to make sure that we are enabling those enterprises to not only run their AI tasks through the frontier APIs in the cloud, but we are providing them infrastructure that they can host open-weight models very efficiently on-prem,” said Suresh Andani, corporate vice president of compute and enterprise AI at AMD, in an interview with theCUBE. “Every enterprise conversation I’m in, that’s a key topic of discussion.”

Another key topic involves AI agents and their growing influence in the enterprise. According to Forrester’s findings, 40% of banks will launch AI assistants next year. The challenge for many financial institutions will be leveraging AI assistants to deliver differentiated guidance using proprietary data, decisioning and specialist expertise to guide customers. This is where keeping proprietary knowledge in-house can become a distinct advantage, according to John Roese, global chief technology officer and chief AI officer of Dell.

“It doesn’t mean you can’t use frontier models and open models,” Roese told theCUBE. “It just means that when you design your AI system, you need to realize that the thing that is your moat is not the actual tools. It’s not even the models. It’s the special knowledge that’s now manifesting in these new forms that really captured what you know and do differently than your competitors.”

#5644. Scientists reveal the hidden danger of missing blood pressure medication

Missing doses of blood pressure medication could significantly reduce its ability to protect against heart attacks, strokes, and other serious cardiovascular problems, according to findings presented at ESC Congress 2026.

An estimated 1.4 billion adults worldwide between the ages of 30 and 79 have high blood pressure (hypertension), a major contributor to illness and death. Although medications that lower blood pressure are proven to reduce the risk of cardiovascular complications, approximately half of patients do not take their prescriptions as directed.

"We have evidence that poor adherence to antihypertensive medication is associated with worse outcomes," explained presenter, Miss Qianqian Yang from the University of Oxford, UK. "However, previous data has come from observational studies and could be confounded by other factors. We undertook an analysis of randomized trial data to assess the true impact of adherence on the benefits of antihypertensive treatment."

Major Study Examines the Impact of Missed Blood Pressure Medication

To better understand how consistently taking medication affects its benefits, researchers analyzed individual patient data from 91,339 participants across nine clinical trials. Each trial compared a blood pressure treatment (intervention group) with an alternative approach (comparator group: either placebo or a less-intensive regimen).

The researchers divided participants into two categories based on how closely they followed their prescribed treatment. Those who took at least 80% of their assigned medication were considered to have higher adherence, while those who took less than 80% were placed in the lower adherence group.

Even with the regular monitoring and structured conditions of clinical trials, patients became less consistent about taking their medication as time passed.

"A decline in adherence over time was apparent, even in the structured setting of trials," noted Miss Yang. Overall, 88% of participants met the higher adherence threshold during the first year, but that figure had dropped to just 79% by the fifth year.

Skipping Blood Pressure Pills Reduces Treatment Benefits

The difference in medication adherence was reflected in how much patients' blood pressure improved.

Among participants with higher adherence, systolic blood pressure, the top number in a blood pressure reading, was 5.2 mmHg lower in the intervention group than in the comparator group. For those with lower adherence, the difference was considerably smaller at just 3.0 mmHg.

Researchers then examined whether these differences translated into protection against major cardiovascular problems. The outcomes included strokes, heart attacks (myocardial infarction), ischemic heart disease, and heart failure that resulted in hospitalization or death.

The findings revealed a striking contrast. Among patients who consistently followed their treatment plans, the intervention group experienced an 11% lower incidence of major cardiovascular events compared with the comparator group. However, among patients with lower adherence, there was no statistically significant reduction in these events.

"Notably, our results reinforce the saying that 'drugs don't work in patients who don't take them.' Patients with lower adherence derived little or no cardiovascular benefit, whereas those with higher adherence had greater reductions in blood pressure and prevention of cardiovascular events," said Miss Yang.

Helping Patients Get Lifesaving Heart Protection

The researchers believe that helping people take their medication consistently should become a greater priority in the treatment of high blood pressure. They recommend more routine assessments of medication adherence, along with better patient education and practical strategies to make treatment easier to follow.

Possible approaches include simplifying medication schedules, combining multiple treatments into a single pill, and prescribing longer-acting drugs that can help limit the consequences of an occasional missed dose.

Professor Felix Mahfoud, Chair of the ESC Communication Committee, emphasized that missed medication has received too little attention as a contributor to poorly controlled blood pressure.

"For years, we have neglected non-adherence to medication as a cause for uncontrolled hypertension. Assessment of adherence should become a routine part of hypertension care so patients do not miss out on life-saving benefits. As healthcare providers, we are here to have open, non-judgmental conversations with our patients about any barriers they may have to taking medication, to help improve adherence."

Materials provided by European Society of Cardiology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

WASHINGTON – Democrats’ landslide victory in the midterm elections may have significant implications for the upcoming negotiations over a key funding source for the Food and Drug Administration, in part by empowering a major critic of the program.

The FDA collects user fees from pharmaceutical companies to fund the agency’s reviews of their medicines. The Prescription User Fee Drug Act must be renewed before the current law expires on Sept. 30. Otherwise, it could disrupt the FDA’s ability to approve medicines.

#5642. Just two drinks a day may be far riskier than you think

Even alcohol consumption that many Americans would describe as moderate may carry significant health risks, including a greater likelihood of premature death, disability, cancer, and heart disease. That is the conclusion of a new study published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, a journal published at Rutgers University.

The research, known as the Alcohol Intake and Health Study, was originally commissioned by the U.S. federal government to help shape updated national dietary recommendations. Researchers estimated that people who consume an average of 14 alcoholic drinks per week face a 1 in 25 lifetime risk of dying from alcohol-related causes. By comparison, consuming up to seven drinks weekly was linked to only small increases in risk for most health conditions.

"Even low levels of alcohol use come with health risks," says lead study author Kevin Shield, Ph.D., an associate professor at the University of Toronto and a senior scientist who leads the World Health Organization (WHO)/Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) Collaborating Centre in Addiction and Mental Health. "And that risk continues to increase the more someone drinks."

How Scientists Measured the Health Risks of Alcohol

To better understand the long-term consequences of drinking, Shield and his colleagues in the United States and Canada investigated how alcohol consumption over a lifetime contributes to disease and premature death among Americans.

Medical experts first examined more than 7,200 scientific publications covering illnesses and injuries associated with alcohol. Using this evidence, they estimated the risks for individual health conditions and combined those findings with large national health data sets. Statistical models then allowed the team to calculate how different levels of alcohol consumption affect the likelihood of developing serious health problems or dying prematurely.

The findings provide specific estimates that are missing from the latest U.S. Dietary Guidelines. The updated recommendations simply encourage Americans to "limit alcoholic beverages" without identifying a particular consumption threshold. Earlier versions advised men to drink no more than two alcoholic beverages per day and women no more than one.

"While the new U.S. Dietary Guidelines contain a useful 'less-is-best' message, they provide no quantitative framework. Our study was designed to do just that across the drinking spectrum," says study co-author Timothy Naimi, M.D., M.P.H., director of the University of Victoria's Canadian Institute for Substance Use Research and an adjunct professor at Boston University.

"It turns out that two drinks per day, which might be considered 'moderate' from a social standpoint, is associated with a substantially elevated risk of a premature death caused by alcohol," explains Naimi.

Moderate Drinking Offers No Significant Overall Health Benefits

The researchers looked beyond the risk of premature death to examine alcohol's connection to a wide range of immediate and long-term health problems. These included cancers (e.g., esophageal, oral, and breast), cardiovascular disease, liver disease, and injuries.

One of the study's most important findings challenges the longstanding belief that consuming small amounts of alcohol can improve health, particularly heart health.

"We did not observe a significant protective effect of alcohol on health at any level of consumption," says Shield. "At low levels, alcohol may be associated with a reduced risk of ischemic heart disease and stroke. But when you look across the full range of health outcomes, including cancer and other chronic diseases, those potential benefits are outweighed by the risks even at 7 drinks per week."

In other words, while some studies have suggested that light drinking may benefit certain aspects of cardiovascular health, those possible advantages do not translate into an overall health benefit once alcohol's links to cancer and other diseases are taken into account.

Although the analysis drew on extensive scientific evidence, the researchers emphasize that its estimates describe risks across populations rather than predicting precisely what will happen to any particular person.

Shield says the statistical calculations relied on "the best possible data." However, he cautions that individual circumstances can substantially influence the results.

"However, we can't assume that means one person's individual health risk is the same as what is reported here -- that depends on other factors like lifestyle, genetics, drinking patterns, and other choices that differ person to person."

To estimate alcohol's overall impact, the researchers calculated risks for health conditions already known to be caused by alcohol and combined them into a broader assessment. However, scientists are continuing to investigate additional possible consequences of drinking, including emerging evidence connecting alcohol consumption to pancreatic cancer.

"Understanding those relationships, and how much alcohol contributes to those risks, is an area that still needs further work," says Shield.

What the Findings Mean for U.S. Drinking Guidelines

The results suggest that alcohol-related health risks become more pronounced when consumption exceeds one drink per day, regardless of whether the person is male or female. This provides a more specific reference point for people trying to understand how their drinking habits might affect their long-term health.

Rather than suggesting that any particular amount is completely safe, the findings show how risks increase with greater consumption and why drinking less generally reduces exposure to alcohol-related harm.

"Having a clearer threshold helps people better understand what level of drinking is associated with increased risk and make more informed decisions when drinking," says Shield.

The study has also raised questions about how scientific evidence was incorporated into federal dietary recommendations.

In an accompanying editorial, Robert M. Vincent, a former Associate Administrator for the U.S. Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, offers his perspective on the circumstances surrounding the research and its role in the development of national guidance.

"The Alcohol Intake and Health report was explicitly invited to inform alcohol guidance during development of the Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2025-2030," he writes. "Despite the study's adherence to its mandate, its findings were sidelined."

Materials provided by Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5641. Opinion: I’m a neurosurgeon. I’ve learned pain and suffering are very different things

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Doran is the author of “To Die Well: A Catholic Neurosurgeon’s Guide to the End of Life.”

John (not his real name) was in his mid-60s, a VA patient with chronic back pain. After three surgeries by three different surgeons over about five years, he was no better off; his lumbar spine was littered with arthritis and titanium implants. He had made the rounds again, to physical therapists, chiropractors, and pain providers, and now he was in my office. The last thing he needed was more surgery.

The more gently I explained, the angrier he became. He left looking like a man betrayed by the system. He wanted me to “do something” and to “fix it.” I could do neither.

After 30 years in practice, you would think that I would have perfected the “I can’t help you” speech. I haven’t, and God forbid I fall into the trap of a canned speech to a suffering patient whom I cannot make better.

I often question myself after such an encounter. Did I help this patient even though I could not fix the problem? Or did I just add another layer of suffering?

In a 1982 essay in The New England Journal of Medicine, “The Nature of Suffering and the Goals of Medicine,” the physician Eric Cassell noted that medicine is obliged to relieve suffering yet gives it little attention. “Suffering occurs when an impending destruction of the person is perceived; it continues until the threat of disintegration has passed or until the integrity of the person can be restored in some other manner,” he wrote.

Pain becomes suffering, he noted, when people “feel out of control, when the pain is overwhelming, when the source of the pain is unknown, when the meaning of the pain is dire, or when the pain is chronic.” Physicians who concentrate only on curing bodily disease, he warned, may “do things that cause the patient as a person to suffer.”

The anatomy and physiology of the brain is consistent with Cassel’s position: Pain and suffering are processed by different pathways. Some people feel intense pain without experiencing suffering, while others continue to suffer greatly even when physical pain is not present.

The distinction between pain and suffering is particularly important now because assisted dying is spreading fast. It is now legal in 13 states and the District of Columbia. New York’s law took effect on Aug. 5, and Illinois’ on Sept. 12. Beneath the policy fight sits an assumption that suffering is a malfunction to be eliminated. Someone needs to “fix it.”

Oregon’s 2025 data illustrate that suffering, and not necessarily pain, motivates patients to seek aid in dying. Among the 400 people who died under the law, the most common concerns were loss of autonomy (89%) and being less able to enjoy life’s activities (89%). Inadequate pain control, or concern about it, was reported by 37%. These patients are suffering, but their suffering goes far beyond physical pain. If personhood is ignored, people suffer.

Cassell proposed that suffering can be relieved, even when pain continues, by making the source of the pain known, changing its meaning, and showing that it can be controlled and that an end is in sight. Then he made a bold claim:

“Transcendence is probably the most powerful way in which one is restored to wholeness after an injury to personhood. … The sufferer is not isolated by pain but is brought closer to a transpersonal source of meaning and to the human community that shares those meanings.”

Such an experience, he added, “need not involve religion in any formal sense; however, in its transpersonal dimension, it is deeply spiritual.” If unrelieved suffering drives people toward assisted dying, and transcendence is the most powerful way to relieve it, how does someone connect with the transcendent? Religious faith by its nature connects the believer with something greater and, in the three monotheistic traditions, with a transcendent someone.

Cassell’s paper challenges physicians to relieve both pain and suffering.

Pain pathways are well described by science and an abundance of medical and surgical options exist to relieve pain. Suffering can be described in physiological terms but only to a point; beyond that, scientific analysis comes up lacking.

Suffering is intensely personal and defies reductionistic “scientism.” Any attempt to address it must take place within a relationship that goes beyond medications, therapies, and surgeries. I could not understand the meaning of John’s pain unless I had a relationship with him. Did I take the time to develop that relationship? Did I offer to keep seeing him even though I could not “fix it”? If I’m honest with myself, the answer to both questions is no.

While there remain many good things about the delivery of health care, a chasm has opened between patients and those who care for them. What was once a covenantal relationship has become transactional. A person in need once placed his trust in someone who promised to serve his good. Now expertise and service are doled out in exchange for relative value units. More time is spent looking at a computer screen than at the face of the patient.

At the root of this lies a single issue: the depersonalization of medicine. The patient is too often reduced to a bystander, a medical problem to be solved. They become the occurrence of a disease rather than a person in need of help. Medications, therapies, and surgeries are our weapons in the battle against disease. When the battle is lost (and at some point it will be), we move on to the next skirmish, and the patient is left isolated and abandoned.

While it is apparent that patients suffer as the result of the depersonalization of medicine, the physician is diminished too. If I neglect the person in front of me, my skills may persist, but I am reduced from an instrument of healing to a technician Relief of pain does not require me to be in relation with the person in front of me. All I need to do is write a prescription for a painkiller.

But if I desire to relieve suffering, I must be willing to enter that sacred space, approaching with reverence the one who cries out to be heard. The former is easy; the latter is rich.

So where do we go from here? Often, the response is to encourage health care providers to accompany their patients, but what does that even mean? The word companion comes from the Latin com (with) and panis (bread): A companion is one who shares bread with you. You cannot accompany someone from afar. It demands a close, intimate relationship. To accompany means to love. We must love our patients.

The objections are predictable: That crosses a professional boundary; we need to maintain objectivity; we will burn out. But love, in the classic sense, is to will the good of the other for the sake of the other. It is not a sentiment. It is a decision. If I will the good of my patients for the sake of my needs (money, prestige), then I am not loving them. That is objectifying them. If I cannot love my patients, I need to quit.

Inevitably, we will encounter patients that we cannot fix. We do not have a solution to their pain and suffering. So then what? When we cannot relieve suffering, we are called to co-suffer. The late Msgr. Lorenzo Albacete, priest, physicist, and theologian, wrote that “to co-suffer — to be a companion with the sufferer — is to walk alongside them to transcendence.” This is precisely what Cassell was advocating: The best way to relieve suffering is a link to the transcendent.

While transcendence is often associated with religious faith, connecting with the transcendent is possible for anyone. In classic philosophy, the transcendentals are the good, the true, and the beautiful. What makes them transcendent is that they point toward something beyond our daily existence, moving to what is more inward than my inward self and higher than my highest self. Participating in the transcendent can bring meaning to suffering.

Truth: Suffering strips away illusions about status and what matters, restoring a dignity when nothing can be fixed.

Goodness: Suffering can become an occasion for love, an opportunity to show courage, patience, and forgiveness.

Beauty: Beauty shows that suffering is not the whole of reality and offers true consolation.

Both Cassel and Albacete connect suffering with the transcendent, but Albacete also warned: “Suffering is a cry that characterizes the human person, and we do violence to the human person if we try to extinguish that cry.” The cruelest response to suffering is to attempt to explain it away. We can only ask “why” together with the one who suffers.

I never saw John again. Earlier this year, I saw an elderly man with osteoporosis suffering from a compression fracture. Stabilizing it was followed by another fracture, then another. His pain is unabated, and he is becoming more and more bent forward. He knows I cannot “fix it,” yet he returns every month to be heard. At the end of each visit, he thanks me for listening even though I offer no solutions. I cannot fix him, but I can accompany him, co-suffer with him, and ask “why” together.

Stephen Doran, M.D., is a neurosurgeon in Omaha, Neb., a permanent deacon and bioethicist for the Archdiocese of Omaha, and the author of “To Die Well: A Catholic Neurosurgeon’s Guide to the End of Life.”
